questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor of capacitance 8$\mu$F is fully charged by connecting it to a source of 200V. It is then disconnected from the supply and connected to an uncharged capacitor of capacitance 4$\mu$F. The electrostatic energy lost in this sharing is:
questions.solution:
Given:

$C_1 = 8 \mu F = 8 \times 10^{-6}\ F$

$V_1 = 200\ V$

$C_2 = 4 \mu F = 4 \times 10^{-6}\ F$

$V_2 = 0\ V$

The loss of electrostatic energy when two capacitors are connected is given by:

$\Delta U = \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2} (V_1 - V_2)^2$

Substituting the values:

$\Delta U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{8 \times 10^{-6} \times 4 \times 10^{-6}}{(8 + 4) \times 10^{-6}} \times (200 - 0)^2$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-12}}{12 \times 10^{-6}} \times 40000$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{16}{12} \times 10^{-6} \times 4 \times 10^4$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{4}{3} \times 4 \times 10^{-2}$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{16}{3} \times 10^{-2} = 5.33 \times 10^{-2}\ J$

Answer: $5.33 \times 10^{-2}\ J$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the charge on $15\mu F$ in the circuit given?
questions.solution:
From the given circuit diagram, the $15\mu F$ and $30\mu F$ capacitors are connected in series.

The equivalent capacitance of this series branch is:
$C_s = \dfrac{15 \times 30}{15 + 30} = \dfrac{450}{45} = 10\mu F$

This series branch is connected directly across the $13\text{ V}$ battery. Therefore, the potential difference across the series combination is $13\text{ V}$.

The charge $Q$ on this series branch is given by:
$Q = C_s \times V = 10\mu F \times 13\text{ V} = 130\mu\text{C}$

In a series circuit, the charge on each capacitor is the same. Thus, the charge on the $15\mu F$ capacitor is equal to the total charge of the series branch, which is $130\mu\text{C}$.

Answer: $130\ \mu\text{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the given figure all the capacitors \(\mathrm{C}_1, \mathrm{C}_2, \mathrm{C}_3\) and \(\mathrm{C}_4\) have the same capacitance \(4 \mu \mathrm{F}\). The emf of the cell is 12 V. What is the effective capacitance ?
questions.solution:
The circuit consists of three parallel branches connected across the 12 V source. Let the left node be A and the right node be B.

Branch 1 consists of capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ in series. Their equivalent capacitance $C_{12}$ is given by $\dfrac{1}{C_{12}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Thus, $C_{12} = 2 \mu F$.

Branch 2 consists of capacitor $C_3$. Thus, $C_{branch2} = C_3 = 4 \mu F$.

Branch 3 consists of capacitor $C_4$. Thus, $C_{branch3} = C_4 = 4 \mu F$.

Since these three branches are connected in parallel between nodes A and B, the effective capacitance $C_{eff}$ is the sum of the capacitances of the individual branches:

$C_{eff} = C_{12} + C_{branch2} + C_{branch3} = 2 \mu F + 4 \mu F + 4 \mu F = 10 \mu F$.

Answer: \(C_{\text {eff }}=10 \mu \mathrm{~F}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The space between the two plates of a parallel plate capacitor is fully filled with a conducting slab. Then the capacitance of the capacitor is :
options: Reduced to half of its original value
questions.solution:
The capacitance $C$ of a parallel plate capacitor with plate area $A$ and separation $d$ is given by $C = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$.

When a conducting slab of thickness $t$ is inserted between the plates, the new capacitance is given by $C' = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 A}{d - t + \dfrac{t}{K}}$, where $K$ is the dielectric constant of the material.

For a conducting slab, the dielectric constant $K$ is infinite, i.e., $K \to \infty$.

Substituting $K \to \infty$ into the formula, the term $\dfrac{t}{K}$ becomes zero.

Since the slab fully fills the space between the plates, the thickness of the slab $t$ is equal to the separation $d$.

Therefore, $C' = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 A}{d - d + 0} = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 A}{0}$.

As the denominator approaches zero, the capacitance $C'$ approaches infinity.

Answer: Infinite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: By connecting two given capacitors, a technician was able to make two new capacitors having the effective capacitance $12.5 \mu \mathrm{F}$ and $2 \mu \mathrm{F}$. What would be the capacitance of the given capacitors?
questions.solution:
Let the capacitances of the two capacitors be $C_1$ and $C_2$.

When connected in parallel, the effective capacitance is $C_p = C_1 + C_2 = 12.5 \mu F$.

When connected in series, the effective capacitance is $C_s = \dfrac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2} = 2 \mu F$.

Substituting $C_1 + C_2 = 12.5$ into the series formula:

$\dfrac{C_1 C_2}{12.5} = 2 \Rightarrow C_1 C_2 = 25$.

We have the sum $S = C_1 + C_2 = 12.5$ and the product $P = C_1 C_2 = 25$. These are the roots of the quadratic equation $x^2 - Sx + P = 0$.

$x^2 - 12.5x + 25 = 0$.

Multiplying by 2 to clear decimals: $2x^2 - 25x + 50 = 0$.

Using the quadratic formula $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$:

$x = \dfrac{25 \pm \sqrt{625 - 4(2)(50)}}{4} = \dfrac{25 \pm \sqrt{625 - 400}}{4} = \dfrac{25 \pm \sqrt{225}}{4} = \dfrac{25 \pm 15}{4}$.

The two roots are $x_1 = \dfrac{40}{4} = 10$ and $x_2 = \dfrac{10}{4} = 2.5$.

Thus, the capacitances are $10 \mu F$ and $2.5 \mu F$.

Answer: $10 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ and $2.5 \mu \mathrm{~F}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a dielectric slab of dielectric constant $\mathrm{k}=2$ is used to fill the space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor, the capacitance of the capacitor is found to be $20 \mu \mathrm{F}$. What will be the capacitance when the slab is replaced with air?
questions.solution:
The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor filled with a dielectric material is given by the formula $C = K C_0$, where $C$ is the capacitance with the dielectric, $K$ is the dielectric constant, and $C_0$ is the capacitance with air as the medium.

Given $C = 20 \mu F$ and $K = 2$, we substitute these values into the equation:

$20 \mu F = 2 \times C_0$

Solving for $C_0$:

$C_0 = \dfrac{20 \mu F}{2} = 10 \mu F$.

Answer: $10 \mu F$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor of capacitance $4 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ is charged to a potential of 24 V and then connected in parallel to an uncharged capacitor of capacitance $6 \mu \mathrm{~F}$. The final potential difference across each capacitor will be:
questions.solution:
The initial charge $Q$ on the capacitor of capacitance $C_1 = 4 \mu \text{F}$ charged to a potential $V_1 = 24 \text{V}$ is given by $Q = C_1 V_1$.

$Q = 4 \mu \text{F} \times 24 \text{V} = 96 \mu \text{C}$.

When this capacitor is connected in parallel to an uncharged capacitor of capacitance $C_2 = 6 \mu \text{F}$, the total charge $Q$ is redistributed between the two capacitors until they reach a common potential $V$.

The total capacitance of the parallel combination is $C_{eq} = C_1 + C_2 = 4 \mu \text{F} + 6 \mu \text{F} = 10 \mu \text{F}$.

Using the principle of conservation of charge, $Q = C_{eq} V$.

$96 \mu \text{C} = 10 \mu \text{F} \times V$.

$V = \dfrac{96 \mu \text{C}}{10 \mu \text{F}} = 9.6 \text{V}$.

Answer: 9.6 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A network of capacitors is as shown below. If the voltage supply is 100 V , find the energy stored in the $6 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ capacitor.
$C_1=3 \mu F, C_2=6 \mu F, C_3=3 \mu F$ and $C_4=4 \mu F$
questions.solution:
The circuit consists of a capacitor $C_4$ in parallel with the series combination of $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$.

First, calculate the equivalent capacitance of the series branch containing $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$. Let this be $C_{series}$.

$\dfrac{1}{C_{series}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \dfrac{1}{C_3} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2+1+2}{6} = \dfrac{5}{6} \mu F^{-1}$

$C_{series} = \dfrac{6}{5} = 1.2 \mu F$

The voltage across the series branch is equal to the supply voltage $V = 100 V$.

The charge $Q$ on the series branch is $Q = C_{series} \times V = 1.2 \mu F \times 100 V = 120 \mu C$.

Since $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$ are in series, they all carry the same charge $Q = 120 \mu C$.

The energy stored in the $C_2 = 6 \mu F$ capacitor is given by $U = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C_2}$.

$U = \dfrac{(120 \times 10^{-6})^2}{2 \times 6 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{14400 \times 10^{-12}}{12 \times 10^{-6}} = 1200 \times 10^{-6} J = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} J = 1.2 mJ$.

Answer: 1.2 mJ

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two capacitors $\mathrm{C}_1$ and $\mathrm{C}_2$ are charged to 100 V and 120 V respectively. It is found that upon connecting them together in parallel, the potential on each one of them is zero. Therefore
questions.solution:
Let the charges on the capacitors be $Q_1 = C_1 V_1$ and $Q_2 = C_2 V_2$. Given $V_1 = 100$ V and $V_2 = 120$ V, the charges are $Q_1 = 100 C_1$ and $Q_2 = 120 C_2$.

When the capacitors are connected in parallel, the total charge is conserved. If the final potential is zero, the total charge must be zero. This implies that the plates of opposite polarity were connected together.

The total charge is $Q_1 - Q_2 = 0$ or $Q_2 - Q_1 = 0$.

Substituting the values, $100 C_1 - 120 C_2 = 0$ or $120 C_2 - 100 C_1 = 0$.

This simplifies to $100 C_1 = 120 C_2$, which reduces to $5 C_1 = 6 C_2$.

Answer: $5 C_1=6 C_2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $5.80 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ parallel plate air capacitor has a plate separation of 5 mm and is charged to a potential difference of 400 V . The energy density in the region between the plates is
questions.solution:
The energy density in the region between the plates is given by
$\begin{aligned} \\ u & =\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E^2 \\ \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0\left(\frac{V}{d}\right)^2 \quad\left(\because E=\frac{V}{d}\right) \\ \\ \Rightarrow \quad u & =\frac{1}{2} \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times\left(\frac{400}{5 \times 10^{-3}}\right)^2 \\ \\ & =283.2 \times 10^{-12} \times 10^6 \\ \\ & =283.2 \times 10^{-6} \\ \\ & =2.83 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{m}^3 \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor of $2 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ is charged as shown in the figure. When the switch $S$ is turned to position 2 , the percentage of its stored energy dissipated is
questions.solution:
Consider the given figure,
When the switch $S$ is connected to point 1, then initial energy stored in the capacitor can be given as
$=\frac{1}{2}(2 \mu \mathrm{~F}) \times V^2$
When the switch $S$ is connected to point 2, energy dissipated on connection across $8 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ will be

Therefore, % loss of energy

questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor having a dielectric constant 5 and dielectric strength $10^6 \mathrm{~V} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$ is to be designed with voltage rating of $2 \mathrm{~kV}$. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is $400 \mathrm{~pF}$. It is connected to an ac source of $100 \mathrm{~V}$ having an angular frequency $100 \mathrm{~rad~s}^{-1}$. If the rms value of the current is $4 \mu \mathrm{A}$, the displacement current is:
questions.solution:
The displacement current $I_d$ in a parallel plate capacitor is defined as the current flowing through the circuit, which is equal to the conduction current $I_c$ in the connecting wires.

The relationship between the conduction current and the displacement current is given by $I_d = I_c$.

Given that the rms value of the current in the circuit is $I_{rms} = 4 \mu \text{A}$, this current represents the conduction current flowing through the wires connected to the capacitor plates.

According to the principle of continuity of current, the displacement current between the plates of the capacitor must be equal to the conduction current in the external circuit.

Therefore, $I_d = I_{rms} = 4 \mu \text{A}$.

Answer: 4 $\mu$A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor is filled by a dielectric whose relative permittivity varies with the applied voltage (U) as $\epsilon=2 U$. A similar capacitor with no dielectric is charged to $U_0=78 \mathrm{~V}$. It is then connected to the uncharged capacitor with the dielectric. Find the final voltage on the capacitors.
questions.solution:
Let $C_0$ be the capacitance of the capacitor without the dielectric. The charge on this capacitor is $Q_0 = C_0 U_0$, where $U_0 = 78$ V.

When the two capacitors are connected in parallel, the total charge $Q_0$ is shared between them. Let $U$ be the final common voltage. The charge on the first capacitor is $Q_1 = C_0 U$.

The second capacitor has a dielectric with relative permittivity $\epsilon = 2U$. The capacitance of this capacitor is $C = \epsilon C_0 = (2U) C_0$. The charge on this capacitor is $Q_2 = C U = (2U) C_0 U = 2 C_0 U^2$.

By the principle of conservation of charge, $Q_0 = Q_1 + Q_2$.

$C_0 U_0 = C_0 U + 2 C_0 U^2$.

Dividing by $C_0$, we get $U_0 = U + 2U^2$.

Substituting $U_0 = 78$, we have $2U^2 + U - 78 = 0$.

Solving the quadratic equation for $U$ using the quadratic formula $U = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$:

$U = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1^2 - 4(2)(-78)}}{2(2)} = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 624}}{4} = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{625}}{4} = \dfrac{-1 \pm 25}{4}$.

Since voltage must be positive, $U = \dfrac{24}{4} = 6$ V.

Answer: 6V

questions.q: If $C$ be the capacitance and $V$ be the electric potential, then the dimensional formula of $\mathrm{CV}^2$ is
questions.solution:
The energy $U$ stored in a capacitor is given by the formula $U = \dfrac{1}{2} CV^2$.

Since $U$ represents energy, its dimensional formula is the same as that of work or energy, which is $[ML^2T^{-2}]$.

The factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ is a dimensionless constant and does not affect the dimensions.

Therefore, the dimensional formula of $CV^2$ is the same as the dimensional formula of energy, which is $[ML^2T^{-2}A^0]$.

Answer: $\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2} \mathrm{~A}^0\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A dielectric of dielectric constant $K$ is introduced such that half of its area of a capacitor of capacitance $C$ is occupied by it. The new capacity is
questions.solution:
The initial capacitance of the parallel plate capacitor is $C = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$, where $A$ is the area of the plates and $d$ is the distance between them.

When a dielectric of dielectric constant $K$ is introduced such that it occupies half the area, the capacitor can be viewed as two capacitors connected in parallel. One capacitor has area $A/2$ with air (dielectric constant 1) and the other has area $A/2$ with the dielectric (dielectric constant $K$).

The capacitance of the air-filled part is $C_1 = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 (A/2)}{d} = \dfrac{C}{2}$.

The capacitance of the dielectric-filled part is $C_2 = \dfrac{K \epsilon_0 (A/2)}{d} = \dfrac{KC}{2}$.

Since these are in parallel, the total capacitance is $C_{new} = C_1 + C_2 = \dfrac{C}{2} + \dfrac{KC}{2} = \dfrac{C(1+K)}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{(1+K) C}{2}$

questions.q: A capacitor of capacity $2 ~\mu \mathrm{F}$ is charged upto a potential $14 \mathrm{~V}$ and then connected in parallel to an uncharged capacitor of capacity $5 ~\mu \mathrm{F}$. The final potential difference across each capacitor will be
questions.solution:
The initial charge $Q$ on the first capacitor is given by $Q = C_1 V_1$.

$Q = 2 \mu \text{F} \times 14 \text{V} = 28 \mu \text{C}$.

When the two capacitors are connected in parallel, the total charge $Q$ is conserved and is shared between the two capacitors. Let $V$ be the common potential difference across the capacitors.

$Q = (C_1 + C_2) V$.

Substituting the given values:

$28 \mu \text{C} = (2 \mu \text{F} + 5 \mu \text{F}) \times V$.

$28 = 7 \times V$.

$V = \dfrac{28}{7} \text{V} = 4 \text{V}$.

Answer: 4 V

questions.q: The formula of capacitative reactance is
questions.solution:
The capacitive reactance $X_{C}$ of a capacitor in an alternating current circuit is defined as the opposition offered by the capacitor to the flow of alternating current.

The formula for capacitive reactance is given by $X_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$, where $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the AC source and $C$ is the capacitance.

Since the angular frequency $\omega$ is related to the frequency $f$ by the relation $\omega = 2 \pi f$, substituting this into the expression for $X_{C}$ yields $X_{C} = \dfrac{1}{2 \pi f C}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2 \pi f C}$

questions.solution:
Given, capacitance of air filled parallel plate capacitor,
$C_{0}=2 \mathrm{pF}\Rightarrow \quad=2 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~F}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\varepsilon_{0} A}{d}=2 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~F}...(i)$
When the separation between the plates is doubled, i.e., $\quad d^{\prime}=2 d$
And wax of dielectric constant $k$ is filled between the plates of capacitor, then,
$\begin{aligned}
C^{\prime} &=6 \mathrm{pF} \\
\frac{\varepsilon_{0} k A}{d^{\prime}} &=6 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~F}
\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\varepsilon_{0} k A}{2 d}=6 \times 10^{-12} \quad\left[\because d^{\prime}=2 d\right]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\varepsilon_{0} A}{d} \times \frac{k}{2}=6 \times 10^{-12}\Rightarrow 2 \times 10^{-12} \times \frac{k}{2}=6 \times 10^{-12}$
[from $\mathrm{Eq} .$ (i)]
$\Rightarrow \quad k=6$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A machine gun fires a bullet of mass m with a velocity of 1000 m/min. The man holding the gun can exert a force of 200 N on the gun. The product of mass of each bullet and the number of bullets fired in one sec is
questions.solution:
Velocity of the bullet, $v = 1000 \text{ m/min} = \dfrac{1000}{60} \text{ m/s} = \dfrac{50}{3} \text{ m/s}$

Force exerted by the man, $F = 200 \text{ N}$

The force required to hold the gun is equal to the rate of change of momentum of the bullets.

$F = n \cdot m \cdot v$

where $n$ is the number of bullets fired per second and $m$ is the mass of each bullet.

We need to find the product $n \cdot m$.

$n \cdot m = \dfrac{F}{v}$

Substituting the given values:

$n \cdot m = \dfrac{200}{\dfrac{50}{3}} = \dfrac{200 \times 3}{50} = 12 \text{ kg/s}$

The product of the mass of each bullet and the number of bullets fired in one second is $12$.

Answer: $12$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A bullet of 0.02 kg moving with a speed of $100 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ hits a surface and comes to rest in 0.1 s What is the magnitude of the impulse of the force?
questions.solution:
The impulse $J$ is defined as the change in linear momentum of the object.

$J = \Delta p = m(v_f - v_i)$

Given mass $m = 0.02 \text{ kg}$, initial velocity $v_i = 100 \text{ ms}^{-1}$, and final velocity $v_f = 0 \text{ ms}^{-1}$ (since the bullet comes to rest).

$J = 0.02 \times (0 - 100)$

$J = 0.02 \times (-100) = -2 \text{ kg ms}^{-1}$

The magnitude of the impulse is $|J| = |-2| = 2 \text{ N.s}$.

Answer: 2 N.s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A bullet of momentum $p$ is fired into a door and gets embedded exactly at the center of the door. The door is 1.0 m wide and weighs 12 kg . It is hinged at one end and rotates about a vertical axis practically without friction. The angular speed of the door just after the bullet embeds into it is (Assume the mass of bullet is negligible compared to the mass of door)
questions.solution:
Let $M = 12$ kg be the mass of the door and $L = 1.0$ m be its width. The moment of inertia of the door about the vertical axis passing through the hinge is $I_{door} = \dfrac{1}{3} M L^2 = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 12 \times (1.0)^2 = 4$ kg m$^2$.

Let $m$ be the mass of the bullet and $v$ be its velocity such that $p = mv$. The bullet strikes the center of the door at distance $r = \dfrac{L}{2} = 0.5$ m from the hinge. The angular momentum of the bullet about the hinge just before impact is $L_{bullet} = p \times r = p \times 0.5 = \dfrac{p}{2}$.

Since there is no external torque about the hinge, the angular momentum is conserved. Let $\omega$ be the angular velocity of the door-bullet system after impact. The moment of inertia of the system is $I = I_{door} + I_{bullet} = \dfrac{1}{3} M L^2 + m r^2 = 4 + m(0.5)^2 = 4 + 0.25m$.

Assuming the mass of the bullet $m$ is negligible compared to the mass of the door ($m \ll M$), the moment of inertia is dominated by the door, $I \approx 4$ kg m$^2$.

Equating angular momentum: $L_{bullet} = I \omega \Rightarrow \dfrac{p}{2} = 4 \omega \Rightarrow \omega = \dfrac{p}{8}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{p}{8}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: The separation between C and O atoms in CO is 0.12 nm . The distance of C atom from the centre of mass is
questions.solution:
Let $m_{C}$ be the mass of the carbon atom and $m_{O}$ be the mass of the oxygen atom. The atomic mass of carbon is $12 \text{ u}$ and the atomic mass of oxygen is $16 \text{ u}$.

Let the position of the carbon atom be $x_{C} = 0$ and the position of the oxygen atom be $x_{O} = d = 0.12 \text{ nm}$.

The centre of mass $X_{CM}$ is given by the formula $X_{CM} = \dfrac{m_{C}x_{C} + m_{O}x_{O}}{m_{C} + m_{O}}$.

Substituting the values, $X_{CM} = \dfrac{12 \times 0 + 16 \times 0.12}{12 + 16} = \dfrac{16 \times 0.12}{28}$.

$X_{CM} = \dfrac{4 \times 0.12}{7} = \dfrac{0.48}{7} \approx 0.06857 \text{ nm}$.

Rounding to 2 decimal places, the distance of the carbon atom from the centre of mass is approximately $0.07 \text{ nm}$.

Answer: 0.07 nm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Select the correct statement from the following: The position of the centre of mass of a system:
options: Does not depend on the shape and size of the system
Depend on the choice of coordinates
Depends on the distribution of its mass.
Remains the same in any translatory motion
questions.solution:
The position of the centre of mass of a system of particles is defined by the vector $\vec{R}_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}$.

This definition shows that the location of the centre of mass is determined by the individual masses $m_i$ and their respective position vectors $\vec{r}_i$ relative to the chosen origin.

Since the position vectors $\vec{r}_i$ depend on the distribution of mass within the system, the centre of mass is fundamentally a property of the mass distribution of the body or system.

While the numerical coordinates of the centre of mass change if the origin of the coordinate system is shifted, the physical location of the centre of mass relative to the body itself is fixed by the mass distribution, making the statement regarding mass distribution the most fundamental physical description.

Answer: Depends on the distribution of its mass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: The velocity - mass graph of body with constant linear momentum is represented by the graph:
questions.solution:
Linear momentum $p$ is defined as the product of mass $m$ and velocity $v$, given by the equation $p = mv$.

For a body with constant linear momentum, $p$ is a constant. Therefore, we can write the relationship between velocity and mass as $v = \dfrac{p}{m}$.

This equation represents an inverse proportionality between velocity and mass, which is of the form $v \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$.

The graph of $v$ versus $m$ for this relationship is a rectangular hyperbola, where $v$ decreases as $m$ increases, approaching zero as $m$ approaches infinity, and approaching infinity as $m$ approaches zero.

Answer:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Momentum of a body is increased to three times its original value. By what percentage will its kinetic energy change?
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy $K$ of a body is related to its momentum $p$ by the formula $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, where $m$ is the mass of the body.

Let the initial momentum be $p_1 = p$ and the initial kinetic energy be $K_1 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$.

The momentum is increased to three times its original value, so the new momentum is $p_2 = 3p$.

The new kinetic energy $K_2$ is given by $K_2 = \dfrac{p_2^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(3p)^2}{2m} = \dfrac{9p^2}{2m} = 9K_1$.

The change in kinetic energy is $\Delta K = K_2 - K_1 = 9K_1 - K_1 = 8K_1$.

The percentage change in kinetic energy is $\dfrac{\Delta K}{K_1} \times 100\% = \dfrac{8K_1}{K_1} \times 100\% = 800\%$.

Answer: $800 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: From a circular disc of radius 2 R , a smaller circular disc is cut with radius of the larger disc as its diameter. The centre of the hole is at a distance of $R$ from the centre of the original disc. The distance of the centre of mass of the remaining portion from the centre is:
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the original disc be $r_1 = 2R$. The area of the original disc is $A_1 = \pi (2R)^2 = 4\pi R^2$.

The smaller disc cut from it has a diameter equal to the radius of the larger disc, so its diameter is $2R$ and its radius is $r_2 = R$. The area of the smaller disc is $A_2 = \pi R^2$.

Let the centre of the original disc be at the origin $(0, 0)$. The centre of the smaller disc is at a distance $R$ from the origin, so its coordinates are $(R, 0)$.

The centre of mass of the remaining portion is given by the formula $X_{cm} = \dfrac{A_1 x_1 - A_2 x_2}{A_1 - A_2}$, where $(x_1, y_1)$ is the centre of the original disc and $(x_2, y_2)$ is the centre of the cut-out disc.

Substituting the values: $X_{cm} = \dfrac{(4\pi R^2)(0) - (\pi R^2)(R)}{4\pi R^2 - \pi R^2}$.

$X_{cm} = \dfrac{-\pi R^3}{3\pi R^2} = -\dfrac{R}{3}$.

The magnitude of the distance of the centre of mass from the centre of the original disc is $\dfrac{R}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A bomb of mass 20 kg at rest explodes into two pieces of masses 12 kg and 8 kg . If the velocity of 8 kg mass is $6 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$, then the kinetic energy of the other mass is:
questions.solution:
Let $M = 20$ kg be the mass of the bomb, $m_1 = 12$ kg, and $m_2 = 8$ kg be the masses of the two pieces. Let $v_1$ and $v_2$ be the velocities of the two pieces respectively. Initially, the bomb is at rest, so the initial momentum is zero.

According to the law of conservation of linear momentum, the final momentum must also be zero:

$m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = 0$

Given $m_2 = 8$ kg and $v_2 = 6$ m/s, we have:

$12 v_1 + 8 \times 6 = 0$

$12 v_1 = -48$

$v_1 = -4$ m/s.

The kinetic energy of the 12 kg mass is given by:

$K_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2$

$K_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times (-4)^2$

$K_1 = 6 \times 16 = 96$ J.

Answer: 96 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Which of the following statement is true regarding the centre of mass of a system?
options: The centre of mass of a body always lies inside the body.
The centre of mass depends on the size and shape but does not depend on the distribution of mass of the body.
The centre of mass depends on the coordinate system.
The centre of mass of a system depends on the size and shape of the body but independent of the co-ordinate system
questions.solution:
The centre of mass of a system is defined by the position vector $\vec{R}_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}$.

The centre of mass is a point that represents the average position of the mass in a system. It depends on the distribution of mass, the size, and the shape of the body. However, the location of the centre of mass is a physical property of the body itself and is independent of the choice of the coordinate system used to describe it.

Option (1) is incorrect because the centre of mass can lie outside the body (e.g., a ring or a hollow sphere).

Option (2) is incorrect because the centre of mass is highly dependent on the distribution of mass.

Option (3) is incorrect because the physical location of the centre of mass is invariant under a change of coordinate system.

Option (4) correctly states that the centre of mass depends on the size, shape, and mass distribution of the body, while being independent of the coordinate system chosen.

Answer: The centre of mass of a system depends on the size and shape of the body but independent of the co-ordinate system

questions.subject: Physics

questions.q: Which of the following graph shows the variation of velocity with mass for the constant momentum?
questions.solution:
The relationship between momentum $p$, mass $m$, and velocity $v$ is given by the formula $p = mv$.

For a constant momentum $p$, the equation becomes $v = \dfrac{p}{m}$.

This equation represents an inverse proportionality between velocity $v$ and mass $m$, which is of the form $v \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$.

The graph of $v$ versus $m$ for an inverse relationship $v = \dfrac{k}{m}$ (where $k$ is a positive constant) is a rectangular hyperbola in the first quadrant, which corresponds to Fig 1.

Answer: Fig 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A neutron makes a head on elastic collision with a lead nucleus. The ratio of nuclear mass to neutron mass is 206 . The fractional change in kinetic energy of a neutron is
questions.solution:
Let $m$ be the mass of the neutron and $M$ be the mass of the lead nucleus. Given $M = 206m$.

In a head-on elastic collision, the final velocity $v_1'$ of the neutron is given by $v_1' = \dfrac{m - M}{m + M} v_1$, where $v_1$ is the initial velocity of the neutron.

The ratio of the final kinetic energy $K'$ to the initial kinetic energy $K$ is $\dfrac{K'}{K} = \left( \dfrac{v_1'}{v_1} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{m - M}{m + M} \right)^2$.

Substituting $M = 206m$, we get $\dfrac{K'}{K} = \left( \dfrac{m - 206m}{m + 206m} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{-205m}{207m} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{205}{207} \right)^2$.

The fractional change in kinetic energy is $\dfrac{\Delta K}{K} = \dfrac{K' - K}{K} = \left( \dfrac{205}{207} \right)^2 - 1 = \dfrac{205^2 - 207^2}{207^2} = \dfrac{(205 - 207)(205 + 207)}{207^2} = \dfrac{-2 \times 412}{42849} = \dfrac{-824}{42849}$.

Calculating the value, $\dfrac{-824}{42849} \approx -0.0192$, which is approximately $-0.02$ or a $2\%$ decrease.

Answer: 2% decrease

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: In the diagram shown below, $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the masses of two particles and $x_1$ and $x_2$ are their respective distances from the origin $O$. The centre of mass of the system is
questions.solution:
The position of the centre of mass $X_{cm}$ for a system of particles with masses $m_1, m_2, ..., m_n$ at positions $x_1, x_2, ..., x_n$ along a line is given by the formula:

$X_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i}$

For the given system with two particles of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ at distances $x_1$ and $x_2$ from the origin $O$, the formula becomes:

$X_{cm} = \dfrac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2}{m_1 + m_2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{m_1 x_1+m_2 x_2}{m_1+m_2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: In the figure, pendulum bob on left side is pulled a side to a height $h$ from its initial position. After it is released it collides with the right pendulum bob at rest, which is of same mass. After the collision, the two bobs stick together and rise to a height
questions.solution:
Let $m$ be the mass of each pendulum bob and $L$ be the length of the strings. When the left bob is released from height $h$, its velocity $v$ just before the collision is found using the conservation of mechanical energy:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2gh}$

The collision is perfectly inelastic because the two bobs stick together. Let $V$ be the velocity of the combined mass $2m$ immediately after the collision. By the principle of conservation of linear momentum:

$mv + m(0) = (m + m)V$

$mv = 2mV \Rightarrow V = \dfrac{v}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2gh}}{2}$

After the collision, the combined mass rises to a new height $H$. Using the conservation of mechanical energy for the combined system:

$\dfrac{1}{2}(2m)V^2 = (2m)gH$

$H = \dfrac{V^2}{2g} = \dfrac{(\dfrac{\sqrt{2gh}}{2})^2}{2g} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2gh}{4}}{2g} = \dfrac{h}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{h}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: If kinetic energy of a body is increased by $300 \%$, then percentage change in momentum will be
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy $K$ and momentum $p$ of a body are related by the expression $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, where $m$ is the mass of the body.

Let the initial kinetic energy be $K_1$ and the initial momentum be $p_1$. Then $K_1 = \dfrac{p_1^2}{2m}$.

The kinetic energy is increased by $300 \%$, so the new kinetic energy $K_2$ is $K_2 = K_1 + 300 \% K_1 = K_1 + 3K_1 = 4K_1$.

Let the new momentum be $p_2$. Then $K_2 = \dfrac{p_2^2}{2m}$.

Substituting $K_2 = 4K_1$ and $K_1 = \dfrac{p_1^2}{2m}$, we get $\dfrac{p_2^2}{2m} = 4 \times \dfrac{p_1^2}{2m}$, which simplifies to $p_2^2 = 4p_1^2$, or $p_2 = 2p_1$.

The percentage change in momentum is given by $\dfrac{p_2 - p_1}{p_1} \times 100 \%$.

Substituting $p_2 = 2p_1$, we get $\dfrac{2p_1 - p_1}{p_1} \times 100 \% = \dfrac{p_1}{p_1} \times 100 \% = 100 \%$.

Answer: $100 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: A bullet of mass $m$ hits a mass $M$ and gets embedded in it. If the block rises to a height $h$ as a result of this collision, the velocity of the bullet before collision is
questions.solution:
Let $V$ be the common velocity of bullet and block just after collision.

By conservation of momentum:
$mv = (m + M)V$
$V = \dfrac{mv}{m+M}$

After collision, the combined mass rises to height $h$. By conservation of energy:
$\dfrac{1}{2}(m+M)V^2 = (m+M)gh$
$V = \sqrt{2gh}$

Substituting back:
$\sqrt{2gh} = \dfrac{mv}{m+M}$

$v = \dfrac{m+M}{m}\sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2gh}\left(1 + \dfrac{M}{m}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: From a circular disc of radius $R$, a square is cut out with a radius as its diagonal. The centre of mass of remaining portion is at a distance (from the centre)
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the circular disc be $R$. The area of the disc is $A_1 = \pi R^2$. The centre of mass of the disc is at the origin $(0, 0)$.

A square is cut out such that its diagonal is equal to the radius $R$. Let the side of the square be $a$. Then, $a\sqrt{2} = R$, which implies $a = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$. The area of the square is $A_2 = a^2 = \dfrac{R^2}{2}$.

The centre of mass of the square is at the centre of the disc $(0, 0)$. However, the problem implies the square is cut from the disc such that its diagonal lies along a radius. Let the centre of the square be at a distance $d$ from the centre of the disc. Since the diagonal is $R$, the distance from the centre of the square to its vertex is $\dfrac{R}{2}$. If the vertex is at the edge of the disc, the centre of the square is at $d = R - \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

The centre of mass of the remaining portion is given by $X_{cm} = \dfrac{A_1 x_1 - A_2 x_2}{A_1 - A_2}$. Here $x_1 = 0$ and $x_2 = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

$X_{cm} = \dfrac{(\pi R^2)(0) - (R^2/2)(R/2)}{\pi R^2 - R^2/2} = \dfrac{-R^3/4}{R^2(\pi - 1/2)} = \dfrac{-R/4}{(\pi - 1/2)} = \dfrac{-R}{4\pi - 2}$.

The magnitude of the distance is $\dfrac{R}{4\pi - 2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{(4 \pi-2)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Centre of mass of the given system of particles will be at
questions.solution:
Let the square $ABCD$ have side length $a$. We place the origin at the center $O$ of the square. The coordinates of the vertices are $A(-a/2, a/2)$, $B(a/2, a/2)$, $C(a/2, -a/2)$, and $D(-a/2, -a/2)$.

The masses at the vertices are $m_A = 2m$, $m_B = 4m$, $m_C = 2m$, and $m_D = 2m$.

The coordinates of the center of mass $(X_{cm}, Y_{cm})$ are given by:

$X_{cm} = \dfrac{m_A x_A + m_B x_B + m_C x_C + m_D x_D}{m_A + m_B + m_C + m_D} = \dfrac{2m(-a/2) + 4m(a/2) + 2m(a/2) + 2m(-a/2)}{2m + 4m + 2m + 2m} = \dfrac{-ma + 2ma + ma - ma}{10m} = \dfrac{ma}{10m} = \dfrac{a}{10}$

$Y_{cm} = \dfrac{m_A y_A + m_B y_B + m_C y_C + m_D y_D}{m_A + m_B + m_C + m_D} = \dfrac{2m(a/2) + 4m(a/2) + 2m(-a/2) + 2m(-a/2)}{2m + 4m + 2m + 2m} = \dfrac{ma + 2ma - ma - ma}{10m} = \dfrac{ma}{10m} = \dfrac{a}{10}$

The center of mass is at $(a/10, a/10)$. Since the diagonal $OB$ lies along the line $y = x$ in the first quadrant, and the point $(a/10, a/10)$ lies on the segment $OB$, the center of mass lies on $OB$.

Answer: $O B$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Newton's second law of rotational motion of a system particles having angular momentum $L$ is given by
questions.solution:
For a system of particles, the total angular momentum $\vec{L}$ is the sum of the angular momenta of individual particles. The rate of change of the total angular momentum is given by the sum of the torques acting on the system.

The total torque $\vec{\tau}$ acting on the system is the sum of external torques $\vec{\tau}_{ext}$ and internal torques $\vec{\tau}_{int}$.

According to Newton's third law in rotational form, the internal torques between particles in a system occur in equal and opposite pairs, such that their vector sum is zero, i.e., $\vec{\tau}_{int} = 0$.

Therefore, the rate of change of the total angular momentum of the system is equal to the sum of the external torques acting on the system:

$\dfrac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{\tau}_{ext}$

Answer: $\dfrac{d L}{d t}=\tau_{\text {ext }}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Two masses of $1 g$ and $9 g$ are moving with equal kinetic energy. The ratio of magnitude of their momentum is
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy $K$ of a body of mass $m$ and momentum $p$ is given by the relation $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$.

Given that the two masses $m_1 = 1 \text{ g}$ and $m_2 = 9 \text{ g}$ have equal kinetic energies $K_1 = K_2$, we have:

$\dfrac{p_1^2}{2m_1} = \dfrac{p_2^2}{2m_2}$

Rearranging the terms to find the ratio of the magnitudes of their momenta $\dfrac{p_1}{p_2}$:

$\dfrac{p_1^2}{p_2^2} = \dfrac{m_1}{m_2}$

Substituting the given values $m_1 = 1$ and $m_2 = 9$:

$\dfrac{p_1^2}{p_2^2} = \dfrac{1}{9}$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$\dfrac{p_1}{p_2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{9}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Thus, the ratio of the magnitude of their momentum is $1:3$.

Answer: $1: 3$

questions.solution:
A collision in which the total kinetic energy of the system remains conserved is defined as an elastic collision.

In an inelastic collision, the total kinetic energy of the system is not conserved, as some part of the kinetic energy is converted into other forms of energy such as heat, sound, or deformation energy.

Answer: elastic

questions.q: The voltage – current graph for a metal wire of uniform area of cross section at two different temp T and T' is shown. Then choose the correct statement:
options: Temperature T' is greater than temperature T
Resistance of the conductor at temperature T is greater than resistance of the conductor at temperature T'
Temperature T is greater than temperature T'
questions.solution:
From Ohm's law, $V = IR$, which gives $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$.

The given graph is an $I-V$ plot. The slope of this graph is $\dfrac{I}{V} = \dfrac{1}{R}$.

From the graph, for a given voltage $V$, the current $I$ at temperature $T$ is greater than the current $I'$ at temperature $T'$ ($I \gt I'$).

Therefore, the slope of the line for $T$ is greater than the slope of the line for $T'$.

This implies $\dfrac{1}{R_T} \gt \dfrac{1}{R_{T'}}$, which means $R_T \lt R_{T'}$.

For a metal wire, resistance increases with an increase in temperature. Since the resistance at $T'$ is greater than the resistance at $T$, the temperature $T'$ must be greater than $T$ ($T' \gt T$).

Answer: Temperature T' is greater than temperature T

Let the potential of the common right wire be $0$ V.

Observe the battery symbols to determine their polarities. For the $10$ V battery, the longer line is on the right, so its positive terminal is on the right. For the $5$ V battery, the longer line is on the left, so its positive terminal is on the left.

Therefore, the potential at the node between the $30 \Omega$ resistor and the $10$ V battery is $-10$ V. The potential at the bottom-left node, connected to the positive terminal of the $5$ V battery, is $+5$ V.

Let $V_A$ be the potential at the junction of the $5 \Omega$, $30 \Omega$, and $40 \Omega$ resistors.

Assume the diode is reverse-biased (OFF) so no current flows through the top branch.

Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at node $V_A$:

$\dfrac{V_A - (-10)}{30} + \dfrac{V_A - 5}{40} = 0$

$\dfrac{V_A + 10}{30} + \dfrac{V_A - 5}{40} = 0$

Multiplying the equation by $120$ to clear denominators:

$4(V_A + 10) + 3(V_A - 5) = 0$

$4V_A + 40 + 3V_A - 15 = 0$

$7V_A + 25 = 0 \Rightarrow V_A = -\dfrac{25}{7} \text{ V} \approx -3.57 \text{ V}$

The anode is at $V_A = -3.57$ V and the cathode is at $0$ V. Since $V_{anode} \lt V_{cathode}$, the diode is reverse-biased.

The magnitude of the current through the $40 \Omega$ resistor is:

$I = \dfrac{5 - V_A}{40} = \dfrac{5 - \left(-\dfrac{25}{7}\right)}{40}$

$I = \dfrac{\dfrac{35}{7} + \dfrac{25}{7}}{40} = \dfrac{\dfrac{60}{7}}{40} = \dfrac{60}{280} = \dfrac{3}{14} \text{ A}$

$I \approx 0.214 \text{ A}$

This matches the option $0.21$ A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A series combination of 'n' cells of emf 'E' and internal resistance 'r' each, are connected across the external resistance 'R'. If the internal resistance 'r' is negligibly small, then the current 'I' through the external resistance is:
questions.solution:
The equivalent electromotive force of $n$ cells connected in series is $nE$.

The equivalent internal resistance of the series combination is $nr$.

The total resistance of the circuit is the sum of the external resistance and the equivalent internal resistance, which is $R + nr$.

By Ohm's law, the current $I$ flowing through the circuit is given by the ratio of total electromotive force to total resistance:

$I = \dfrac{nE}{R + nr}$

It is given that the internal resistance $r$ is negligibly small, so the term $nr$ can be neglected in comparison to the external resistance $R$.

Therefore, the total resistance simplifies to approximately $R$.

Substituting this into the expression for current, we get:

$I = \dfrac{nE}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric coil is rated 400W, 200V. It is cut into two equal parts and connected in parallel to the same source of 200V. Calculate the percentage increase in energy produced per second.
questions.solution:
Let the original resistance of the coil be $R$.

The original power is $P_1 = \dfrac{V^2}{R} = 400$ W.

When the coil is cut into two equal parts, the resistance of each part becomes $\dfrac{R}{2}$.

When these two parts are connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ is given by:

$R_{eq} = \dfrac{\dfrac{R}{2} \times \dfrac{R}{2}}{\dfrac{R}{2} + \dfrac{R}{2}} = \dfrac{R}{4}$

The new power $P_2$ when connected to the same voltage source $V$ is:

$P_2 = \dfrac{V^2}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{V^2}{\dfrac{R}{4}} = 4 \dfrac{V^2}{R} = 4 P_1$

The increase in power is $\Delta P = P_2 - P_1 = 4 P_1 - P_1 = 3 P_1$.

The percentage increase in energy produced per second is:

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P_1} \times 100\% = \dfrac{3 P_1}{P_1} \times 100\% = 300\%$

Answer: $300\ \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance 50$\Omega$ is having 30 divisions and a current sensitivity 10 mA/div. What should be the shunt resistance so that it can be converted into an ammeter of range 10A?
questions.solution:
The full scale deflection current of the galvanometer is given by:

$I_g = \text{Number of divisions} \times \text{Current sensitivity}$

$I_g = 30 \times 10 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 0.3\ \text{A}$

The shunt resistance $S$ required to convert the galvanometer into an ammeter of range $I$ is:

$S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g}$

Substituting the given values $G = 50\ \Omega$ and $I = 10\ \text{A}$:

$S = \dfrac{0.3 \times 50}{10 - 0.3}$

$S = \dfrac{15}{9.7}$

$S \approx 1.55\ \Omega$

Answer: $1.55\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Current in a conductor is expressed as $I = 8t^3 + 3t^2 + 1$, where current I is measured in amperes and time t is measured in seconds. What is the charge that flows through a cross-section of the conductor between time t = 1s to t = 2s?
questions.solution:
The current in the conductor is given by $I = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = 8t^3 + 3t^2 + 1$

The charge $q$ that flows through a cross-section is the integral of current with respect to time.

$dq = I dt = (8t^3 + 3t^2 + 1) dt$

Integrating both sides from $t = 1$ s to $t = 2$ s:

$q = \int_{1}^{2} (8t^3 + 3t^2 + 1) dt$

$q = \left[ \dfrac{8t^4}{4} + \dfrac{3t^3}{3} + t \right]_{1}^{2}$

$q = \left[ 2t^4 + t^3 + t \right]_{1}^{2}$

$q = (2(2)^4 + (2)^3 + 2) - (2(1)^4 + (1)^3 + 1)$

$q = (2(16) + 8 + 2) - (2 + 1 + 1)$

$q = (32 + 8 + 2) - 4$

$q = 42 - 4 = 38 \text{ C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the given circuit, an ideal voltmeter connected across $6\Omega$ reads 5V. The internal resistance r of each cell is:
questions.solution:
The equivalent resistance of the upper branch is $9\ \Omega + 3\ \Omega = 12\ \Omega$.

The equivalent resistance of the parallel combination is $R_p = \dfrac{12 \times 6}{12 + 6} = 4\ \Omega$.

The voltage across the parallel combination is given as $V_p = 5\text{ V}$.

The main circuit current is $I = \dfrac{V_p}{R_p} = \dfrac{5}{4} = 1.25\text{ A}$.

The total external resistance is $R_{\text{ext}} = 2 + 4 = 6\ \Omega$.

The total EMF of the circuit is $E = 4 + 4 = 8\text{ V}$ and total internal resistance is $2r$.

Applying Ohm's law for the complete circuit:

$I = \dfrac{E}{R_{\text{ext}} + 2r}$

$1.25 = \dfrac{8}{6 + 2r}$

$6 + 2r = \dfrac{8}{1.25} = 6.4$

$2r = 0.4 \Rightarrow r = 0.2\ \Omega$

Answer: $0.2\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length 1m has a resistance of $20\ \Omega$ at $0^\circ$C. It is uniformly stretched so that its length increases by 21%. Assuming the volume of the wire remains constant, the percentage change in resistance is $n\%$. Alternatively, if the wire is heated [without stretching] through a temperature of $27^\circ$ C and if the temperature coefficient of resistance of the material of wire is $0.004K^{-1}$, the percentage change in resistance is $m\%$. The values of $m$ and $n$ are:
questions.solution:
For stretching of the wire, the volume $V = A \cdot L$ remains constant.

Resistance $R = \rho \dfrac{L}{A} = \rho \dfrac{L^2}{V} \Rightarrow R \propto L^2$

Given that the length increases by $21\%$, the new length is $L' = 1.21 L$.

New resistance $R' = R (1.21)^2 = 1.4641 R$

Percentage change in resistance $n = \dfrac{R' - R}{R} \times 100 = (1.4641 - 1) \times 100 = 46.41 \approx 46.4$

For heating the wire, the change in resistance is given by $\Delta R = R \alpha \Delta T$.

Percentage change in resistance $m = \dfrac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100 = \alpha \Delta T \times 100$

Given $\alpha = 0.004 K^{-1}$ and $\Delta T = 27^\circ C = 27 K$.

$m = 0.004 \times 27 \times 100 = 10.8$

The values of $m$ and $n$ are $10.8$ and $46.4$.

Answer: 10.8 and 46.4

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A current of 3A enters one vertex P of an equilateral triangle PQR having three resistors of $1\Omega$ each forming the sides of the equilateral triangle as shown. The value of $i_2$ in amperes is:
questions.solution:
The current of $3\text{A}$ enters at node P and leaves at node R. The circuit consists of two parallel paths between P and R.

The first path is the direct branch PR with resistance $R_1 = 1\Omega$.

The second path is the branch PQR, which has two $1\Omega$ resistors in series, giving an equivalent resistance $R_2 = 1\Omega + 1\Omega = 2\Omega$.

The current $i_2$ flows through the branch PQR. Using the current divider rule, the current $i_2$ is:

$i_2 = I \times \dfrac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}$

Substituting the given values:

$i_2 = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{1 + 2} = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 1\text{A}$

Answer: $1\text{A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $50\ \Omega$ galvanometer is shunted by a resistance of $S\Omega$. If 8% of total current passes through the galvanometer, the value of S is:
questions.solution:
Let the total current in the circuit be $I$.

The current passing through the galvanometer is $I_g = 8\%$ of $I = 0.08 I$.

The current passing through the shunt is $I_s = I - I_g = I - 0.08 I = 0.92 I$.

Since the galvanometer and the shunt are connected in parallel, the potential difference across them is equal:

$I_g G = I_s S$

Substituting the given values, $G = 50\ \Omega$:

$0.08 I \times 50 = 0.92 I \times S$

$4 = 0.92 S$

$S = \dfrac{4}{0.92} = \dfrac{400}{92} = \dfrac{100}{23} \approx 4.35\ \Omega$

Answer: $4.35\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cell of emf 5 V and negligible internal resistance is connected across a conducting wire of cross-sectional area $2 \mathrm{~mm}^2$. If the electron density in the wire is $5 \times 10^{28}$ and the drift velocity of the electrons is $0.125 \mathrm{mms}^{-1}$ then the resistance offered by the wire is:
questions.solution:
The current $I$ in a conductor is given by the relation $I = nAev_d$, where $n$ is the electron density, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $v_d$ is the drift velocity.

Given values are:
$n = 5 \times 10^{28} \text{ m}^{-3}$
$A = 2 \text{ mm}^2 = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$
$v_d = 0.125 \text{ mm s}^{-1} = 0.125 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 1.25 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m s}^{-1}$
$e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$

Substituting these values into the formula for current:
$I = (5 \times 10^{28}) \times (2 \times 10^{-6}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \times (1.25 \times 10^{-4})$
$I = (5 \times 2 \times 1.6 \times 1.25) \times 10^{28 - 6 - 19 - 4}$
$I = 20 \times 10^{-1} = 2 \text{ A}$

Using Ohm's law, $V = IR$, where $V = 5 \text{ V}$ is the emf of the cell:
$R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5 \Omega$

Answer: $2.5 \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the potential difference between A and B in the above circuit element?
questions.solution:
The circuit consists of a series combination of resistors and voltage sources. The current $I = 1\text{ A}$ flows from A to B.

Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) starting from point A to point B:

$V_A - I(18) - 10 - I(3) + 5 - I(9) = V_B$

Substituting the value of current $I = 1\text{ A}$:

$V_A - 1(18) - 10 - 1(3) + 5 - 1(9) = V_B$

$V_A - 18 - 10 - 3 + 5 - 9 = V_B$

$V_A - 35 = V_B$

$V_A - V_B = 35\text{ V}$

Answer: 35 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the figure shown above, a cell of negligible internal resistance and emf 22 V is connected to a network of resistors. If the power dissipated in the whole circuit is $\dfrac{x}{10 R}$, then the value of $x$ is:
questions.solution:
The diamond network forms a Wheatstone bridge. Left arm ratio: $\dfrac{4R}{8R} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, Right arm ratio: $\dfrac{2R}{4R} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Since ratios are equal, the bridge is balanced — no current flows through the horizontal branch ($R + R = 2R$), so it is removed.

Remaining three parallel paths in the diamond:
Left path: $4R + 8R = 12R$
Right path: $2R + 4R = 6R$
Vertical path: $R + R = 2R$

Combining left and right paths in parallel:
$R_{outer} = \dfrac{12R \times 6R}{12R + 6R} = \dfrac{72R^2}{18R} = 4R$

Combining with vertical path:
$R_{diamond} = \dfrac{4R \times 2R}{4R + 2R} = \dfrac{8R^2}{6R} = \dfrac{4}{3}R$

Total resistance (including top $R$ and bottom $R$ in series):
$R_{total} = R + \dfrac{4}{3}R + R = \dfrac{10}{3}R$

Total power: $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R_{total}} = \dfrac{(22)^2}{\dfrac{10}{3}R} = \dfrac{484 \times 3}{10R} = \dfrac{1452}{10R}$

Comparing with $\dfrac{x}{10R}$: $x = 1452$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A galvanometer having 20 divisions has a resistance of $50 \Omega$. A deflection of one division in this galvanometer needs a current of 0.2 mA . What should be the resistance that needs to be connected to this galvanometer to convert it to a voltmeter of range (0-20) volts?
questions.solution:
The full scale deflection current $I_g$ of the galvanometer is calculated by multiplying the number of divisions by the current per division.

$I_g = 20 \times 0.2 \text{ mA} = 20 \times 0.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A} = 0.004 \text{ A}$.

The resistance of the galvanometer is $G = 50 \Omega$.

To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter of range $V$, a high resistance $R$ must be connected in series with the galvanometer.

The formula for the series resistance is $V = I_g(G + R)$.

Substituting the given values, $20 = 0.004(50 + R)$.

Dividing both sides by $0.004$, we get $\dfrac{20}{0.004} = 50 + R$.

$5000 = 50 + R$.

$R = 5000 - 50 = 4950 \Omega$.

Thus, a resistance of $4950 \Omega$ must be connected in series with the galvanometer.

Answer: $4950 \Omega$ in series with the galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of $24 \Omega$ resistance is bent to form a square loop. A 10 V battery negligible internal resistance is connected across the diagonals of the square loop. The potential drop across one of its sides is:
questions.solution:
The total resistance of the wire is $R = 24 \Omega$. Since the wire is bent into a square loop, each side of the square has a resistance of $r = \dfrac{24}{4} = 6 \Omega$.

When a battery is connected across the diagonals of the square, the loop is divided into two parallel branches. Each branch consists of two sides of the square connected in series. Thus, the resistance of each branch is $R_{branch} = 6 \Omega + 6 \Omega = 12 \Omega$.

The two branches are connected in parallel across the 10 V battery. Therefore, the potential difference across each branch is 10 V.

In one branch, there are two resistors of $6 \Omega$ each connected in series. Since the resistors are equal, the potential drop across each resistor is half of the total potential drop across the branch.

Potential drop across one side = $\dfrac{10 V}{2} = 5 V$.

Answer: 5 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Across the 220 V source of internal resistance $20 \Omega$, how many lamps of $40 \mathrm{~W}, 100 \mathrm{~V}$ can be connected in parallel so that all the lamps may glow with full brightness.
questions.solution:
Each lamp is rated $40 \text{ W}$ at $100 \text{ V}$. The resistance of each lamp is $R_L = \dfrac{V^2}{P} = \dfrac{100^2}{40} = \dfrac{10000}{40} = 250 \Omega$.

Let $n$ be the number of lamps connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance of $n$ lamps is $R_p = \dfrac{R_L}{n} = \dfrac{250}{n} \Omega$.

The circuit consists of the source voltage $V_s = 220 \text{ V}$ with internal resistance $r = 20 \Omega$ in series with the parallel combination of lamps. For the lamps to glow with full brightness, the voltage across the parallel combination must be $100 \text{ V}$.

The current flowing through the circuit is $I = \dfrac{V_s - V_L}{r} = \dfrac{220 - 100}{20} = \dfrac{120}{20} = 6 \text{ A}$.

The current through each lamp is $I_L = \dfrac{P}{V_L} = \dfrac{40}{100} = 0.4 \text{ A}$.

The total current is the sum of currents through $n$ lamps, so $I = n \times I_L$.

$6 = n \times 0.4 \Rightarrow n = \dfrac{6}{0.4} = 15$.

Answer: 15

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A galvanometer of $50 \Omega$ resistance is converted into an ammeter using a shunt resistance of $10 \Omega$. If the same resistance is used to convert the same galvanometer in to a voltmeter, what would be the ratio of the resistance of the ammeter to the resistance of the voltmeter?
questions.solution:
Let $G = 50 \Omega$ be the resistance of the galvanometer and $S = 10 \Omega$ be the shunt resistance.

The resistance of an ammeter $R_{A}$ is given by the parallel combination of the galvanometer and the shunt resistance:

$R_{A} = \dfrac{G \times S}{G + S} = \dfrac{50 \times 10}{50 + 10} = \dfrac{500}{60} = \dfrac{50}{6} \Omega = \dfrac{25}{3} \Omega$.

When the same resistance $S = 10 \Omega$ is used to convert the galvanometer into a voltmeter, it is connected in series with the galvanometer. The resistance of the voltmeter $R_{V}$ is given by:

$R_{V} = G + S = 50 + 10 = 60 \Omega$.

The ratio of the resistance of the ammeter to the resistance of the voltmeter is:

$\dfrac{R_{A}}{R_{V}} = \dfrac{25/3}{60} = \dfrac{25}{3 \times 60} = \dfrac{25}{180}$.

Dividing both numerator and denominator by 5, we get:

$\dfrac{R_{A}}{R_{V}} = \dfrac{5}{36}$.

Answer: $5: 36$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wires A and B made of same material having length 10 cm and 40 cm respectively are connected in parallel to the same source of emf 10 V . What will be the ratio of the drift velocity of the electrons in the wire $A$ to the drift velocity in the wire $B$ ?
questions.solution:
The drift velocity $v_{d}$ of electrons in a conductor is given by the formula $v_{d} = \dfrac{I}{neA}$, where $I$ is the current, $n$ is the electron density, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area. Since the wires are made of the same material, $n$ is the same for both.

The current $I$ in a wire is given by $I = \dfrac{V}{R}$, where $V$ is the potential difference and $R$ is the resistance. The resistance $R$ is given by $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$, where $\rho$ is the resistivity and $l$ is the length. Substituting this into the expression for current, $I = \dfrac{VA}{\rho l}$.

Substituting $I$ into the drift velocity formula, $v_{d} = \dfrac{VA}{neA\rho l} = \dfrac{V}{ne\rho l}$.

Since both wires are connected to the same source of emf, $V$ is the same for both. The material is the same, so $n$ and $\rho$ are constant. Therefore, $v_{d} \propto \dfrac{1}{l}$.

The ratio of drift velocities is $\dfrac{v_{dA}}{v_{dB}} = \dfrac{l_{B}}{l_{A}}$.

Given $l_{A} = 10$ cm and $l_{B} = 40$ cm, we have $\dfrac{v_{dA}}{v_{dB}} = \dfrac{40}{10} = \dfrac{4}{1}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{V_{d A}}{V_{d B}}=4: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Ten cells, each having internal resistance $1 \Omega$ and emf 1.5 V are connected in series. But unknowingly 3 cells are connected wrongly in series. The effective internal resistance and emf of the series combination are respectively:
questions.solution:
The total number of cells is $n = 10$. Each cell has an emf $E = 1.5$ V and internal resistance $r = 1 \Omega$.

When cells are connected in series, the total internal resistance is the sum of individual resistances, regardless of their polarity. Thus, the effective internal resistance $R_{eq} = n \times r = 10 \times 1 = 10 \Omega$.

For the effective emf, if $m$ cells are connected wrongly, they oppose the remaining $(n - m)$ cells. The effective emf is given by $E_{eq} = (n - m)E - mE = (n - 2m)E$.

Given $n = 10$ and $m = 3$, the effective emf is $E_{eq} = (10 - 2 \times 3) \times 1.5 = (10 - 6) \times 1.5 = 4 \times 1.5 = 6$ V.

Therefore, the effective internal resistance is $10 \Omega$ and the effective emf is 6 V.

Answer: $10 \Omega$ and 6 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resistance of the conductor is $\sqrt{3} \Omega$ the angle made by the V-I graph with the voltage axis is $\theta$
questions.solution:
The resistance $R$ of a conductor is given by the slope of the $V-I$ graph, where $V$ is on the y-axis and $I$ is on the x-axis. Thus, $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \tan(\phi)$, where $\phi$ is the angle made with the current axis (x-axis).

The problem states that the angle made with the voltage axis (y-axis) is $\theta$. Therefore, the angle made with the current axis is $\phi = 90^{\circ} - \theta$.

Given $R = \sqrt{3} \Omega$, we have $\tan(\phi) = \sqrt{3}$.

Since $\tan(60^{\circ}) = \sqrt{3}$, it follows that $\phi = 60^{\circ}$.

Substituting $\phi = 90^{\circ} - \theta$, we get $60^{\circ} = 90^{\circ} - \theta$, which implies $\theta = 30^{\circ}$.

Answer: $\theta=30^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resistance of a heating element is found to be $120 \Omega$ at room temperature which is $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the temperature coefficient of the material of the resistor is $1.6 \times 10^{-4} C^{-1}$ and the resistance is found to be $160 \Omega$, the temperature of the element is:
questions.solution:
The resistance of a conductor at a temperature $T$ is given by the formula $R_T = R_0 [1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$, where $R_0$ is the resistance at room temperature $T_0$, $R_T$ is the resistance at temperature $T$, and $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient of resistance.

Given values are $R_0 = 120 \Omega$, $T_0 = 20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, $R_T = 160 \Omega$, and $\alpha = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$160 = 120 [1 + 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)]$

Dividing both sides by $120$:

$\dfrac{160}{120} = 1 + 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)$

$\dfrac{4}{3} = 1 + 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)$

$\dfrac{4}{3} - 1 = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)$

$\dfrac{1}{3} = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)$

$T - 20 = \dfrac{1}{3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-4}}$

$T - 20 = \dfrac{1}{4.8 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{10000}{4.8} \approx 2083.33$

$T = 2083.33 + 20 = 2103.33 \approx 2103^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

Answer: $2103^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The power dissipated across the $16 \Omega$ resistor in the circuit is 2 watts. The power dissipated in watt units across the $4 \Omega$ resistor is:
questions.solution:
The circuit consists of two parallel branches. The top branch contains a $16 \Omega$ resistor. The bottom branch contains a $6 \Omega$ resistor and a $4 \Omega$ resistor in series.

Let $V$ be the potential difference across the parallel branches. The power dissipated in the $16 \Omega$ resistor is given by $P_{16} = \dfrac{V^2}{R_{16}} = 2$ W. Substituting $R_{16} = 16 \Omega$, we get $\dfrac{V^2}{16} = 2$, which implies $V^2 = 32$ V$^2$.

The bottom branch has a total resistance $R_{bottom} = 6 \Omega + 4 \Omega = 10 \Omega$. The current flowing through the bottom branch is $I_{bottom} = \dfrac{V}{R_{bottom}} = \dfrac{V}{10}$.

The power dissipated in the $4 \Omega$ resistor is $P_4 = I_{bottom}^2 \times R_4 = \left(\dfrac{V}{10}\right)^2 \times 4 = \dfrac{V^2}{100} \times 4$.

Substituting $V^2 = 32$, we get $P_4 = \dfrac{32}{100} \times 4 = \dfrac{128}{100} = 1.28$ W.

Answer: 1.28 W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A galvanometer having a resistance of $50 \Omega$ is shunted by a wire of resistance $10 \Omega$. If the total current is 2 A , the current passing through the shunt is:
questions.solution:
Let $G$ be the resistance of the galvanometer and $S$ be the resistance of the shunt wire. Given $G = 50 \Omega$ and $S = 10 \Omega$. The total current $I = 2 \text{ A}$.

The current $I_S$ passing through the shunt is given by the current divider rule:

$I_S = I \times \dfrac{G}{G + S}$

Substituting the given values:

$I_S = 2 \times \dfrac{50}{50 + 10}$

$I_S = 2 \times \dfrac{50}{60}$

$I_S = 2 \times \dfrac{5}{6}$

$I_S = \dfrac{5}{3} \text{ A}$

Answer: $\dfrac{5}{3} \mathrm{~A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A student measures the terminal potential difference $V$ of a cell of $\operatorname{emf} \varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ as a function of the current I flowing through it. Which of the following graphs will give the values of emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ ?
questions.solution:
The terminal potential difference $V$ of a cell with emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ is given by the equation $V = \varepsilon - Ir$.

This equation represents a linear relationship between $V$ and $I$, which can be written in the form $y = mx + c$ as $V = -rI + \varepsilon$.

Comparing this with the equation of a straight line, the intercept on the $V$-axis (when $I = 0$) is $\varepsilon$, and the slope of the line is $-r$.

Graph 1 shows $V$ on the vertical axis and $I$ on the horizontal axis with a negative slope, which matches the equation $V = -rI + \varepsilon$. The $V$-intercept is $\varepsilon$ and the magnitude of the slope gives the internal resistance $r$.

Answer: $1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The net resistance between the points A and B in the circuit given below is:
questions.solution:
A and E are the same node. The circuit forms a Wheatstone bridge with D and C as middle junctions.

Arms: $R_{ED} = 4R$, $R_{EC} = 2R$, $R_{DB} = 4R$, $R_{CB} = 2R$, cross resistor $= 5R$

Balance check: $\dfrac{R_{ED}}{R_{EC}} = \dfrac{4R}{2R} = 2$ and $\dfrac{R_{DB}}{R_{CB}} = \dfrac{4R}{2R} = 2$

Bridge is balanced \Rightarrow no current through $5R$, so it is removed.

Upper branch (E-D-B): $4R + 4R = 8R$
Lower branch (E-C-B): $2R + 2R = 4R$

$\dfrac{1}{R_{AB}} = \dfrac{1}{8R} + \dfrac{1}{4R} = \dfrac{3}{8R}$

$R_{AB} = \dfrac{8R}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resistance of a wire is 5 ohm at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 7 ohm at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The resistance of the wire at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is
questions.solution:
The resistance of a wire at temperature $t$ is given by the formula $R_t = R_0(1 + \alpha t)$, where $R_0$ is the resistance at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient of resistance.

Given $R_{25} = 5 \, \Omega$ at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $R_{100} = 7 \, \Omega$ at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, we have the following equations:

$5 = R_0(1 + 25\alpha)$ (1)

$7 = R_0(1 + 100\alpha)$ (2)

Dividing equation (2) by equation (1):

$\dfrac{7}{5} = \dfrac{1 + 100\alpha}{1 + 25\alpha}$

$7(1 + 25\alpha) = 5(1 + 100\alpha)$

$7 + 175\alpha = 5 + 500\alpha$

$2 = 325\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{2}{325}$

Substituting $\alpha$ back into equation (1):

$5 = R_0(1 + 25 \times \dfrac{2}{325})$

$5 = R_0(1 + \dfrac{50}{325}) = R_0(1 + \dfrac{2}{13})$

$5 = R_0(\dfrac{15}{13})$

$R_0 = 5 \times \dfrac{13}{15} = \dfrac{13}{3} \, \Omega$

Answer: $\dfrac{13}{3} \mathrm{ohm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If voltage across a bulb rated $220 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~W}$ drops by $5 \%$ of its rated value, the percentage of the rated value by which the power would decrease is
questions.solution:
The power $P$ consumed by a bulb is related to the voltage $V$ by the formula $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$, where $R$ is the constant resistance of the bulb.

Taking the logarithmic derivative of both sides, we get $\dfrac{dP}{P} = 2 \dfrac{dV}{V}$.

Given that the voltage drops by $5 \%$, we have $\dfrac{dV}{V} = -0.05$.

Substituting this into the expression for the fractional change in power:

$\dfrac{dP}{P} = 2 \times (-0.05) = -0.10$.

The negative sign indicates a decrease in power. Thus, the power decreases by $10 \%$ of its rated value.

Answer: $10 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A student measures the terminal potential difference V of a cell (emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance r) as a function of current I flowing through it, and draws V versus I graph. The slope and intercept of the graph respectively are
questions.solution:
The terminal potential difference $V$ of a cell with emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ when a current $I$ is drawn from it is given by the equation:

$V = \varepsilon - Ir$

Rearranging this equation to match the linear form $y = mx + c$, where $y = V$ and $x = I$, we get:

$V = -rI + \varepsilon$

Comparing this with the equation of a straight line $V = mI + c$, the slope $m$ is $-r$ and the y-intercept $c$ is $\varepsilon$.

Answer: $-r, \varepsilon$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical conductors of lengths $l$ and 3$l$ respectively are maintained at the same temperature. They are given potential differences in the ratio $1: 3$. The ratio of their drift velocities is
questions.solution:
The drift velocity $v_d$ of electrons in a conductor is given by the formula $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$, where $E$ is the electric field, $e$ is the charge of an electron, $\tau$ is the relaxation time, and $m$ is the mass of the electron.

The electric field $E$ is related to the potential difference $V$ and length $l$ by $E = \dfrac{V}{l}$.

Substituting this into the drift velocity formula, we get $v_d = \dfrac{eV\tau}{ml}$.

For two conductors, the ratio of drift velocities is $\dfrac{v_{d1}}{v_{d2}} = \dfrac{V_1}{l_1} \times \dfrac{l_2}{V_2}$.

Given $l_1 = l$ and $l_2 = 3l$, and the ratio of potential differences $\dfrac{V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

Substituting these values, we get $\dfrac{v_{d1}}{v_{d2}} = \dfrac{1}{l} \times \dfrac{3l}{3} = \dfrac{1}{1}$.

Answer: $1: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance $50 \Omega$ is connected to a battery of 4 V along with a resistance of $3950 \Omega$ in series. A full-scale deflection of 30 divisions is obtained in the galvanometer. In order to reduce this deflection to 10 divisions, the resistance in series should be equal to:
questions.solution:
The current $I$ flowing through the galvanometer for a full-scale deflection of $30$ divisions is given by Ohm's law:

$I = \dfrac{V}{R_{g} + R_{s}} = \dfrac{4}{50 + 3950} = \dfrac{4}{4000} = 10^{-3} \text{ A}$

The current per division is $\dfrac{10^{-3}}{30} \text{ A/division}$.

To obtain a deflection of $10$ divisions, the new current $I'$ required is:

$I' = 10 \times \dfrac{10^{-3}}{30} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 10^{-3} \text{ A}$

Let the new series resistance be $R'_{s}$. The circuit equation is:

$I' = \dfrac{V}{R_{g} + R'_{s}}$

$\dfrac{1}{3} \times 10^{-3} = \dfrac{4}{50 + R'_{s}}$

$50 + R'_{s} = 4 \times 3 \times 10^{3} = 12000$

$R'_{s} = 12000 - 50 = 11950 \Omega$

Answer: 11950 ohm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric bulb is rated at 220 V and 100 W . Power consumed by bulb when operated at 110 V will be
questions.solution:
$\quad P_{\text {rated }}=\frac{V_{\text {rated }}^2}{R}$ or $R=\frac{(220)^2}{100}$
Now, power consumed
$=\frac{V^2}{R}=\frac{(110)^2 \times 100}{(220)^2}=25 \mathrm{~W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A battery of emf 12 V and negligible resistance is connected across the diagonally opposite corners of a cubical network consisting of 12 resistors each of resistance $2 \Omega$. The equivalent resistance of the network is
questions.solution:
In a closed loop, say $A B C C^{\prime} E A$ and apply Kirchhoffs second rule, $-I R-\left(\frac{I}{2}\right) R-I R+\varepsilon=0$

where, $R$ is the resistance of each edge and $\varepsilon$ the emf of battery.
Thus, $\varepsilon=\frac{5}{2} I R$
The equivalent resistance $R_{\text {eq }}$ of the network is
$R_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{\varepsilon}{3 I}=\frac{5}{6} R=\frac{5}{6} \times 2=\frac{5}{3} \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resistor of resistance $R$ is connected to 25 V supply and heat produced in it is $25 \mathrm{Js}^{-1}$. The value of $R$ is
questions.solution:
Given,
$\begin{aligned} \\ & \frac{H}{t}=25 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{s}=25 \mathrm{~W} \\ \\ & V=25 \mathrm{~V} \\ \end{aligned}$
We know that,
$\begin{aligned} \\ & H=\frac{V^2}{R} t \\ \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \frac{H}{t}=\frac{V^2}{R} \\ \\ \Rightarrow \quad & 25=\frac{25^2}{R} \\ \\ \Rightarrow \quad & R=\frac{25^2}{25}=25 \Omega \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the length of a wire is increased by $20 \%$ by stretching it, then its resistance is increased to
questions.solution:
Given
$\begin{aligned} \\ & l_1=l, A_1=A \\ \\ & l_2=l\left(1+\frac{20}{100}\right)=\frac{6 l}{5}, A_2=A^{\prime} \\ \end{aligned}$
We have,
$\begin{aligned} \\ & A_1 l_1=A_2 l_2 \\ \\ & A l=A^{\prime} \frac{6 l}{5} \Rightarrow A^{\prime}=\frac{5 A}{6} \\ \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{R_2}{R_1}=\frac{\frac{\rho_2}{A_2}}{\frac{\rho_1}{A_1}}=\frac{l_2}{l_1} \cdot \frac{A_1}{A_2}=\frac{\frac{6 l}{5}}{l} \cdot \frac{6}{5 \mathrm{~A}}=\frac{36}{25} \\ \end{aligned}$
Increase in the resistance,
$\left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}-1\right) \times 100=\left(\frac{36}{25}-1\right) \times 100=44 \%$

questions.q:
For a cell, $V$ - $I$ graph is given below.

Which of the following options gives correct value of emf of cell and its internal resistance?
questions.solution:
From graph, $V=1.5 \mathrm{~V}$ at $I=0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The drift velocity of free electrons in a conducting wire is the order of $10^{-4} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Yet, the bulb glows very quickly after the switch is put ON because
options: the random speed of electrons is very high of order of $10^6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
the electrons transfer their energy very quickly through collisions
electric field is set-up in the wire with a speed of light producing a current through each cross-section, almost instantaneously
the random speed of electrons is very low of order of $10^{-6} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
questions.solution:
When electric field is applied, the random motion of all free electrons converted into uni-directional within very short duration of time of order $10^{-9} \mathrm{~s}$. Which in turn sets up on electric field instantaneously. Thus, a current through each cross-section is produced almost instantaneously.
Hence, the bulb glows very quickly.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A storage battery of emf $28.0 \mathrm{~V}$ and internal resistance $0.5 \Omega$ is being charged by a $140 \mathrm{~V}$ dc supply using a series resistor of $27.5 \Omega$. The terminal voltage of the battery during charging is
questions.solution:
The circuit consists of a DC supply of $V_{s} = 140 \text{ V}$, a series resistor $R = 27.5 \Omega$, and a battery being charged with emf $E = 28.0 \text{ V}$ and internal resistance $r = 0.5 \Omega$.

The total resistance in the circuit is $R_{total} = R + r = 27.5 \Omega + 0.5 \Omega = 28.0 \Omega$.

The charging current $I$ is given by the formula $I = \dfrac{V_{s} - E}{R_{total}}$.

Substituting the values, $I = \dfrac{140 \text{ V} - 28.0 \text{ V}}{28.0 \Omega} = \dfrac{112 \text{ V}}{28.0 \Omega} = 4 \text{ A}$.

The terminal voltage $V$ of the battery during charging is given by $V = E + Ir$.

Substituting the values, $V = 28.0 \text{ V} + (4 \text{ A} \times 0.5 \Omega) = 28.0 \text{ V} + 2.0 \text{ V} = 30.0 \text{ V}$.

Answer: 30V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The mobility of the charge carriers increases with
options: Decrease in the charge of the mobile carriers
Increase in the mass of the charge
questions.solution:
The mobility $\mu$ of charge carriers in a conductor is defined as the ratio of the drift velocity $v_d$ to the applied electric field $E$.

The expression for drift velocity is $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$, where $e$ is the charge of the carrier, $\tau$ is the average relaxation time (average collision time), and $m$ is the mass of the carrier.

Substituting this into the definition of mobility: $\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E} = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}$.

From the relation $\mu = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}$, it is evident that the mobility $\mu$ is directly proportional to the average collision time $\tau$. Therefore, mobility increases as the average collision time increases.

Answer: The average collision time

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of uniform cross section and resistance 4 ohms is bent in the shape of square ABCD. Point A is connected to a point $\mathrm{P}$ on DC by a wire AP of resistance $1 \mathrm{ohm}$. When a potential difference is applied between $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{C}$, the points $\mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{P}$ are seen to be in same potential. What is the resistance of part $\mathrm{DP}$ ?
questions.solution:
Each side of the square has resistance $\dfrac{4}{4} = 1\ \Omega$. Let $R_{DP} = x$, so $R_{PC} = 1-x$.

Since B and P are at the same potential, the A-P section resistance equals the P-C section resistance (by symmetry of the voltage divider).

From A to P: direct wire AP $(1\ \Omega)$ is in parallel with path A\to D\to P $(1+x)\ \Omega$:

$R_{AP(eq)} = \dfrac{1 \cdot (1+x)}{1+(1+x)} = \dfrac{1+x}{2+x}$

Setting $R_{AP(eq)} = R_{PC}$:

$\dfrac{1+x}{2+x} = 1-x$

$1+x = (1-x)(2+x) = 2+x-2x-x^2$

$x^2 + 2x - 1 = 0$

$x = \dfrac{-2+\sqrt{8}}{2} = -1+\sqrt{2}$

$R_{DP} = \sqrt{2}-1\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical moving coil galvanometers have $10 \Omega$ resistance and full-scale deflection at $2 \mu \mathrm{A}$ current. One of them is converted into a voltmeter of range $10 \mathrm{~mV}$ and the other into an ammeter of range $1 \mathrm{~mA}$ using appropriate resistors. The ratio of resistance of the converted voltmeter to that of the ammeter is
questions.solution:
The resistance of the galvanometer is $G = 10 \Omega$ and the full-scale deflection current is $I_g = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$.

For the voltmeter, the range is $V = 10 \text{ mV} = 10^{-2} \text{ V}$. The total resistance of the voltmeter is $R_V = \dfrac{V}{I_g} = \dfrac{10^{-2}}{2 \times 10^{-6}} = 5000 \Omega$.

For the ammeter, the range is $I = 1 \text{ mA} = 10^{-3} \text{ A}$. The shunt resistance $S$ is connected in parallel with $G$ such that $I_g G = (I - I_g) S$. Thus, $S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 10}{10^{-3} - 2 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-5}}{0.998 \times 10^{-3}} \approx \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-5}}{10^{-3}} = 0.02 \Omega$. The total resistance of the ammeter is $R_A = \dfrac{G \times S}{G + S} \approx S = 0.02 \Omega$.

The ratio of the resistance of the voltmeter to the ammeter is $\dfrac{R_V}{R_A} = \dfrac{5000}{0.02} = \dfrac{5000 \times 100}{2} = 250000$.

Answer: 250000 : 1
