questions.solution:
The universal gravitational constant $G$ was first experimentally determined by Henry Cavendish in 1798 using a torsion balance apparatus. This experiment is famously known as the Cavendish experiment, which allowed for the measurement of the extremely weak gravitational force between two lead spheres, thereby enabling the calculation of the value of $G$.

Answer: Cavendish

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spherical planets $P$ and $Q$ have the same uniform density $\rho$, and masses $M_P$ and $M_Q$ and surface areas $A$ and $4 A$ respectively. Another spherical planet R also has the same uniform density $\rho$, and its mass is $\mathrm{Mp}+\mathrm{MQ}$. The escape velocities from these planets is
questions.solution:
The surface area of a sphere is $A = 4 \pi R^2$. Given $A_P = A$ and $A_Q = 4A$, we have $4 \pi R_P^2 = A$ and $4 \pi R_Q^2 = 4A$. This implies $R_Q^2 = 4 R_P^2$, so $R_Q = 2 R_P$.

The mass of a planet with uniform density $\rho$ is $M = \rho \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3$. Thus, $M \propto R^3$. Given $R_Q = 2 R_P$, we have $M_Q = (2)^3 M_P = 8 M_P$.

The escape velocity from a planet is $V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$. Since $M = \rho \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3$, we have $V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G \rho \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3}{R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3} \pi G \rho} R$. Thus, $V \propto R$.

Since $R_Q = 2 R_P$, it follows that $V_Q = 2 V_P$, so $V_Q \gt V_P$.

For planet R, $M_R = M_P + M_Q = M_P + 8 M_P = 9 M_P$. Since $M_R = \rho \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_R^3$, we have $R_R^3 = \dfrac{M_R}{\rho \dfrac{4}{3} \pi} = \dfrac{9 M_P}{\rho \dfrac{4}{3} \pi} = 9 R_P^3$. Thus, $R_R = 9^{1/3} R_P$.

Since $V \propto R$, $V_R = 9^{1/3} V_P$. Comparing the values: $V_P = 1 V_P$, $V_Q = 2 V_P$, and $V_R = 9^{1/3} V_P \approx 2.08 V_P$.

Therefore, $V_R \gt V_Q \gt V_P$.

Answer: $V_R \gt V_Q \gt V_P$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the radius of earth were to shrink by two percent, its mass remaining the same, the acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface would
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity $g$ on the surface of the earth is given by the formula $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ is the mass of the earth, and $R$ is the radius of the earth.

Given that the mass $M$ remains constant, $g$ is inversely proportional to the square of the radius, $g \propto R^{-2}$.

Taking the logarithmic derivative of the relation $g = GM R^{-2}$, we get $\dfrac{dg}{g} = -2 \dfrac{dR}{R}$.

The radius shrinks by two percent, which means $\dfrac{dR}{R} = -0.02$.

Substituting this value into the expression for the fractional change in $g$:

$\dfrac{dg}{g} = -2 \times (-0.02) = 0.04$.

Therefore, the acceleration due to gravity increases by $0.04$ or $4 \%$.

Answer: Increase by \(4 \%\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
If the distance between the Sun and Earth is doubled ,then the duration of the year on earth will be:
[Given actual duration of the year $=\mathrm{T}$ ]
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's third law of planetary motion, the square of the time period $T$ of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis $r$ of its orbit, which is given by $T^2 \propto r^3$.

Let the initial distance be $r_1 = r$ and the initial time period be $T_1 = T$. The new distance is $r_2 = 2r$.

Using the relation $\dfrac{T_2^2}{T_1^2} = \left( \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} \right)^3$, we substitute the values:

$\dfrac{T_2^2}{T^2} = \left( \dfrac{2r}{r} \right)^3 = 2^3 = 8$.

Taking the square root on both sides, we get $\dfrac{T_2}{T} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$.

Therefore, the new duration of the year is $T_2 = 2\sqrt{2}T$.

Answer: $2 \sqrt{2} T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The unit of universal gravitational constant is :
questions.solution:
The law of universal gravitation is given by the formula $F = G \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, where $F$ is the gravitational force, $G$ is the universal gravitational constant, $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the masses of the two objects, and $r$ is the distance between them.

Rearranging the formula to solve for $G$, we get $G = \dfrac{F r^2}{m_1 m_2}$.

Substituting the SI units for each quantity: $F$ is in Newtons ($\mathrm{N}$), $r$ is in meters ($\mathrm{m}$), and $m$ is in kilograms ($\mathrm{kg}$).

The unit of $G$ is $\dfrac{\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m}^2}{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{kg}} = \mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m}^2 \cdot \mathrm{kg}^{-2}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{m}^2 \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A planet is 121 times heavier than moon and has a diameter 9 times that of moon. If the escape velocity on the planet is v , then the escape velocity on the moon will be:
questions.solution:
The escape velocity $v_e$ of a body is given by the formula $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, where $M$ is the mass and $R$ is the radius of the body.

Let $M_p$ and $R_p$ be the mass and radius of the planet, and $M_m$ and $R_m$ be the mass and radius of the moon. Given $M_p = 121 M_m$ and the diameter $D_p = 9 D_m$, which implies $R_p = 9 R_m$.

The escape velocity on the planet is $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_p}{R_p}}$.

The escape velocity on the moon is $v_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_m}{R_m}}$.

Taking the ratio of the escape velocities:

$\dfrac{v_m}{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_m}{R_m} \times \dfrac{R_p}{M_p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_m}{R_m} \times \dfrac{9 R_m}{121 M_m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{9}{121}} = \dfrac{3}{11}$.

Therefore, $v_m = \dfrac{3}{11} v$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3 v}{11}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The radius of earth is $R$ and acceleration due to gravity on its surface is $g$. The height at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $\dfrac{g}{8}$ is:
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the Earth is given by the formula $g' = g \left( \dfrac{R}{R+h} \right)^{2}$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface and $R$ is the radius of the Earth.

Given that $g' = \dfrac{g}{8}$, we substitute this into the equation:

$\dfrac{g}{8} = g \left( \dfrac{R}{R+h} \right)^{2}$

Dividing both sides by $g$ gives:

$\dfrac{1}{8} = \left( \dfrac{R}{R+h} \right)^{2}$

Taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{R}{R+h}$

Rearranging the terms to solve for $h$:

$R + h = 2\sqrt{2} R$

$h = 2\sqrt{2} R - R$

$h = (2\sqrt{2} - 1) R$

Answer: $(2 \sqrt{2}-1) R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass 1 kg is kept on the surface of a uniform sphere of mass 20 kg and radius 1.0 m . The work to be done against the gravitational force between them to take the particle away from the sphere is
questions.solution:
Potential at the surface of earth,
$V=-\frac{G M}{R}$
$\begin{aligned} \\ & =-\frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 20}{1} \\ \\ & =-1.334 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{K} \\ \end{aligned}$
i.e., $1.334 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~J}$ work is done to bring a mass of 1 kg from infinity to the surface of sphere. Hence, the same amount of work will have to be done to take the particle away from the surface of sphere.
$\therefore W=1.334 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A planet has double the mass of the earth and double the radius. The gravitational potential at the surface of the Earth is $\mathrm{V}$ and the magnitude of the gravitational field strength is $\mathrm{g}$. The gravitational potential and gravitational field strength on the surface of the planet are
No.PotentialField
AV$\dfrac{g}{4}$
B2V$\dfrac{g}{2}$
CV$\dfrac{g}{2}$
D2V$\dfrac{g}{4}$
questions.solution:
The gravitational potential $V$ at the surface of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is given by $V = -\dfrac{GM}{R}$.

The gravitational field strength $g$ at the surface is given by $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$.

For the Earth, $V_E = -\dfrac{GM_E}{R_E} = V$ and $g_E = \dfrac{GM_E}{R_E^2} = g$.

For the given planet, $M_P = 2M_E$ and $R_P = 2R_E$.

The gravitational potential at the surface of the planet is $V_P = -\dfrac{GM_P}{R_P} = -\dfrac{G(2M_E)}{2R_E} = -\dfrac{GM_E}{R_E} = V$.

The gravitational field strength at the surface of the planet is $g_P = \dfrac{GM_P}{R_P^2} = \dfrac{G(2M_E)}{(2R_E)^2} = \dfrac{2GM_E}{4R_E^2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{GM_E}{R_E^2} \right) = \dfrac{g}{2}$.

Answer: C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Energy required for moving a body of mass $\mathrm{m}$ from a circular orbit of radius 3R to a higher orbit of radius 4R around the earth is.
questions.solution:
The total mechanical energy $E$ of a body of mass $m$ in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around the Earth of mass $M$ is given by the expression $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$.

The energy in the initial orbit of radius $r_1 = 3R$ is $E_1 = -\dfrac{GMm}{2(3R)} = -\dfrac{GMm}{6R}$.

The energy in the final orbit of radius $r_2 = 4R$ is $E_2 = -\dfrac{GMm}{2(4R)} = -\dfrac{GMm}{8R}$.

The energy required to move the body from the initial orbit to the final orbit is the change in total mechanical energy, $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1$.

Substituting the values, $\Delta E = -\dfrac{GMm}{8R} - \left(-\dfrac{GMm}{6R}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{6R} - \dfrac{GMm}{8R}$.

Taking the common denominator, $\Delta E = \dfrac{4GMm - 3GMm}{24R} = \dfrac{GMm}{24R}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\mathrm{GMm}}{24 \mathrm{R}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite is revolving around the earth in a circular orbit with kinetic energy of $1.69 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~J}$. The additional kinetic energy required for just escaping into the outer space is
questions.solution:
For a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around the earth of mass $M$, the gravitational potential energy is $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ and the kinetic energy is $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$.

The total mechanical energy of the satellite in the orbit is $E = K + U = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r} = -K$.

Given $K = 1.69 \times 10^{10} \text{ J}$, the total energy is $E = -1.69 \times 10^{10} \text{ J}$.

To escape into outer space, the final total energy of the satellite must be at least $0$.

The required additional energy $\Delta E$ is given by $E_{final} - E_{initial} = 0 - E = -(-K) = K$.

Therefore, the additional kinetic energy required is equal to the current kinetic energy, which is $1.69 \times 10^{10} \text{ J}$.

Answer: $1.69 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity at pole and equator can be related as
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity $g$ at a point on the surface of the Earth at a latitude $\lambda$ is given by the formula $g_{\lambda} = g - R\omega^2 \cos^2 \lambda$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the poles, $R$ is the radius of the Earth, and $\omega$ is the angular velocity of the Earth.

At the poles, the latitude $\lambda = 90^{\circ}$. Substituting this into the formula, we get $g_p = g - R\omega^2 \cos^2(90^{\circ}) = g - 0 = g$.

At the equator, the latitude $\lambda = 0^{\circ}$. Substituting this into the formula, we get $g_e = g - R\omega^2 \cos^2(0^{\circ}) = g - R\omega^2$.

Since $R\omega^2 \gt 0$, it follows that $g - R\omega^2 \lt g$. Therefore, $g_e \lt g_p$.

Answer: $g_e \lt g_p$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $\mathrm{A}$ is the areal velocity of a planet of mass $\mathrm{M}$, then its angular momentum is
questions.solution:
The areal velocity of a planet is defined as the rate at which the area is swept by the radius vector, given by $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$.

The angular momentum $L$ of a planet of mass $M$ moving in an orbit is given by $L = mvr = mr^2 \omega$, where $\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$.

Substituting $\omega$ into the expression for angular momentum, we get $L = M r^2 \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$.

Comparing this with the expression for areal velocity $A = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$, we see that $r^2 \dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = 2A$.

Therefore, $L = M(2A) = 2MA$.

Answer: $2 \mathrm{MA}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the earth has a mass nine times and radius four times that of planet X, the ratio of the maximum speed required by a rocket to pull out of the gravitational force of planet $\mathrm{X}$ to that of the earth is
questions.solution:
The escape velocity $v_{e}$ of a planet with mass $M$ and radius $R$ is given by the formula $v_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

Let $M_{E}$ and $R_{E}$ be the mass and radius of the Earth, and $M_{X}$ and $R_{X}$ be the mass and radius of planet X. Given $M_{E} = 9M_{X}$ and $R_{E} = 4R_{X}$.

The escape velocity for Earth is $v_{E} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_{E}}{R_{E}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G(9M_{X})}{4R_{X}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{9}{4}} \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_{X}}{R_{X}}} = \dfrac{3}{2} v_{X}$, where $v_{X}$ is the escape velocity for planet X.

The ratio of the escape velocity of planet X to that of the Earth is $\dfrac{v_{X}}{v_{E}} = \dfrac{v_{X}}{\dfrac{3}{2} v_{X}} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{3}$

questions.q: Starting from the centre of the earth having radius $R$, the variation of $g$ (acceleration due to gravity) is shown by

Acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ below the surface of the earth is given by

Also, for a point at height $h$ above surface,

Therefore, we can say that value of $g$ increases from centre to maximum at the surface and then decreases as depicted in graph (b).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If escape velocity on earth surface is $11.1 \mathrm{kmh}^{-1}$, then find the escape velocity on moon surface. If mass of moon is $\frac{1}{81}$ times of mass of earth and radius of moon is $\frac{1}{4}$ times radius of earth.
questions.solution:
Given, Escape velocity on the surface of the earth is given by i.e. $v_\rho=\sqrt{2 g R_e}$
Mass of the moon, $M_m=\frac{M_e}{81}$ Radius of the moon, $R_m=\frac{R_e}{4}\therefore$ Escape velocity on the surface of the moon $v_m=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M_m}{R_m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G\left(\frac{M e}{81}\right)}{\frac{R_e}{4}}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{9} \sqrt{\frac{G M_e}{R_e}}$ From Eq. (i), $=\frac{2}{9} \sqrt{\frac{2 G M_e}{R_e}}=\frac{2}{9} v_e$ Escape velocity $v_e=11.1 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}=\frac{2}{9} \times 11.1=2.46 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An uniform sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ exerts a force of $F$ on a small mass $m$ placed at a distance of 3R from the centre of the sphere. A spherical portion of diameter $R$ is cut from the sphere as shown in the fig. The force of attraction between the remaining part of the disc and the mass $\mathrm{m}$ is
questions.solution:
The force exerted by the original sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ on a mass $m$ at a distance $d = 3R$ from its center is given by $F = \dfrac{GMm}{(3R)^2} = \dfrac{GMm}{9R^2}$.

The mass of the original sphere is $M = \rho \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3$, where $\rho$ is the density. The spherical portion cut out has a radius $r = R/2$. Its mass $M'$ is $M' = \rho \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi (R/2)^3 = \rho \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi \dfrac{R^3}{8} = \dfrac{M}{8}$.

The center of the cut-out sphere is at a distance $x = R/2$ from the center of the original sphere. The mass $m$ is at a distance $d = 3R$ from the center of the original sphere. The distance of $m$ from the center of the cut-out sphere is $d' = 3R - R/2 = 2.5R = \dfrac{5R}{2}$.

The force exerted by the cut-out portion on $m$ is $F' = \dfrac{GM'm}{(d')^2} = \dfrac{G(M/8)m}{(5R/2)^2} = \dfrac{GMm}{8 \times (25R^2/4)} = \dfrac{GMm}{50R^2}$.

Expressing $F'$ in terms of $F$: Since $F = \dfrac{GMm}{9R^2}$, we have $\dfrac{GMm}{R^2} = 9F$. Substituting this into the expression for $F'$, we get $F' = \dfrac{9F}{50}$.

The force exerted by the remaining part is $F_{rem} = F - F' = F - \dfrac{9F}{50} = \dfrac{41F}{50}$.

Answer: 41F/50

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity at a height of $7 \mathrm{~km}$ above the earth is the same as at a depth d below the surface of the earth. Then d is
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the earth is given by $g_h = g \left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface and $R$ is the radius of the earth.

The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ below the surface of the earth is given by $g_d = g \left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$.

Given that $g_h = g_d$, we equate the two expressions:

$g \left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) = g \left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$

$1 - \dfrac{2h}{R} = 1 - \dfrac{d}{R}$

$\dfrac{2h}{R} = \dfrac{d}{R}$

$d = 2h$

Given $h = 7 \text{ km}$, we have $d = 2 \times 7 \text{ km} = 14 \text{ km}$.

Answer: 14 km

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If escape velocity on earth surface is $11.1 \mathrm{~kmh}^{-1}$, then find the escape velocity on moon surface. If mass of moon is $\dfrac{1}{81}$ times of mass of earth and radius of moon is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ times radius of earth.
questions.solution:
The escape velocity $v_e$ from the surface of a planet is given by the formula $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, where $M$ is the mass of the planet and $R$ is its radius.

Let $M_e$ and $R_e$ be the mass and radius of the Earth, and $M_m$ and $R_m$ be the mass and radius of the Moon. Given $M_m = \dfrac{M_e}{81}$ and $R_m = \dfrac{R_e}{4}$.

The escape velocity on the Moon $v_m$ is given by $v_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_m}{R_m}}$.

Substituting the given ratios into the expression for $v_m$:

$v_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G(M_e/81)}{R_e/4}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_e}{R_e} \times \dfrac{4}{81}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_e}{R_e}} \times \sqrt{\dfrac{4}{81}}$.

Since $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_e}{R_e}} = 11.1 \text{ km/h}$, we have $v_m = 11.1 \times \dfrac{2}{9}$.

$v_m = 11.1 \times 0.2222... = 2.4666... \text{ km/h}$.

Rounding to two decimal places, $v_m \approx 2.47 \text{ km/h}$.

Answer: $2.47 \mathrm{~kmh}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Starting from the centre of the earth having radius $R$, the variation of $g$ (acceleration due to gravity) is shown by
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity $g$ at a distance $r$ from the centre of the Earth is given by two different expressions depending on whether the point is inside or outside the Earth.

For $r \lt R$ (inside the Earth), assuming uniform density, the acceleration due to gravity is given by $g_{in} = \dfrac{GMr}{R^3}$. This shows that $g$ is directly proportional to $r$, i.e., $g \propto r$. The graph is a straight line passing through the origin with a positive slope.

For $r \ge R$ (outside the Earth), the acceleration due to gravity is given by $g_{out} = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$. This shows that $g$ is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, i.e., $g \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$. The graph is a curve that decreases as $r$ increases.

At the surface of the Earth ($r = R$), both expressions yield the same value $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, which is the maximum value of $g$.

Combining these, the graph starts from the origin, increases linearly until $r = R$, and then decreases following an inverse-square law for $r \gt R$. This matches the fourth graph provided in the options.

Answer:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The height vertically above the earth's surface at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $1 \%$ of its value at the surface is
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the earth is given by the formula $g_h = g \left( \dfrac{R}{R+h} \right)^2$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface and $R$ is the radius of the earth.

Given that $g_h = 1 \% \text{ of } g$, we have $g_h = \dfrac{1}{100} g$.

Substituting this into the formula:

$\dfrac{1}{100} g = g \left( \dfrac{R}{R+h} \right)^2$

$\dfrac{1}{100} = \left( \dfrac{R}{R+h} \right)^2$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{R}{R+h}$

$R + h = 10R$

$h = 9R$

Answer: 9R

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the earth were to spin faster, acceleration due to gravity at the poles
options: depends on how fast it spins
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity $g'$ at a latitude $\lambda$ is given by the formula $g' = g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} \lambda$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the poles (or in the absence of rotation), $\omega$ is the angular velocity of the earth, and $R$ is the radius of the earth.

At the poles, the latitude $\lambda = 90^{\circ}$.

Substituting $\lambda = 90^{\circ}$ into the formula, we get $\cos 90^{\circ} = 0$, so $g' = g - \omega^{2} R (0)^{2} = g$.

Since the term involving $\omega$ becomes zero at the poles, the acceleration due to gravity at the poles is independent of the angular velocity of the earth's rotation. Therefore, if the earth were to spin faster, the acceleration due to gravity at the poles remains the same.

Answer: remains the same

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The height at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $\dfrac{g}{16}$ (where, $g=$ acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth) in terms of $R$ is, if $R$ is the radius of earth.
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the earth is given by the formula $g_h = g \left( \dfrac{R}{R + h} \right)^2$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface and $R$ is the radius of the earth.

Given that $g_h = \dfrac{g}{16}$, we substitute this into the equation:

$\dfrac{g}{16} = g \left( \dfrac{R}{R + h} \right)^2$

Dividing both sides by $g$ and taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{R}{R + h}$

Cross-multiplying gives:

$R + h = 4R$

$h = 3R$

Answer: $3 R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The escape velocity of a projectile on the earth's surface is $11.2 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$. A body is projected out with thrice this speed. The speed of the body far away from the earth will be
questions.solution:
Let $v_e$ be the escape velocity on the earth's surface, where $v_e = 11.2 \text{ km/s}$. The energy conservation principle states that the total energy at the surface equals the total energy at infinity.

The initial velocity of the body is $v = 3v_e$. The total energy at the surface is $E_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2}m(3v_e)^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R}$.

Since $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, we have $\dfrac{GM}{R} = \dfrac{v_e^2}{2}$. Substituting this into the energy equation:

$E_i = \dfrac{1}{2}m(9v_e^2) - m\left(\dfrac{v_e^2}{2}\right) = \dfrac{9}{2}mv_e^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2 = 4mv_e^2$.

At a large distance from the earth, the potential energy is zero. Let $v_f$ be the final velocity at infinity. The total energy is $E_f = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2$.

Equating $E_i = E_f$:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2 = 4mv_e^2 \Rightarrow v_f^2 = 8v_e^2 \Rightarrow v_f = v_e \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}v_e$.

Substituting $v_e = 11.2 \text{ km/s}$:

$v_f = 2 \times 1.414 \times 11.2 \text{ km/s} = 2.828 \times 11.2 \text{ km/s} \approx 31.67 \text{ km/s}$.

Rounding to the nearest value, we get $31.7 \text{ km/s}$.

Answer: $31.7 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Kepler's second law of planetary motion corresponds to
questions.solution:
Kepler's second law states that the radius vector joining a planet to the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.

The area swept by the radius vector in a small time interval $dt$ is given by $dA = \dfrac{1}{2} |\vec{r} \times d\vec{r}|$.

Since $d\vec{r} = \vec{v} dt$, the rate of area sweeping is $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2} |\vec{r} \times \vec{v}|$.

Multiplying and dividing by the mass of the planet $m$, we get $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2m} |\vec{r} \times m\vec{v}| = \dfrac{L}{2m}$, where $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$ is the angular momentum of the planet.

Since the gravitational force exerted by the sun on the planet is a central force, the torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = 0$.

Because $\vec{\tau} = \dfrac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = 0$, the angular momentum $\vec{L}$ remains constant.

Therefore, $\dfrac{dA}{dt}$ is constant, which confirms that Kepler's second law is a direct consequence of the conservation of angular momentum.

Answer: conservation of angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A constant potential energy of a satellite is given as

\mathrm{PE}=r(\mathrm{KE})

where, $\mathrm{PE}=$ potential energy
and $\mathrm{KE}=$ kinetic energy.
The value of $r$ will be
questions.solution:
For a satellite orbiting a planet of mass $M$ at a distance $R$ with orbital speed $v$, the gravitational potential energy is given by $PE = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}$.

The kinetic energy of the satellite is given by $KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. Since the centripetal force is provided by the gravitational force, we have $\dfrac{mv^2}{R} = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2}$, which implies $mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{R}$.

Substituting this into the expression for kinetic energy, we get $KE = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{GMm}{R} \right) = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$.

Comparing the expressions for potential energy and kinetic energy, we observe that $PE = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}$ and $KE = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$.

Therefore, $PE = -2 \times \left( \dfrac{GMm}{2R} \right) = -2(KE)$.

Given the relation $PE = r(KE)$, we find that $r = -2$.

Answer: $-2$

questions.q: A stone weight $100 \mathrm{~N}$ on the surface of the earth. The ratio of its weight at a height of half the radius of the earth to a depth of half the radius of the earth will be approximately
questions.solution:
Weight of stone at the surface of the earth, $w=100 \mathrm{~N}$ At height $h$ from the surface of earth, gravitational acceleration,

g_{h}=\frac{g}{\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)^{2}}

At depth $d$ from the surface of the earth, gravitational acceleration,

g_{d}=g\left(1-\frac{d}{R}\right)

According to question,
$\frac{\text { Weight at } h=R / 2}{\text { Weight at } d=R / 2}=\frac{m_{h}(\text { at } h=R / 2)}{m g_{d}(\text { at } h=R / 2)}=\frac{\frac{g}{\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)^{2}}(\text { at } h=R / 2)}{g\left(1-\frac{d}{R}\right) \text { at }(d=R / 2)}=\frac{\frac{1}{\left(1+\frac{R / 2}{R}\right)^{2}}}{1-\frac{R / 2}{R}}=\frac{4 / 9}{1 / 2}=\frac{8}{9}=0.9$

questions.q: The gravitational field strength at the surface of a certain planet is $g$. Which of the following is the gravitational field strength at the surface of a planet with twice the radius and twice the mass?
questions.solution:
At the surface of the planet, gravitational acceleration,

\begin{aligned}
\qquad g=\frac{G M}{R^{2}} \quad \text{...(i)} \\
\text { where, } M &=\text { mass of the planet } \\
R &=\text { radius of the planet. } \\
\text { When } M^{\prime} &=2 M \text { and } R^{\prime}=2 R \text {, then } \\
\qquad g^{\prime} &=\frac{G M^{\prime}}{R^{2}} \\
&=\frac{G \cdot 2 M}{(2 R)^{2}}=\frac{G M}{2 R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot g \quad \text{[from Eq. (i)]}\\
\end{aligned}

$\Rightarrow \quad g^{\prime}=\frac{g}{2}$

questions.solution:
The given situation is shown below

$a_{\max }=1.4 \times 10^{12} \mathrm{~m}a_{\min }=7 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~m}$ The velocity of the comet is maximum, when it is nearest to the sun and minimum when it is farthest from the sun. $\therefore \quad v_{\max }=6 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Applying the law of conservation of angular momentum at points $A$ and $B$, we get \begin{aligned} &m v_{\min } a_{\max }=m v_{\max } a_{\min } \quad(\quad L=m v r) \\ &\Rightarrow \quad v_{\min }=\frac{v_{\max } \times a_{\min }}{a_{\max }} \\ &=\frac{6 \times 10^{14} \times 7 \times 10^{10}}{1.4 \times 10^{12}} \\ &=3 \times 10^{13} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} \end{aligned} No option is correct.

Let $v_{m}$ be escape velocity from moon and $v_{e}$ be the escape velocity from Earth. Then,
$\frac{v_{m}}{v_{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times g_{m} \times R_{m}}{2 \times g_{e} \times R_{e}}}=\sqrt{\frac{g_{m} \times D_{m}}{g_{e} \times D_{e}}} \quad {(\because D=2 R)}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{g_{e}}{6} \times \frac{D_{e}}{4}}{g_{e} D_{e}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{24}}\therefore \quad v_{m}=\frac{v_{e}}{\sqrt{24}}=\frac{11.2}{\sqrt{24}} \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s} \quad\left(\because v_{e}=11.2 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel of volume $27 \times 10^4$ cc, contains a mixture of Hydrogen (molar mass $= 2\ g\ mol^{-1}$) and oxygen (molar mass $= 32\ g\ mol^{-1}$) gas at standard temperature and pressure. If the mass of hydrogen is 16 g, find the mass of oxygen gas contained in the vessel.
questions.solution:
Volume of the vessel, $V = 27 \times 10^4$ cc $= 270$ L

At STP, the volume of $1$ mole of an ideal gas is $22.4$ L.

Total number of moles in the mixture, $n = \dfrac{270}{22.4} \approx 12.054$

Number of moles of hydrogen, $n_{H_2} = \dfrac{16}{2} = 8$

Number of moles of oxygen, $n_{O_2} = n - n_{H_2} = 12.054 - 8 = 4.054$

Mass of oxygen, $m_{O_2} = n_{O_2} \times 32 = 4.054 \times 32 \approx 129.7$ g

Answer: $129.7$ g

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Find the mass of oxygen gas with which $1.882 \times 10^{23}$ degrees of freedom are associated at N.T.P.
Given: Molar mass of diatomic gas, oxygen is $32\ g\ mol^{-1}$ and oxygen molecule possess three translational and two rotational degrees of freedom.
questions.solution:
Total degrees of freedom of the gas = $1.882 \times 10^{23}$

Degrees of freedom per oxygen molecule = $3$ (translational) + $2$ (rotational) = $5$

Number of oxygen molecules = $\dfrac{1.882 \times 10^{23}}{5} = 0.3764 \times 10^{23}$

Number of moles of oxygen gas = $\dfrac{0.3764 \times 10^{23}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} = 0.0625$

Mass of oxygen gas = $0.0625 \times 32 = 2$ g

Answer: $2$g

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas has molar specific heat $\dfrac{5R}{2}$ at constant pressure. If 1662 J of heat brings about 50 K temperature change, the number of moles of gas is
questions.solution:
Given the molar specific heat at constant pressure, $C_p = \dfrac{5R}{2}$

The heat supplied at constant pressure is given by:

$Q = n C_p \Delta T$

Substituting the given values ($Q = 1662$ J, $\Delta T = 50$ K, and $R = 8.31$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$):

$1662 = n \left(\dfrac{5 \times 8.31}{2}\right) \times 50$

$1662 = n \times 125 \times 8.31$

$1662 = n \times 1038.75$

$n = \dfrac{1662}{1038.75} = 1.6$

Answer: $1.6$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas bubble of volume $2 \mathrm{~cm}^3$ rises from the bottom of a pond of depth 10 m at $17^0 \mathrm{C}$. What will be the volume of the bubble when it reaches the surface of the pond? Atmospheric temperature is $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the pressure at the bottom of the pond is double that of the pressure at the surface.
questions.solution:
Let $P_1$ and $V_1$ be the pressure and volume at the bottom of the pond, and $P_2$ and $V_2$ be the pressure and volume at the surface. Given $V_1 = 2 \text{ cm}^3$.

The temperature at the bottom is $T_1 = 17 + 273 = 290 \text{ K}$. The temperature at the surface is $T_2 = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$.

The pressure at the bottom is given as double the atmospheric pressure, so $P_1 = 2P_2$.

Using the ideal gas law in the form $\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$, we substitute the known values:

$\dfrac{2P_2 \times 2}{290} = \dfrac{P_2 \times V_2}{300}$

Canceling $P_2$ from both sides:

$\dfrac{4}{290} = \dfrac{V_2}{300}$

$V_2 = \dfrac{4 \times 300}{290} = \dfrac{1200}{290} \approx 4.137 \text{ cm}^3$.

Rounding to the nearest value provided in the options, we get $4.1 \text{ cm}^3$.

Answer: $4.1 \mathrm{~cm}^3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the ratio of the mean free paths of the molecules of two gases $A$ and $B$ having the molecular diameters $2 \mathrm{~A}^0$ and $3 \mathrm{~A}^0$ respectively under the identical conditions of pressure, temperature and volume?
questions.solution:
The mean free path $\lambda$ of a gas molecule is given by the formula $\lambda = \dfrac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 P}$, where $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ is the temperature, $d$ is the molecular diameter, and $P$ is the pressure.

Under identical conditions of pressure, temperature, and volume, the variables $k_B$, $T$, and $P$ are constant for both gases $A$ and $B$.

Therefore, the mean free path is inversely proportional to the square of the molecular diameter: $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}$.

Given the diameters $d_A = 2 \text{ \AA}$ and $d_B = 3 \text{ \AA}$, the ratio of the mean free paths is:

$\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = \dfrac{d_B^2}{d_A^2} = \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{4}$.

Thus, $\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = 9:4$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B}=9: 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The rms velocity of the gas molecule at $327^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is same as the rms velocity of the oxygen molecules at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the molecular weight of oxygen is 32 then the molecular weight of the given gas molecule is:
questions.solution:
The root mean square velocity of a gas is given by the formula $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$, where $R$ is the universal gas constant, $T$ is the absolute temperature in Kelvin, and $M$ is the molar mass of the gas.

Given that the rms velocity of the gas at $T_1 = 327^{\circ}C$ is equal to the rms velocity of oxygen at $T_2 = 27^{\circ}C$, we have:

$\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT_1}{M_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT_2}{M_2}}$

Squaring both sides and simplifying, we get:

$\dfrac{T_1}{M_1} = \dfrac{T_2}{M_2}$

Convert the temperatures to Kelvin:

$T_1 = 327 + 273 = 600 \text{ K}$

$T_2 = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$

The molar mass of oxygen $M_2 = 32$. Substituting the values into the equation:

$\dfrac{600}{M_1} = \dfrac{300}{32}$

$M_1 = \dfrac{600 \times 32}{300}$

$M_1 = 2 \times 32 = 64$

Answer: $64$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The total number of degrees of freedom associated with $2 \mathrm{~cm}^3$ of Nitrogen gas at normal temperature and pressure is:
[Given Avogadro number as ' N ' ]
questions.solution:
At normal temperature and pressure (NTP), the molar volume of an ideal gas is $22400 \text{ cm}^3$.

The number of moles $n$ in $2 \text{ cm}^3$ of Nitrogen gas is given by $n = \dfrac{V}{V_{m}} = \dfrac{2}{22400} = \dfrac{1}{11200}$ moles.

Nitrogen ($N_2$) is a diatomic gas. The degrees of freedom $f$ for a diatomic molecule at room temperature is $5$ (3 translational and 2 rotational).

The total number of molecules $N_{total}$ is $n \times N$, where $N$ is the Avogadro number. Thus, $N_{total} = \dfrac{N}{11200}$.

The total degrees of freedom is given by $f \times N_{total} = 5 \times \dfrac{N}{11200} = \dfrac{N}{2240}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{N}{2240}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The mean energy per molecule for a diatomic gas is:
questions.solution:
A diatomic gas molecule at moderate temperatures possesses 5 degrees of freedom: 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom.

According to the law of equipartition of energy, each degree of freedom contributes $\dfrac{1}{2} K_{B} T$ to the average energy of the molecule.

The total mean energy per molecule $E$ is given by the sum of the energies associated with each degree of freedom:

$E = f \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2} K_{B} T\right)$

Substituting $f = 5$ for a diatomic gas:

$E = 5 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2} K_{B} T\right) = \dfrac{5}{2} K_{B} T$

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right) \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cubical box of side $2 \mathrm{~m}$ contains helium gas. It was observed that in a time of 1 second, an atom travelling with the root-mean-square speed parallel to one of the edges of the cube, made 250 hits with one of the walls, without any collision with other atoms. The average kinetic energy of the helium gas is Take $R=\dfrac{25}{3} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{mol}-\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{kB}=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{JK}{ }^{-1}$
questions.solution:
The side length of the cubical box is $L = 2 \text{ m}$.

An atom travelling with root-mean-square speed $v_{rms}$ parallel to one of the edges makes 250 hits in 1 second. The distance covered by the atom between two consecutive hits on the same wall is $2L$.

The time taken for one round trip is $\Delta t = \dfrac{2L}{v_{rms}}$.

The number of hits per second is $n = \dfrac{1}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v_{rms}}{2L}$.

Given $n = 250 \text{ s}^{-1}$ and $L = 2 \text{ m}$, we have $250 = \dfrac{v_{rms}}{2 \times 2} = \dfrac{v_{rms}}{4}$.

$v_{rms} = 250 \times 4 = 1000 \text{ m/s}$.

The average kinetic energy of a single helium atom is $K_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_{rms}^2$.

The molar mass of helium is $M = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg/mol}$. The mass of one atom is $m = \dfrac{M}{N_A} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \text{ kg}$.

Alternatively, using $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3k_B T}{m}}$, we have $v_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{3k_B T}{m}$, so $\dfrac{1}{2} m v_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{3}{2} k_B T$.

From $v_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{3RT}{M}$, we get $T = \dfrac{M v_{rms}^2}{3R} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-3} \times (1000)^2}{3 \times (25/3)} = \dfrac{4000}{25} = 160 \text{ K}$.

The average kinetic energy per atom is $K_{avg} = \dfrac{3}{2} k_B T = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 160$.

$K_{avg} = 1.5 \times 1.38 \times 160 \times 10^{-23} = 331.2 \times 10^{-23} = 3.312 \times 10^{-21} \text{ J}$.

Answer: $3.31 \times 10^{-21} \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If pressure of an ideal gas is increased by keeping temperature constant the kinetic energy will
questions.solution:
The average kinetic energy of an ideal gas molecule is given by the formula $K.E. = \dfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T$, where $k_{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature of the gas.

Since the temperature $T$ is kept constant, the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules depends only on the temperature and remains independent of the pressure or volume of the gas.

Therefore, when the pressure of an ideal gas is increased at a constant temperature, the kinetic energy of the gas does not change.

Answer: Not change

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Internal energy of $\mathrm{n}_1$ moles of hydrogen at temperature T is equal to internal energy of $\mathrm{m}_2$ moles of helium at temperature 2T. The ratio $\dfrac{n_1}{n_2}$ is
questions.solution:
The internal energy $U$ of an ideal gas is given by $U = n C_V T$, where $n$ is the number of moles, $C_V$ is the molar heat capacity at constant volume, and $T$ is the temperature.

For hydrogen ($H_2$), which is a diatomic gas, the degrees of freedom $f = 5$. Thus, $C_{V, H_2} = \dfrac{f}{2} R = \dfrac{5}{2} R$. The internal energy is $U_1 = n_1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} R \times T$.

For helium ($He$), which is a monatomic gas, the degrees of freedom $f = 3$. Thus, $C_{V, He} = \dfrac{f}{2} R = \dfrac{3}{2} R$. The internal energy is $U_2 = n_2 \times \dfrac{3}{2} R \times (2T)$.

Equating the internal energies $U_1 = U_2$:

$n_1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} R \times T = n_2 \times \dfrac{3}{2} R \times 2T$

Simplifying the equation by cancelling $R$ and $T$ from both sides:

$n_1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} = n_2 \times 3$

Rearranging to find the ratio $\dfrac{n_1}{n_2}$:

$\dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{3}{5/2} = \dfrac{3 \times 2}{5} = \dfrac{6}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{6}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cubical box of side $1 \mathrm{~m}$ contains Boron gas at a pressure of $100 \mathrm{~Nm}^{-2}$. During an observation time of 1 second, an atom travelling with the rms speed parallel to one of the edges of the cube, was found to make 500 hits with a particular wall, without any collision with other atoms. The total mass of gas in the box in gram is
questions.solution:
The side length of the cubical box is $L = 1 \text{ m}$. The volume of the box is $V = L^3 = 1 \text{ m}^3$.

An atom travels with rms speed $v_{rms}$ parallel to an edge. In 1 second, it makes 500 hits on a wall. Since it travels back and forth between two opposite walls, the distance covered in one round trip is $2L = 2 \text{ m}$. The number of hits in 1 second is $N = 500$. The time taken for one round trip is $t = \dfrac{2L}{v_{rms}}$. The number of hits per second is $\dfrac{1}{t} = \dfrac{v_{rms}}{2L}$.

Given $\dfrac{v_{rms}}{2L} = 500$, we have $v_{rms} = 500 \times 2 \times 1 = 1000 \text{ m/s}$.

The pressure of an ideal gas is given by $P = \dfrac{1}{3} \rho v_{rms}^2$, where $\rho = \dfrac{M}{V}$ is the density and $M$ is the total mass of the gas.

Substituting the given values: $100 = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{M}{1} \times (1000)^2$.

$100 = \dfrac{M \times 10^6}{3} \Rightarrow M = \dfrac{300}{10^6} = 3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg}$.

Converting the mass to grams: $M = 3 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^3 \text{ g} = 0.3 \text{ g}$.

Answer: 0.3

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The molecules of a given mass of a gas have root mean square speed of $120 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ at $88^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 1 atmospheric pressure. The root mean square speed of the molecules at $127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and 2 atmospheric pressure is
questions.solution:
The root mean square speed $v_{rms}$ of gas molecules is given by the formula $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$.

From this formula, it is evident that $v_{rms}$ depends only on the temperature $T$ and the molar mass $M$ of the gas. It is independent of the pressure $P$ of the gas.

Given $v_{rms,1} = 120 \text{ m/s}$ at $T_1 = 88^{\circ}\text{C} = 88 + 273 = 361 \text{ K}$.

We need to find $v_{rms,2}$ at $T_2 = 127^{\circ}\text{C} = 127 + 273 = 400 \text{ K}$.

Taking the ratio of the two speeds:

$\dfrac{v_{rms,2}}{v_{rms,1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}$

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{v_{rms,2}}{120} = \sqrt{\dfrac{400}{361}}$

$\dfrac{v_{rms,2}}{120} = \dfrac{20}{19}$

$v_{rms,2} = 120 \times \dfrac{20}{19} = \dfrac{2400}{19} \approx 126.315 \text{ m/s}$.

Answer: 126.3 m/s

questions.q: The gases carbon monoxide $(\mathrm{CO})$ and nitrogen at the same temperature have kinetic energies $E_1$ and $E_2$, respectively. Then,
questions.solution:
The average kinetic energy of a gas molecule is given by the formula $E = \dfrac{3}{2} k_B T$, where $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature of the gas.

Since both carbon monoxide (CO) and nitrogen ($N_2$) are at the same temperature $T$, the kinetic energy depends only on the temperature and the Boltzmann constant.

Therefore, $E_1 = \dfrac{3}{2} k_B T$ and $E_2 = \dfrac{3}{2} k_B T$.

Comparing the two expressions, we find $E_1 = E_2$.

Answer: $E_1=E_2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The mean energy per molecule for a diatomic gas is
questions.solution:
A diatomic gas molecule at a temperature $T$ possesses degrees of freedom associated with its motion. For a rigid diatomic molecule, there are 3 translational degrees of freedom and 2 rotational degrees of freedom, totaling 5 degrees of freedom ($f = 5$).

According to the law of equipartition of energy, each degree of freedom contributes $\dfrac{1}{2} k_B T$ to the average energy of a molecule.

Therefore, the mean energy per molecule $E$ is given by $E = f \times \dfrac{1}{2} k_B T$.

Substituting $f = 5$, we get $E = 5 \times \dfrac{1}{2} k_B T = \dfrac{5 k_B T}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{5 k_B T}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The average kinetic energy of a molecule in air at room temperature of $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
questions.solution:
The average kinetic energy of a molecule is given by the formula $K_{avg} = \dfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T$, where $k_{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature in Kelvin.

Given temperature $T = 20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} = 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 \mathrm{~K}$.

The Boltzmann constant $k_{B} \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J/K}$.

Substituting the values into the formula:

$K_{avg} = \dfrac{3}{2} \times (1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J/K}) \times 293.15 \mathrm{~K}$

$K_{avg} = 1.5 \times 1.38 \times 293.15 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J}$

$K_{avg} = 2.07 \times 293.15 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J}$

$K_{avg} \approx 606.82 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J}$

$K_{avg} \approx 6.0682 \times 10^{-21} \mathrm{~J}$

Rounding to three significant figures, we get $6.07 \times 10^{-21} \mathrm{~J}$.

Answer: $6.07 \times 10^{-21} \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following is not a green house gas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is (3) $N_2$.

$N_2$ makes up about 78% of the Earth's atmosphere but is not a greenhouse gas. Being a symmetrical diatomic molecule (two identical atoms), it does not absorb infrared radiation radiating from the Earth's surface.

In contrast, $CO_2$, $CH_4$, and $N_2O$ have asymmetric molecular structures that allow them to absorb and trap heat in the atmosphere.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The collision of the molecules of an ideal gas is taken as
questions.solution:
In the kinetic theory of gases, the molecules of an ideal gas are assumed to be point masses that do not exert any intermolecular forces of attraction or repulsion on each other, except during collisions.

The collisions between these molecules are assumed to be perfectly elastic, meaning that both the total kinetic energy and the total linear momentum of the system are conserved during the collision process.

Answer: elastic

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The average energy associated with a monoatomic molecule is
questions.solution:
A monoatomic gas molecule has 3 degrees of freedom ($f = 3$) corresponding to its translational motion along the $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes.

According to the law of equipartition of energy, each degree of freedom contributes $\dfrac{1}{2} K_{B} T$ to the average kinetic energy of the molecule.

Therefore, the total average energy $E$ is given by $E = f \times \dfrac{1}{2} K_{B} T = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{2} K_{B} T = \dfrac{3}{2} K_{B} T$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{2} K_{B} T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Equal volumes of two gases, having their densities in the ratio of $1: 16$ exert equal pressures on the walls of two containers. The ratio of their rms velocities $\left(\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}\right)$
questions.solution:
Densities ratio of two gases,

\rho_{1}: \rho_{2}=1: 16

\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\rho_{1}}{\rho_{2}}=\frac{1}{16}

Since, pressure of both gases are equal.
$\therefore \quad p_{1}=p_{\mathrm{g}}\frac{1}{3} \rho_{1} c_{1}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \rho_{2} c_{2}^{2}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{c_{1}^{2}}{c_{2}^{2}}=\frac{\rho_{2}}{\rho_{1}}=\frac{16}{1}=\left(\frac{4}{1}\right)^{2}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}=\frac{4}{1}\Rightarrow \quad c_{1}: c_{2}=4: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gaseous mixture consists of $16 \mathrm{~g}$ of helium and $16 \mathrm{~g}$ of oxygen. The ratio $C_{p} / C_{V}$ of the mixture is
questions.solution:
Mass of helium, $m_{1}=16 \mathrm{~g}$
Mass of oxygen, $m_{2}=16 \mathrm{~g}\therefore$ Number of moles of He gas,

n_{1}=\frac{m_{1}}{4}=\frac{16}{4}=4

Number of moles of $\mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{gas}$,

n_{2}=\frac{m_{2}}{32}=\frac{16}{32}=\frac{1}{2}

We know that for the mixture,
$\begin{aligned} C_{V} &=\frac{n_{1} C_{V}+n_{2} C_{V_{2}}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}, \text { where } C_{V}=\frac{f R}{2} \\ \text { and } C_{p} &=\frac{n_{1} C_{p_{1}}+n_{2} C_{p_{2}}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}, \text { where } C_{p}=\left(\frac{f}{2}+1\right) R \end{aligned}$
For He gas, $f=3, n_{1}=4$
For $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ gas, $f=5, n_{2}=\frac{1}{2}$
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}} &=\frac{n_{1} C_{p_{1}}+n_{2} C_{p_{2}}}{n_{1} C_{V_{1}}+n_{2} C_{V_{2}}} \\
&=\frac{4 \times\left(\frac{3}{2}+1\right) R+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{5}{2}+1\right) R}{4 \times \frac{3}{2} R+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{5}{2} R} \\
&=\frac{\left(4 \times \frac{5}{2} R\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{7}{2} R\right)}{\left(4 \times \frac{3}{2} R\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{5}{2} R\right)}=\frac{47}{29} \\
&=1.62
\end{aligned}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of metal, of 25g mass moves down without acceleration when the plane is inclined at an angle of $30^\circ$. When the inclination is increased by $30^\circ$, find the downward acceleration of the block.
questions.solution:
When the block moves down without acceleration at an angle $\theta = 30^\circ$, the net force is zero.

$mg \sin 30^\circ = \mu_k mg \cos 30^\circ$

$\mu_k = \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

When the inclination is increased by $30^\circ$, the new angle is $\theta' = 60^\circ$.

The downward acceleration $a$ is given by:

$ma = mg \sin 60^\circ - \mu_k mg \cos 60^\circ$

$a = g \left( \sin 60^\circ - \mu_k \cos 60^\circ \right)$

Substituting the values of $\mu_k$ and $g = 9.8\ ms^{-2}$:

$a = 9.8 \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \right)$

$a = 9.8 \left( \dfrac{3 - 1}{2\sqrt{3}} \right) = \dfrac{9.8}{\sqrt{3}}$

$a = \dfrac{9.8}{1.732} \approx 5.66\ ms^{-2}$

Answer: $5.66\ ms^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the maximum speed with which a vehicle can take the turn on a curved frictionless smooth road of width 4 m , without skidding, if the radius of the circular curve of the road is 9 m and the outer edge of the road above the inner edge is 40 cm high? [given $g=\mathrm{1 0} \mathrm{ms}^{-2}$ ]
questions.solution:
For a vehicle moving on a banked road without skidding, the required centripetal force is provided by the horizontal component of the normal reaction. The angle of banking $\theta$ is given by $\tan \theta = \dfrac{h}{b}$, where $h$ is the height of the outer edge above the inner edge and $b$ is the width of the road.

Given $h = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$ and $b = 4 \text{ m}$, we have $\tan \theta = \dfrac{0.4}{4} = 0.1$.

The maximum speed $v$ for a banked road without friction is given by $v = \sqrt{rg \tan \theta}$, where $r$ is the radius of the curve and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Substituting the given values $r = 9 \text{ m}$, $g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$, and $\tan \theta = 0.1$:

$v = \sqrt{9 \times 10 \times 0.1} = \sqrt{9} = 3 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{3} \mathrm{ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Pick out the weakest force from the four given fundamental forces in nature.
questions.solution:
The four fundamental forces in nature are the strong nuclear force, the electromagnetic force, the weak nuclear force, and the gravitational force.

The relative strengths of these forces are typically compared by considering the interaction between two protons at a distance of $10^{-15}$ m. The strong nuclear force is the strongest, followed by the electromagnetic force, then the weak nuclear force, and finally the gravitational force.

The gravitational force is the weakest among the four fundamental forces, as its coupling constant is extremely small compared to the others.

Answer: Gravitational force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass 125 kg just slides down a rough inclined plane that rises 1 m in every 2 m. What is the angle of friction?
questions.solution:
The plane rises 1 m in every 2 m, so:

$\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = 30°$

When a body just slides down, it is at limiting equilibrium, so angle of friction $\phi =$ angle of inclination $\theta$.

$\phi = 30° = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radians

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coin is placed on a disc rotating with an angular velocity $\omega$. The co-efficient of friction between the disc and the coin is $\mu$. The maximum distance of the coin from the centre of the disc up to which it will rotate with the disc is
questions.solution:
For the coin to rotate with the disc without slipping, the centripetal force required for circular motion must be provided by the static frictional force.

Let $m$ be the mass of the coin, $r$ be the distance from the centre, and $\omega$ be the angular velocity. The centripetal force is $F_c = m \omega^2 r$.

The maximum static frictional force available is $f_{max} = \mu N$, where $N = mg$ is the normal force. Thus, $f_{max} = \mu mg$.

For the coin to remain stationary relative to the disc, the condition is $F_c \le f_{max}$.

$m \omega^2 r \le \mu mg$.

Solving for the maximum distance $r$, we get $r \le \dfrac{\mu g}{\omega^2}$.

Therefore, the maximum distance is $r_{max} = \dfrac{\mu g}{\omega^2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu g}{\omega^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass 10 kg is moving up on an inclined plane of $30^{\circ}$ with an acceleration $2 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$. Find the force required, if the coefficient of friction between the object and the plane surface is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$, [given $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$ ].
questions.solution:
The forces acting on the body of mass $m = 10$ kg moving up the inclined plane are the applied force $F$ (acting up the plane), the component of gravitational force $mg \sin \theta$ (acting down the plane), and the frictional force $f_k$ (acting down the plane).

The equation of motion is $F - mg \sin \theta - f_k = ma$.

The normal force $N$ exerted by the plane is $N = mg \cos \theta$.

The frictional force is $f_k = \mu N = \mu mg \cos \theta$.

Given $m = 10$ kg, $g = 10$ ms$^{-2}$, $\theta = 30^{\circ}$, $a = 2$ ms$^{-2}$, and $\mu = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$.

Calculating the components:
$mg \sin 30^{\circ} = 10 \times 10 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 50$ N.
$f_k = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6} \times 10 \times 10 \times \cos 30^{\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6} \times 100 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{3 \times 100}{12} = \dfrac{300}{12} = 25$ N.

Substituting these values into the equation of motion:
$F - 50 - 25 = 10 \times 2$
$F - 75 = 20$
$F = 95$ N.

Answer: 95 N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If no external force acts on particle, then Which of the following statements is incorrect about particle?
options: Particle moves with uniform velocity on linear path.
Particle moves with uniform speed on circle.
questions.solution: The statement given in option (3) is incorrect and it can be corrected as, When particle moves in a circle even with uniform or constant speed, it faces an external force towards its centre called centripetal force.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block slides on rough horizontal surface with a velocity of $20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. It comes to rest after travelling a distance of 80 m . The coefficient of kinetic friction between block and surface is (Take, $\left.g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$
questions.solution:
Friction force, $F=\mu N$
and acceleration, $a=\frac{-F}{m}=-\frac{\mu m g}{m}$
$a=-\mu g=-10 \mu$
Using third equation of motion,
$\begin{array}{ll}
& v^2=u^2+2 a s \\
\text { or } & 0^2=(20)^2+2(-10 \mu) 80 \\
\text { or } & \mu=\frac{(20)^2}{2 \times 10 \times 80}=\frac{1}{4} \\
\text { or } & \mu=0.25
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cube bar slides thrice the time with friction than that without friction when it slides on an inclined plane of inclination $45^{\circ}$. The coefficient of friction between the block and the surface is
questions.solution:
For a block sliding down an inclined plane of angle $\theta$ without friction, the acceleration is $a_1 = g \sin \theta$. The time taken to cover a distance $s$ is $t_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{a_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{g \sin \theta}}$.

For a block sliding down with friction, the acceleration is $a_2 = g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)$. The time taken to cover the same distance $s$ is $t_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{a_2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)}}$.

Given $t_2 = 3t_1$, we have $\sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{g(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)}} = 3 \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{g \sin \theta}}$.

Squaring both sides, $\dfrac{1}{\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta} = \dfrac{9}{\sin \theta}$.

Rearranging gives $9(\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta) = \sin \theta$, which simplifies to $8 \sin \theta = 9 \mu \cos \theta$.

Thus, $\mu = \dfrac{8}{9} \tan \theta$.

Given $\theta = 45^{\circ}$, $\tan 45^{\circ} = 1$, so $\mu = \dfrac{8}{9} \approx 0.888$.

Answer: 0.88

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body initially at rest undergoes rectilinear motion. The forcetime (F-t) graph for the motion of the body is given below. Find the linear momentum gained by the body in $2 \mathrm{~s}$.
questions.solution:
The impulse $J$ delivered to a body is equal to the change in its linear momentum $\Delta p$.

The impulse is given by the area under the force-time ($F-t$) graph.

For the interval $t = 0$ to $t = 2$ s, the graph represents a semi-circle below the time axis with radius $r = 1$ s and amplitude $A = 4$ N.

The area of this semi-circle is $A_{area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \pi r^2$.

Since the area is below the time axis, the impulse is negative: $J = -\dfrac{1}{2} \pi (1)^2 = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ N-s.

The magnitude of the linear momentum gained is $|J| = \left| -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right| = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ N-s.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Action and reaction can never balance out because
options: They are equal in magnitude but not opposite always.
They are unequal in magnitudes even though opposite in direction
Though they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction they act on different bodies.
questions.solution:
According to Newton's third law of motion, for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

These two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

However, the fundamental reason they do not balance each other out is that they act on two different bodies. Since the forces are applied to different objects, they cannot result in the net force on a single body being zero.

Answer: Though they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction they act on different bodies.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stone of mass $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ is hung from the ceiling of the room using two strings. If the strings make an angle $60^{\circ}$ and $30^{\circ}$ respectively with the horizontal surface of the roof then the tension on the longer string is : $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$
questions.solution:
The string making $30°$ with the horizontal is longer. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be tensions in strings at $60°$ and $30°$ respectively. Weight $W = mg = 20$ N.

Horizontal equilibrium:
$T_1\cos60° = T_2\cos30°$
$T_1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = T_2 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow T_1 = \sqrt{3}T_2$

Vertical equilibrium:
$T_1\sin60° + T_2\sin30° = 20$

Substituting $T_1 = \sqrt{3}T_2$:
$\sqrt{3}T_2 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + T_2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 20$

$T_2\left(\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 20 \Rightarrow 2T_2 = 20 \Rightarrow T_2 = 10$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A balloon with mass $m$ is descending down with an acceleration $a$ (where, $a \lt  g$ ). How much mass should be removed from it so that it starts moving up with an acceleration $a$ ?
questions.solution:
When the balloon is descending down with an acceleration $a$,

where, $B=$ buoyant force. Here, we should assume that while removing some mass the volume of balloon and hence buoyant force will not change. Let the new mass of the balloon is $m^{\prime}$, so
On solving Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} & m g-m^{\prime} g=m a+m^{\prime} a \\ \Rightarrow \quad & m(g-a)=m^{\prime}(g+a) \Rightarrow m^{\prime}=\frac{m(g-a)}{g+a} \end{aligned}$ So, mass removed, $\Delta m=m-m^{\prime}=m\left[1-\frac{(g-a)}{(g+a)}\right]=m\left[\frac{g+a-g+a}{g+a}\right]=\frac{2 m a}{g+a}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}}, \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}}$ and $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{C}}$ are three forces acting at point $\mathrm{P}$ as shown in figure. The whole system is in equilibrium state. The magnitude of $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}}$ is
questions.solution:
The system is in equilibrium at point P. We resolve the forces $F_A$ and $F_B$ into their horizontal and vertical components.

For horizontal equilibrium:
$F_B \cos(45^{\circ}) - F_A \cos(30^{\circ}) = 0$
$F_B \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = F_A \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$F_B = F_A \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}} = F_A \sqrt{1.5}$

For vertical equilibrium:
$F_A \sin(30^{\circ}) + F_B \sin(45^{\circ}) = F_C$
Since $F_C = 100$ N, we have:
$F_A \sin(30^{\circ}) + (F_A \sqrt{1.5}) \sin(45^{\circ}) = 100$
$F_A (0.5) + F_A \sqrt{1.5} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 100$
$F_A (0.5) + F_A \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 100$
$F_A (0.5) + F_A \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 100$
$F_A (0.5 + 0.866) = 100$
$F_A (1.366) = 100$
$F_A = \dfrac{100}{1.366} \approx 73.206$ N.

Answer: 73.2 N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the resultant of all external forces acting on a system of particles is zero, then from an inertial frame one can surely say that
options: Potential energy of the system does not change in time.
Kinetic energy of the system does not change in time.
Angular momentum of the system does not change in time
Linear momentum of the system does not change in time
questions.solution:
The net external force acting on a system of particles is given by the rate of change of the total linear momentum of the system, expressed as $\vec{F}_{ext} = \dfrac{d\vec{P}}{dt}$.

Given that the resultant of all external forces is zero, $\vec{F}_{ext} = 0$.

Substituting this into the equation, we get $\dfrac{d\vec{P}}{dt} = 0$.

Integrating with respect to time, we find that the total linear momentum $\vec{P}$ of the system remains constant over time. This is the principle of conservation of linear momentum.

Answer: Linear momentum of the system does not change in time

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A spring of force constant $k$ is cut into lengths of ratio $1 : 3 : 4$. They are connected in series and the new force constant is $k'$. Then they are connected in parallel and force constant is $k''$. Then $k' : k''$ is
questions.solution:
Let the total length of the spring be $L$. The spring is cut into three parts with lengths $l_1 = \dfrac{1}{8}L$, $l_2 = \dfrac{3}{8}L$, and $l_3 = \dfrac{4}{8}L$.

The force constant of a spring is inversely proportional to its length, $k \propto \dfrac{1}{l}$. Thus, $k_1 = 8k$, $k_2 = \dfrac{8}{3}k$, and $k_3 = 2k$.

When connected in series, the equivalent force constant $k'$ is given by $\dfrac{1}{k'} = \dfrac{1}{k_1} + \dfrac{1}{k_2} + \dfrac{1}{k_3} = \dfrac{1}{8k} + \dfrac{3}{8k} + \dfrac{1}{2k} = \dfrac{1+3+4}{8k} = \dfrac{8}{8k} = \dfrac{1}{k}$. Therefore, $k' = k$.

When connected in parallel, the equivalent force constant $k''$ is given by $k'' = k_1 + k_2 + k_3 = 8k + \dfrac{8}{3}k + 2k = 10k + \dfrac{8}{3}k = \dfrac{30k + 8k}{3} = \dfrac{38k}{3}$.

The ratio $k' : k'' = k : \dfrac{38k}{3} = 1 : \dfrac{38}{3} = 3 : 38$.

The ratio is $3:38$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A balloon with mass $m$ is descending down with an acceleration $a$ (where, $a \lt  g$ ). How much mass should be removed from it so that it starts moving up with an acceleration $a$ ?
questions.solution:
Let $F$ be the upward buoyant force acting on the balloon. When the balloon of mass $m$ is descending with acceleration $a$, the equation of motion is $mg - F = ma$.

From this, $F = m(g - a)$.

Let $m'$ be the mass to be removed, so the new mass is $m - m'$. When the balloon moves up with acceleration $a$, the equation of motion is $F - (m - m')g = (m - m')a$.

Substituting $F = m(g - a)$ into the equation, we get $m(g - a) - (m - m')g = (m - m')a$.

$mg - ma - mg + m'g = ma - m'a$.

$m'g + m'a = 2ma$.

$m'(g + a) = 2ma$.

$m' = \dfrac{2ma}{g + a}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2 m a}{g+a}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: With what minimum acceleration can a fireman slide down a rope while breaking strength of the rope is $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of the weight?
questions.solution:
Let $m$ be the mass of the fireman and $g$ be the acceleration due to gravity. The weight of the fireman is $W = mg$.

The breaking strength of the rope is given as $T_{max} = \dfrac{2}{3} mg$.

When the fireman slides down with an acceleration $a$, the equation of motion is $mg - T = ma$, where $T$ is the tension in the rope.

To prevent the rope from breaking, the tension $T$ must not exceed $T_{max}$. Thus, $T \le \dfrac{2}{3} mg$.

Substituting the maximum tension into the equation of motion: $mg - \dfrac{2}{3} mg = ma$.

Solving for $a$: $\dfrac{1}{3} mg = ma$, which gives $a = \dfrac{1}{3} g$.

Since the fireman must slide with at least this acceleration to keep the tension within the breaking limit, the minimum acceleration required is $\dfrac{1}{3} g$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3} g$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resultant of two forces acting at an angle of $120^{\circ}$ is $10 \mathrm{~kg}-\mathrm{W}$ and is perpendicular to one of the forces. That force is
questions.solution:
Let the two forces be $F_1$ and $F_2$. The angle between them is $\theta = 120^{\circ}$. The resultant $R = 10 \text{ kg-W}$ is perpendicular to $F_1$.

The formula for the angle $\alpha$ that the resultant makes with $F_1$ is given by $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{F_2 \sin \theta}{F_1 + F_2 \cos \theta}$.

Since the resultant is perpendicular to $F_1$, $\alpha = 90^{\circ}$, which implies $\tan 90^{\circ} = \infty$. This occurs when the denominator is zero:

$F_1 + F_2 \cos 120^{\circ} = 0$

$F_1 + F_2 (-0.5) = 0 \Rightarrow F_1 = 0.5 F_2 \Rightarrow F_2 = 2 F_1$.

The magnitude of the resultant $R$ is given by $R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2 F_1 F_2 \cos 120^{\circ}$.

Substituting $R = 10$ and $F_2 = 2 F_1$:

$10^2 = F_1^2 + (2 F_1)^2 + 2 F_1 (2 F_1) (-0.5)$

$100 = F_1^2 + 4 F_1^2 - 2 F_1^2$

$100 = 3 F_1^2$

$F_1^2 = \dfrac{100}{3} \Rightarrow F_1 = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ kg-W}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{3}} \mathrm{~kg}-\mathrm{W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The motion of a particle of mass $m$ is described by $y=u t+g t^{2}$. The force acting on the particle will be
questions.solution:
The displacement of the particle is given by $y = ut + gt^2$.

The velocity $v$ is the first derivative of displacement with respect to time $t$:

$v = \dfrac{dy}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(ut + gt^2) = u + 2gt$.

The acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity with respect to time $t$:

$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(u + 2gt) = 2g$.

The force $F$ acting on the particle is given by Newton's second law, $F = ma$:

$F = m(2g) = 2mg$.

Answer: $2 \mathrm{mg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
When a car of mass $m$ is moving with speed $v$ along a circle of radius $r$ on a level road, the centripetal force is provided by $f$, where $f$ denotes
$\left(\mu_{s} \rightarrow\right.$ coefficient of friction, $N \rightarrow$ normal reaction)
questions.solution:
For a car of mass $m$ moving in a circular path of radius $r$ with speed $v$ on a level road, the centripetal force required is given by $F_{c} = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$.

On a level road, this centripetal force is provided by the static frictional force $f$ acting between the tires and the road surface.

The static frictional force $f$ can take any value from $0$ up to the maximum limiting friction, which is given by $f_{max} = \mu_{s}N$, where $\mu_{s}$ is the coefficient of static friction and $N$ is the normal reaction.

For the car to safely negotiate the turn without skidding, the required centripetal force must be less than or equal to the maximum available static friction. Thus, $f = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} \leq \mu_{s}N$.

Answer: $\dfrac{m v^{2}}{r}=f \leq \mu_{s} N$

questions.q: A uniform chain of length $L$ is lying partly on a table, the remaining part hanging down from the edge of the table. If the coefficient of friction between the chain and the table is $0.5$, what is the minimum length of the chain that should lie on the table, to prevent the chain from slipping down to the ground?
questions.solution:
Let length of chain lying the table be $y$.
Mass per unit length of the chain $=\frac{M}{L}$ 
Mass of the chain lying on the table, $M^{\prime}=\frac{M}{L} \cdot y$ 
Mass of the length $(L-y)$ of hanging chain $=\frac{M}{L}(L-y)$
At equilibrium,
Friction force between table and chain $=$ Weight of hanging part of the chain
$\mu\left(\frac{M}{L} y\right) g=\frac{M}{L}(L-y) g\Rightarrow \quad \mu y=L-y\Rightarrow \quad 0.5 y=L-y \quad[\because \mu=0.5]\Rightarrow \quad y=\frac{2 L}{3}$

questions.solution:
Given, initial velocity, $u=3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+4 \hat{\hat{\mathrm{s}}}$
Force, $F=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$
Initial velocity along $X$-axis and $Y_{\text {-axis }}$ are $u_{x}=3 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$
and $u_{y}=4 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$, respectively.
Similarly, $F_{x}=2 \mathrm{~N}$ and $F_{y}=-3 \mathrm{~N}$
If acceleration along $X$ and $Y$-axes are $a_{x}$ and $a_{y}$, then

a_{x}=\frac{F_{x}}{m}=\frac{2}{1}=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \quad[\because F=m a]

\begin{aligned}
a_{y} &=\frac{F_{y}}{m}=\frac{-3}{1}=-3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \\
s_{x} &=u_{x} t+\frac{1}{2} u_{x} l^{2}=3 \times 3+\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 9=18 \mathrm{un} \\
s_{y} &=u_{y} t+\frac{1}{2} a_{y} t^{2}=4 \times 3+\frac{1}{2} \times(-3) \times 9 \\
&=12-13.5=-1.5 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}

So, required $x$ and $y$-coordinates of point $=(18,-15)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monkey of mass $40 \mathrm{~kg}$ climbs up a rope which can stand a maximum tension of $600 \mathrm{~N}$. The rope will break, when the monkey
options: climbs down with an acceleration of $4 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$
climbs up with uniform speed of $5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$
slides down the rope freely under gravity
questions.solution:
Mass of the monkey, $m=40 \mathrm{~kg}$
Maximum tension that the rope can bear, $T_{\max }=600 \mathrm{~N}$
In option (a), acceleration of monkey, $a=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ (upward)
$\therefore$ By equation of motion,

\Rightarrow \quad \begin{array}{ll}
T & -m g=m a \\
T & =m(g+a) \\
& =40(10+6)=640 \mathrm{~N}
\end{array}

Since, $T \gt T_{\text {max }}$, hence in this case, rope will break. Therefore, option (a) is correct.
In option (b), acceleration of monkey, $a=4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ (downward)
$\therefore$ By equation of motion,

T=m(g-a)=40(10-4)=240 \mathrm{~N}

Since, $T \lt  T_{\max }$, then the rope will not break.
In option (c), monkey climbs up with uniform speed, $v=5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\therefore$ Acceleration, $a=0 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$
Hence, by equation of motion, $T=m g$
=40 \times 10=400 \mathrm{~N}

Since, $T \lt  T_{\max }$, hence rope will not break.
In option $(\mathrm{d})$, acceleration, $a=g$
\therefore \quad T=m(g-a)=m(g-g)=0 \mathrm{~N} \text {. }

Since, $T \lt  T_{\max }$, the rope will not break.
Therefore, only option (a) is correct.
