questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are the angles between the vectors $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}, \overrightarrow{\mathrm{Q}}$, and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{R}}$ and $\alpha=90^{\circ}$ as shown in figure. the product of $(\vec{Q} \times \vec{R}) \cdot \vec{Q}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The expression given is $(\vec{Q} \times \vec{R}) \cdot \vec{Q}$.

By the properties of the scalar triple product, the vector $(\vec{Q} \times \vec{R})$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{Q}$ and $\vec{R}$.

Specifically, the cross product $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ results in a vector that is orthogonal to the plane containing $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.

Therefore, $(\vec{Q} \times \vec{R})$ is perpendicular to $\vec{Q}$.

The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is always zero. Thus, $(\vec{Q} \times \vec{R}) \cdot \vec{Q} = 0$.

Answer: Zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The sides of a parallelogram are represented by vectors $\mathbf{p}=5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and $\mathbf{q}=3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ Then, the area of the parallelogram is
questions.solution:
Area of a parallelogram $=|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|$
where, $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are sides of parallelogram.
$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Given, } \quad \mathbf{a}=\mathbf{p}=5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
& \text { and } \quad \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{q}=3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
5 & -4 & 3 \\
3 & 2 & -1
\end{array}\right| \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=\hat{\mathbf{i}}(4-6)-\hat{\mathbf{j}}(-5-9)+\hat{\mathbf{k}}(10+12) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=-2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+14 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+22 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
&
\end{aligned}$
Thus, $|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{(2)^2+(14)^2+(22)^2}=\sqrt{684}$ sq units

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tentative explanation of observations without assuming that it is true is called
questions.solution:
A hypothesis is a tentative explanation of observations or phenomena that can be tested through experimentation or further observation. It does not assume the explanation is true until it is verified by evidence.

Answer: hypothesis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The sides of a parallelogram are represented by vectors $\vec{p}=5 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-4 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+3 \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and $\vec{q}=3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}$. Then, the area of the parallelogram is
questions.solution:
The area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides represented by vectors $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{q}$ is given by the magnitude of their cross product, $|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}|$.

First, calculate the cross product $\vec{p} \times \vec{q}$:
$\vec{p} \times \vec{q} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 5 & -4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding the determinant:
$\vec{p} \times \vec{q} = \hat{i}((-4)(-1) - (3)(2)) - \hat{j}((5)(-1) - (3)(3)) + \hat{k}((5)(2) - (-4)(3))$
$\vec{p} \times \vec{q} = \hat{i}(4 - 6) - \hat{j}(-5 - 9) + \hat{k}(10 + 12)$
$\vec{p} \times \vec{q} = -2\hat{i} + 14\hat{j} + 22\hat{k}$

Now, calculate the magnitude of the resulting vector:
$|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}| = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (14)^2 + (22)^2}$
$|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}| = \sqrt{4 + 196 + 484}$
$|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}| = \sqrt{684}$

The area of the parallelogram is $\sqrt{684}$ sq units.

Answer: $\sqrt{684}$ sq units

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The relative errors in the measurement of two lengths $1.02 \mathrm{~cm} \pm 0.01 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $9.89 \mathrm{~cm} \pm 0.01 \mathrm{~cm}$ is
questions.solution:
The relative error in a measurement $x \pm \Delta x$ is given by $\dfrac{\Delta x}{x}$. The percentage error is given by $\dfrac{\Delta x}{x} \times 100 \%$.

For the first measurement $1.02 \pm 0.01 \text{ cm}$, the relative error is $\dfrac{0.01}{1.02}$. The percentage error is $\dfrac{0.01}{1.02} \times 100 \% \approx 0.98 \% \approx 1 \%$.

For the second measurement $9.89 \pm 0.01 \text{ cm}$, the relative error is $\dfrac{0.01}{9.89}$. The percentage error is $\dfrac{0.01}{9.89} \times 100 \% \approx 0.101 \% \approx 0.1 \%$.

Thus, the relative errors are approximately $\pm 1 \%$ and $\pm 0.1 \%$.

Answer: $\pm 1 \%$ and $\pm 0.1 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If voltage $V=(200 \pm 8) \mathrm{V}$ and current $I=(20 \pm 05) \mathrm{A}$, then the percentage error in resistance $R$ is
questions.solution:
Voltage, $V=\langle 200 \pm 8) \mathrm{V}$
Current, $I=(20 \pm 05) \mathrm{A}\therefore$ Fesistance, $R=\frac{V}{I}=\frac{200}{20}=10 \Omega$
Taking maximum error condition,

\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Delta R}{R} &=\frac{\Delta V}{V}+\frac{\Delta l}{l}=\frac{8}{200}+\frac{05}{20}=\frac{13}{200} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100 &=\frac{13}{200} \times 100 \\
&=\frac{13}{2} \angle=6.5 \%
\end{aligned}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two equal forces ( $p$ each) act at a point inclined to each other at an angle of $120^{\circ}$. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.solution:
The magnitude of the resultant force can be given by parallelogram's law of vector addition i.e.,

\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \quad F_{\text {net }} &=\sqrt{2 p^{2}+2 p^{2} \times \cos \left(120^{\circ}\right)}\left(\because \theta=120^{\circ}\right) \\
&=\sqrt{2 p^{2}+2 p^{2}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)} \\
&=\sqrt{p^{2}} \\
&=p
\end{aligned}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The square of the resultant of two equal forces acting at a point is equal to three times their product. Angle between them is
questions.solution:
Let $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ be the two forces acting at a point, then their resultant,
$\begin{array}{ll} 
& F_{R}=\sqrt{F_{1}^{2}+F_{2}^{2}+2 F_{1} F_{2} \cos \theta} \\
\text { Given, } \quad & F_{1}=F_{2}=F \\
\Rightarrow \quad & F_{R}=\sqrt{2 F^{2}+2 F^{2} \cos \theta} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & F_{R}^{2}=2 F^{2}(1+\cos \theta)...(i) \\
\text { As per question, } \\
\Rightarrow \quad & F_{R}^{2}=3 F_{1} F_{2}=3 F^{2} \\
\Rightarrow & 2 F^{2}(1+\cos \theta)=3 F^{2} \quad[\text { using Eq. (i)] } \\
\Rightarrow \quad 1+\cos \theta=\frac{3}{2} \\
\Rightarrow & \cos \theta=\frac{1}{2} \text { or } \theta=60^{\circ}
\end{array}$

questions.q: Vectors $\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are such that $\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}=0$ and $\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{C}=0$, then the vector parallel to $\mathbf{A}$ is
questions.solution:

questions.q: Two equal forces $(P$ each $)$ act at a point inclined to each other at an angle of $120^{\circ}$. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.solution:
The magnitude of resultant of two forces is given by
$R=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}+2 A B \cos \theta}$
Given, $\quad A=B=P$ and $\theta=120^{\circ}\therefore \quad R=\sqrt{P^{2}+P^{2}+2 P^{2} \cos 120^{\circ}}=\sqrt{2 p^{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)}=p$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Calculate the vapour pressure that can help the formation of a spherical droplet of water of radius $6.25 \times 10^{-5}$ m at 22°C. Given: The surface tension of water at the given temperature is $7.28 \times 10^{-2}$ Nm$^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The excess pressure inside a spherical droplet that helps in its formation is given by the formula:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{r}$

where $T$ is the surface tension and $r$ is the radius of the droplet.

Substituting the given values:
$T = 7.28 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$
$r = 6.25 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}$

$\Delta P = \dfrac{2 \times 7.28 \times 10^{-2}}{6.25 \times 10^{-5}}$

$\Delta P = \dfrac{14.56 \times 10^{-2}}{6.25 \times 10^{-5}}$

$\Delta P = 2.3296 \times 10^3\ \text{Pa}$

$\Delta P \approx 2.33 \times 10^3\ \text{Pa}$

Answer: $2.33 \times 10^3\ Pa$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small hollow vessel which has a small circular hole of radius r in its base, is immersed in a tank of oil of density $\rho$ and surface tension T. The oil will penetrate into the vessel at a depth of
questions.solution:
Let the depth at which the oil penetrates the vessel be $h$.

The hydrostatic pressure exerted by the oil at depth $h$ is given by $P = h\rho g$.

For the oil to enter the vessel through the small hole of radius $r$, this hydrostatic pressure must overcome the excess pressure due to surface tension at the meniscus formed at the hole.

The maximum excess pressure for a meniscus of radius $r$ is $\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{r}$.

Equating the hydrostatic pressure to the excess pressure:

$h\rho g = \dfrac{2T}{r}$

$h = \dfrac{2T}{r\rho g}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2T}{r\rho g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: While falling through the air, twenty seven droplets having the same radius 1 mm and terminal velocity $10 \mathrm{cms}^{-1}$ combine to form a single drop. What is the terminal velocity of the single bigger drop?
questions.solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of each small droplet and $R$ be the radius of the single large drop. Since the volume is conserved, we have $27 \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^{3}$.

This implies $R^{3} = 27 r^{3}$, so $R = 3r$.

The terminal velocity $v$ of a droplet is given by Stokes' Law as $v = \dfrac{2}{9} \dfrac{r^{2} g (\rho - \sigma)}{\eta}$, where $\rho$ is the density of the liquid and $\sigma$ is the density of air.

From this expression, $v \propto r^{2}$.

Let $v_{1}$ be the terminal velocity of the small droplet and $v_{2}$ be the terminal velocity of the large drop. Then $\dfrac{v_{2}}{v_{1}} = \left( \dfrac{R}{r} \right)^{2}$.

Substituting $R = 3r$, we get $\dfrac{v_{2}}{v_{1}} = (3)^{2} = 9$.

Given $v_{1} = 10 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, the terminal velocity of the larger drop is $v_{2} = 9 \times 10 = 90 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $90 \mathrm{cms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water from a tap emerges vertically downwards with an initial speed of $1.0 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. The cross-sectional area of the tap is $1 \mathrm{~cm}^2$. Assume that the pressure is constant throughout the stream of water and that the flow is steady. The cross-sectional area of the stream 15 cm below the tap is $\left(g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Let the initial velocity at the tap be $v_1 = 1.0 \text{ ms}^{-1}$ and the cross-sectional area be $A_1 = 1 \text{ cm}^2$.

Let the velocity at a depth $h = 15 \text{ cm} = 0.15 \text{ m}$ be $v_2$ and the cross-sectional area be $A_2$.

Using the equation of motion $v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2gh$, we have:

$v_2^2 = (1.0)^2 + 2 \times 10 \times 0.15 = 1 + 3 = 4$

$v_2 = 2 \text{ ms}^{-1}$

According to the equation of continuity for steady flow, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.

$1 \text{ cm}^2 \times 1.0 \text{ ms}^{-1} = A_2 \times 2.0 \text{ ms}^{-1}$

$A_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \text{ cm}^2 = 0.5 \text{ cm}^2$

Answer: $0.5 \mathrm{~cm}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In to a vessel containing pure water a clean glass tube of radius $3.6 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}$ is held vertically with 12 cm of the tube above the water level. Now the capillary tube is moved down in to the water so that only 2 cm of its length is above the water surface. Angle of contact $\theta$ at this position is (given surface tension of water $=7.2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ and $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The capillary rise $h$ in a tube of radius $r$ is given by the formula $h = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}$, where $T$ is the surface tension, $\theta$ is the angle of contact, $\rho$ is the density of water, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

First, calculate the maximum capillary rise $h_{max}$ for pure water in a glass tube, where $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ and $\cos 0^{\circ} = 1$. Given $T = 7.2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N/m}$, $r = 3.6 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$, and $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$h_{max} = \dfrac{2 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-2}}{3.6 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000 \times 10} = \dfrac{14.4 \times 10^{-2}}{3.6 \times 10^0} = 4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 4 \text{ cm}$.

When the tube is pushed down such that only $2 \text{ cm}$ is above the water surface, the water cannot rise higher than the top of the tube. The water will rise to the top of the tube, and the meniscus will adjust its curvature to satisfy the equilibrium condition $h' = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}$, where $h' = 2 \text{ cm}$.

Substituting the values: $2 \times 10^{-2} = \dfrac{2 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta}{3.6 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000 \times 10}$.

$2 \times 10^{-2} = \dfrac{14.4 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta}{3.6} = 4 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta$.

Therefore, $\cos \theta = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-2}}{4 \times 10^{-2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

This gives $\theta = 60^{\circ}$.

Answer: $\theta=60^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wooden block floats with $\dfrac{3}{5}$ of its volume submerged in a tank of water. If a denser liquid is poured into the tank, the wooden block floats with half its volume in the liquid and the remaining half in water. The relative density of the liquid is:
questions.solution:
Let $V$ be the volume of the wooden block and $\rho_{w}$ be the density of water. Let $\rho_{b}$ be the density of the block and $\rho_{l}$ be the density of the denser liquid.

In the first case, the block floats in water. By the principle of flotation, the weight of the block equals the weight of the displaced water:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{w} (\dfrac{3}{5} V) g$

$\rho_{b} = \dfrac{3}{5} \rho_{w}$

In the second case, the block floats in a mixture of water and the denser liquid. The total buoyant force equals the weight of the block. The block has half its volume in the liquid and half in water:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{l} (\dfrac{1}{2} V) g + \rho_{w} (\dfrac{1}{2} V) g$

$\rho_{b} = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{l} + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{w}$

Substituting $\rho_{b} = \dfrac{3}{5} \rho_{w}$ into the equation:

$\dfrac{3}{5} \rho_{w} = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{l} + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{w}$

$\dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{l} = (\dfrac{3}{5} - \dfrac{1}{2}) \rho_{w}$

$\dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{l} = (\dfrac{6-5}{10}) \rho_{w} = \dfrac{1}{10} \rho_{w}$

$\rho_{l} = \dfrac{2}{10} \rho_{w} = \dfrac{1}{5} \rho_{w}$

The relative density of the liquid is $\dfrac{\rho_{l}}{\rho_{w}} = \dfrac{1}{5}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylindrical tank 0.5 m in radius, rests on a platform 1.5 m high. Initially the tank is filled with water to a height of 2.5 m. A small plug whose area is $10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$ is removed from an orifice located on the side of the tank at the bottom. The vertical speed with which the water strikes the ground is: [Assume $g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
The orifice is on the side at the bottom, so water emerges horizontally with zero initial vertical velocity.

The platform height $H = 1.5$ m, so water falls 1.5 m vertically.

$v_y^2 = u_y^2 + 2gH = 0 + 2 \times 10 \times 1.5 = 30$

$v_y = \sqrt{30} \approx 5.47 \ ms^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hydraulic automobile lift is designed to lift cars with a maximum mass of 3000 kg . The area of cross-section of the piston carrying the board is $425 \mathrm{~cm}^2$. What maximum pressure would smaller piston have to bear?
questions.solution:
The maximum force, which the bigger piston can bear,
$F=30000 \mathrm{kgf}=3000 \times 9.8 \mathrm{~N}$
Area of piston,
$A=425 \mathrm{~cm}^2=425 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$
$\therefore$ Maximum pressure on the bigger piston,
$p=\frac{F}{A}=\frac{300 \times 9.8}{425 \times 10^{-4}}=6.92 \times 10^4 \mathrm{~Pa}$
Since, the liquid transmits pressure equally, therefore the maximum pressure the smaller piston can bear is $6.92 \times 10^4 \mathrm{~Pa}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water flows from a tap with steady flow, through a cross sectional area of $10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^2$ with a speed of $0.5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. Assume the pressure is constant throughout the stream of water. The cross sectional area of the stream $0.19 \mathrm{~m}$ below the tap is
questions.solution:
Let $A_1 = 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^2$ be the cross-sectional area at the tap and $v_1 = 0.5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ be the speed of water at the tap. Let $A_2$ and $v_2$ be the cross-sectional area and speed at a depth $h = 0.19 \mathrm{~m}$ below the tap.

Using the equation of continuity, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.

Using Bernoulli's equation or the equation of motion for a freely falling body, $v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2gh$.

Given $g = 9.8 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$ (or $10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$ depending on standard convention, here $9.8$ is standard), $v_2^2 = (0.5)^2 + 2 \times 9.8 \times 0.19 = 0.25 + 3.724 = 3.974$.

If we use $g = 10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$, $v_2^2 = 0.25 + 2 \times 10 \times 0.19 = 0.25 + 3.8 = 4.05$.

Taking $v_2 = \sqrt{4} = 2 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ (using $g=10$ and approximating $v_2^2 \approx 4$), we have $v_2 = 2 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$.

Substituting into the continuity equation: $A_2 = \dfrac{A_1 v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{10^{-3} \times 0.5}{2} = 0.25 \times 10^{-3} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$.

Answer: $2.5 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Modulus of rigidity of an incompressible liquid is
questions.solution:
The modulus of rigidity, also known as the shear modulus ($G$), is defined as the ratio of shear stress to shear strain. For a fluid, shear stress is proportional to the rate of shear strain, not the shear strain itself. When a static shear force is applied to a liquid, it continues to deform indefinitely as long as the force is applied, meaning the shear strain is not defined for a static state. Consequently, the resistance to shear deformation in a liquid is zero. Therefore, the modulus of rigidity for any liquid, including an incompressible one, is zero.

Answer: Zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the relation obeyed by the angles of contact $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and $\theta_3$ of 3 liquids of different densities $P_1, P_2$ and $P_3$ respectively $(\mathrm{P}_1 \lt  \mathrm{P}_2 \lt  \mathrm{P}_3$) when they rise to the same capillary height in 3 identical capillaries and having nearly same surface tension $\mathrm{T}$ ?
questions.solution:
From Jurin's law: $h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{rPg}$

Since $h$, $T$, $r$, $g$ are constant: $\cos\theta \propto P$

Given $P_1 \lt P_2 \lt P_3$:

$\cos\theta_1 \lt \cos\theta_2 \lt \cos\theta_3$

Since liquids rise ($h \gt 0$), $\cos\theta \gt 0$, so all angles are acute: $0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

In $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, cosine is decreasing, so smaller cosine means larger angle:

$\theta_1 \gt \theta_2 \gt \theta_3$

Combined: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \gt \theta_1 \gt \theta_2 \gt \theta_3 \geq 0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 64 rain drops of the same radius are falling through air with a steady velocity of $0.5 \mathrm{~cm} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. If the drops coalesce, the terminal velocity would be
questions.solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of each small drop and $v$ be its terminal velocity. The terminal velocity of a spherical drop is given by Stokes Law as $v = \dfrac{2}{9} \dfrac{r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{\eta}$, where $\rho$ is the density of the drop, $\sigma$ is the density of air, and $\eta$ is the coefficient of viscosity. This implies $v \propto r^2$.

When $n = 64$ drops coalesce into a single large drop of radius $R$, the volume remains constant. Thus, $\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = n \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$, which gives $R^3 = n r^3$, or $R = n^{1/3} r$.

Substituting $n = 64$, we get $R = (64)^{1/3} r = 4r$.

Let $V$ be the terminal velocity of the large drop. Since $V \propto R^2$ and $v \propto r^2$, we have $\dfrac{V}{v} = \left( \dfrac{R}{r} \right)^2 = (4)^2 = 16$.

Given $v = 0.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, the terminal velocity of the large drop is $V = 16 \times 0.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 8 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

Converting to meters per second, $V = 8 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 0.08 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $0.08 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of wood floats in water with $(4 / 5)$ th of its volume submerged. If the same block just floats in a liquid, the density of the liquid is $\left(\right.$ in $\mathrm{kgm}^{-3}$ )
questions.solution:
Applying Archimedes' principle, submerged part $=$ replaced water
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{4}{5} h \rho_{u s} g=h \times \rho_l \times g$
where, $\rho_w=$ density of water and $\rho_l=$ density of the liquid.
$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \rho_l=\frac{4}{5} \times \rho_w=\frac{4}{5} \times 1000 \\
\Rightarrow & \rho_l=800 \mathrm{kgm}^{-3}
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The speeds of air-flow on the upper and lower surfaces of a wing of an aeroplane $arefv_1$ and $v_2$, respectively. If $A$ is the cross-sectional area of the wing and $\rho$ is the density of air, then the upward lift is
questions.solution:
Due to the specific shape of wings, when the aeroplane runs, air passes at higher speed over it as compared to its lower surface. This difference of air speeds above and below the wings, in accordance with Bernoulli's principle, creates a pressure difference, due to which an upward force called 'dynamic lift' acts on the plate.
$\therefore$ Upward lift $=$ pressure difference \times  area of the wings
$[\because F=p \times A]$
From Bernoulli's equation,
$\begin{aligned}
p_1+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_1{ }^2 & =p_2+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_2{ }^2 \\
\because \quad p_2-p_1 & =\frac{1}{2} \rho\left(v_1{ }^2-v_2{ }^2\right) \\
\text { Hence, upward lift } & =\frac{1}{2} \rho A\left(v_1^2-v_2^2\right)
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water from a tap of cross-sectional area $1 \mathrm{~cm}^2$, falls vertically downwards at $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The cross sectional area of the stream, $20 \mathrm{~cm}$ below the tap is (assume that pressure is constant throughout and the flow is streamlined; $\left(\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Let $A_1 = 1 \text{ cm}^2$ be the cross-sectional area at the tap and $v_1 = 2 \text{ m/s}$ be the velocity at the tap. Let $A_2$ be the cross-sectional area at a depth $h = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$ below the tap, and $v_2$ be the velocity at that point.

Using the equation of continuity, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.

Using the principle of conservation of energy (Bernoulli's equation) for a streamline, $v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2gh$.

Substituting the given values, $v_2^2 = (2)^2 + 2 \times 10 \times 0.2 = 4 + 4 = 8$.

Thus, $v_2 = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2} \text{ m/s} \approx 2 \times 1.414 = 2.828 \text{ m/s}$.

From the continuity equation, $A_2 = \dfrac{A_1 v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1 \times 2}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ cm}^2$.

Calculating the value, $A_2 = \dfrac{1}{1.414} \approx 0.707 \text{ cm}^2$.

Answer: 0.707 cm$^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A spherical metal ball of density '$\rho$' and radius '$r$' is immersed in a liquid of density '$\sigma$'. When an electric field is applied in the upward direction the metal ball remains just suspended in the liquid. Then the expression for the charge on the metal ball is :
questions.solution:
For the metal ball to remain suspended in the liquid, the net force acting on it must be zero. The forces acting on the ball are the gravitational force acting downwards, the buoyant force acting upwards, and the electric force acting upwards.

The gravitational force is $F_g = mg = V \rho g = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho g$.

The buoyant force is $F_b = V \sigma g = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \sigma g$.

The electric force is $F_e = qE$.

Equating the upward forces to the downward force:

$F_e + F_b = F_g$

$qE + \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \sigma g = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho g$

$qE = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 g (\rho - \sigma)$

$q = \dfrac{4 \pi r^3 (\rho - \sigma) g}{3 E}$

Answer: $q=\dfrac{\left[4 \pi r^3(\rho-\sigma) g\right]}{3 E}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The speeds of air-flow on the upper and lower surfaces of a wing of an aeroplane are $v_1$ and $v_2$, respectively. If $A$ is the cross-sectional area of the wing and $\rho$ is the density of air, then the upward lift is
questions.solution:
According to Bernoulli's principle for streamline flow, the pressure $P$ and velocity $v$ at any two points on a streamline are related by $P + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 = \text{constant}$.

Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be the pressures on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing respectively, with corresponding air speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$.

Applying Bernoulli's equation:

$P_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_2^2$

The pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces is:

$P_2 - P_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho (v_1^2 - v_2^2)$

The upward lift force $F$ is the product of the pressure difference and the cross-sectional area $A$ of the wing:

$F = (P_2 - P_1) A$

$F = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho A (v_1^2 - v_2^2)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2} \rho A\left(v_1^2-v_2^2\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of wood floats in water with $(4 / 5)$ th of its volume submerged. If the same block just floats in a liquid, the density of the liquid is (in $\mathrm{kgm}^{-3}$)
questions.solution:
Let $V$ be the volume of the block and $\rho_{w}$ be the density of water. Let $\rho_{b}$ be the density of the block and $\rho_{l}$ be the density of the liquid.

When the block floats in water, the weight of the block equals the weight of the displaced water:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{w} V_{sub} g$

Given $V_{sub} = \dfrac{4}{5} V$, we have:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{w} \left( \dfrac{4}{5} V \right) g$

$\rho_{b} = \dfrac{4}{5} \rho_{w}$

Taking the density of water $\rho_{w} = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^{3}$, we get $\rho_{b} = \dfrac{4}{5} \times 1000 = 800 \text{ kg/m}^{3}$.

When the block just floats in the liquid, the entire volume of the block is submerged, so the weight of the block equals the weight of the displaced liquid:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{l} V g$

$\rho_{l} = \rho_{b} = 800 \text{ kg/m}^{3}$.

Answer: 800

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A raft of density $600 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{m}^3$ and mass $120 \mathrm{~kg}$ floats in water. How much weight can be put on the raft to make it just sink?
questions.solution:
The density of the raft is $\rho_{r} = 600 \text{ kg/m}^3$. The mass of the raft is $M = 120 \text{ kg}$.

The volume of the raft is $V = \dfrac{M}{\rho_{r}} = \dfrac{120}{600} = 0.2 \text{ m}^3$.

For the raft to just sink in water (density $\rho_{w} = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$), the total weight of the raft and the added mass $m$ must be equal to the buoyant force acting on the raft when it is fully submerged.

The buoyant force is $F_{B} = V \rho_{w} g = 0.2 \times 1000 \times g = 200g$.

The total weight is $(M + m)g = (120 + m)g$.

Equating the two, we have $120 + m = 200$.

Therefore, $m = 200 - 120 = 80 \text{ kg}$.

Answer: $80 \mathrm{~kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water is poured in a tank through a cylindrical tube of area of cross-section $A$ and ejecting water at a constant speed $4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The tank contains a hole of area $\dfrac{A}{2}$ at bottom. Level of water in the tank will not go up beyond
questions.solution:
Let $A_{in} = A$ be the area of the inlet tube and $v_{in} = 4 \text{ m/s}$ be the velocity of water entering the tank. Let $A_{out} = \dfrac{A}{2}$ be the area of the hole at the bottom of the tank.

The level of water in the tank stops rising when the rate of water entering the tank equals the rate of water exiting the tank through the hole. This is the condition for steady state.

The rate of volume flow entering the tank is $Q_{in} = A_{in} \times v_{in} = A \times 4 = 4A$.

The rate of volume flow exiting the tank through the hole is $Q_{out} = A_{out} \times v_{out}$, where $v_{out}$ is the velocity of efflux given by Torricelli's law as $v_{out} = \sqrt{2gh}$, with $h$ being the height of the water level.

Equating the flow rates: $4A = \dfrac{A}{2} \times \sqrt{2gh}$.

Dividing both sides by $A$: $4 = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{2gh} \Rightarrow 8 = \sqrt{2gh}$.

Squaring both sides: $64 = 2gh$.

Using $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$: $64 = 2 \times 10 \times h \Rightarrow 64 = 20h$.

$h = \dfrac{64}{20} = 3.2 \text{ m}$.

Answer: $3.2 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: According to Pascal's law, pressure in a fluid at rest is the same at all points, if
options: they are at the same plane
they are at the same height
questions.solution:
Pascal's law states that for a fluid at rest, the pressure at all points at the same horizontal level is identical. In a continuous fluid at rest, the pressure variation with depth is given by $P = P_0 + \rho gh$, where $h$ is the depth measured from the surface. Points at the same vertical height (or same plane) have the same depth $h$, and therefore experience the same pressure.

Answer: they are at the same height

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The surface tension of a liquid at its boiling point
options: is equal to the value at room temperature
is half of the value at room temperature
questions.solution:
Surface tension is a property of liquids that arises due to the cohesive forces between molecules at the surface. As the temperature of a liquid increases, the kinetic energy of the molecules increases, which weakens the intermolecular forces of attraction.

At the boiling point, the liquid is in equilibrium with its vapor phase. The density of the liquid phase decreases while the density of the vapor phase increases as the temperature approaches the critical temperature. At the critical temperature, the distinction between the liquid and vapor phases disappears, and the surface tension becomes zero.

For any liquid, as the temperature reaches its boiling point, the surface tension decreases significantly. Specifically, at the critical temperature, it vanishes. In the context of standard physics problems, the surface tension of a liquid at its boiling point is considered to be zero.

Answer: becomes zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball floats on the surface of water in a container exposed to the atmosphere. When the container is covered and the air is partially removed, then the ball
options: remains immersed at its former depth
questions.solution: In the given situation, the weight of the ball is supported by the buoyant force of water and buoyant force due to air. As the density of air becomes less, the buoyant force due to the air becomes less. Therefore, to compensate a greater buoyant force due to water is required which is achieved by a greater immersion of ball into the water.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A frame made of metallic wire  enclosing a surface area $A$ is covered with a soap film. If the area of the frame of metallic wire is reduced by $50 \%$, then the energy of the soap film will be changed by
questions.solution:
Given, initial surface area, $A_{1}=A$
Final surface area, $A_{2}=A_{1}-50 \%$ of $AA_{2}=A-50 \%$ of $A=A-\frac{A}{2}=\frac{A}{2}$ Initial surface energy, $E_{1}=T \cdot 2 A=2 T A$ Final surface energy, $E_{2}=$ Surface tension \times  Surface $\Rightarrow \quad E_{2}=T \times 2\left(A_{1}-A_{2}\right)=T \times 2\left(A-\frac{A}{2}\right)\Rightarrow \quad \quad E_{2}=T A\therefore$ Percentage change in the energy of soap film

\begin{aligned}
&=\frac{E_{1}-E_{2}}{E_{1}} \times 100 \\
&=\frac{2 T A-T A}{2 T A} \times 100 \\
&=50 \%
\end{aligned}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A fluid is in streamline flow across a horizontal pipe of variable area of cross-section. For this which of the following statements is correct?
options: Velocity of fluid is maximum at narrowest part.
Pressure of the fluid is maximum at widest part.
questions.solution:
According to the equation of continuity,

A v=\text { constant }

Therefore, velocity of the fluid is minimum at the widest part and maximum at the narrowest part of the horizontal pipe.
Again, according to Bernoulli's principle for horizontal pipe,

p+\frac{1}{2} p v^{2}=\text { constant }

Hence, $p$ is more, $v$ is less and vice-versa.
Therefore, when a fluid is flowing through the horizontal pipe of variable area of cross-section, then velocity is maximum at the narrowest part of the pipe and pressure is maximum at the widest part of the pipe.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thread is tied slightly loose to a wire frame as in figure and the frame is dipped into a soap solution and taken out. The frame is completely covered with the film. When the portion $A$ is punctured with a pin, the thread
options: Either (a) or (b) depending on the size of $A$ w.r.t. $B$
questions.solution:
The potential energy due to surface tension is given by the formula $U=S \times A$
where, $S$ is the surface tension and $A$ is the area of film. Since after puncturing, the film will try to minimise its potential energy and hence the surface area. Thus, the thread will become concave towards A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: From the adjacent figure, the correct observation is
options: the pressure on the bottom of tank (I) is greater than at the bottom of (II)
the pressure on the bottom of tank (I) is smaller than at the bottom of $(I)$
the pressure depend on the shape of the container
the pressure on the bottom of (I) and (II) is the same
questions.solution:
The pressure applied at the bottom of a container by a liquid column of height $h$ is given by
$p=h \rho g$
Here, in two cases, the liquid used is same (water), so $\rho$ is same. Also, the height of liquid column is same on both. So, the pressure applied at the bottom is same for both.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a liquid does not wet glass, its angle of contact is
questions.solution: If a liquid does not wet glass, it means that the liquid-liquid interaction (cohesion) is more than liquid - solid interaction (adhesion). So, the angle of contact is obtuse.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: With the addition of impurities, surface tension of a liquid
options: may increase or decrease depending on impurities
questions.solution:
The addition of impurities in a liquid may increase or decrease the surface tension of liquid depending on the nature of impurities.
If the impurities are highly soluble in liquid, then it will increase the surface tension. But if it is less soluble in liquid, then it will decrease the surface tension of liquid.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Viscosity decreases with increase in temperature is the reason for
questions.solution: The viscosity decreases with increase in temperature. Due to this reason, the hot water moves faster than cold water. Since in summer temperature is high, so more viscous oils are used in motorcars.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A soap bubble of radius $r$ is blown up to form a bubble of radius $3 r$ under isothermal conditions. If $\sigma$ is the surface tension of soap solution, then the energy spent in blowing is
questions.solution:
Surface area of bubble of radius, $r=4 \pi r^{2}$
Surface area of bubble of radius, $3 r=4 \pi(3 r)^{2}=36 \pi r^{2}$
Therefore, increase in surface area

=36 \pi r^{2}-4 \pi r^{2}=32 \pi r^{2}

Since, a bubble has two surfaces, the total increase in surface area $=2 \times 32 \pi r^{2}=64 \pi r^{2}\therefore$ Energy spent $=$ Work done $=$ Surface tension \times  Total increase in surface area $=64 \pi \sigma r^{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following cannot be explained on the basis of Bernoulli's principle?
questions.solution: Ink filler works on the principle of both surface tension and pump. Vacuum in the pen pulls the ink in the bottle to the pen. This ink travels in the pen tip through small openings due to surface tension.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire, made of a certain material of length-l and area of cross section-a can withstand a maximum load =W without breaking. If, another wire of the same material and cross-sectional area is used with double the original length, what will be the maximum load that the wire can withstand, without breaking?
questions.solution:
Breaking stress is a property of the material and is independent of the dimensions of the wire.

The maximum load a wire can withstand is given by the product of breaking stress and the cross-sectional area.

Maximum load = Breaking stress \times Area of cross section

Since the material and the cross-sectional area of the new wire are the same as those of the original wire, the breaking stress and area remain unchanged.

Therefore, the maximum load the wire can withstand remains the same, which is $W$.

Answer: Remains the same =W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A light rod of length 1 m is suspended from ceiling horizontally by means of two vertical wires of equal length tied to its ends. One of the wires is made of material X and is of cross-section $0.1\ \text{cm}^2$ and the other of material Y of cross-section $0.3\ \text{cm}^2$. A weight is hung from the wire at a point to produce equal strain in the wires. The ratio of Young's moduli of wires A to B is 3:1. The location of the point from one end of the wire is
questions.solution:
Let the length of the rod be $L = 1\ \text{m}$.

Let the weight be suspended at a distance $x$ from the wire of material X.

For rotational equilibrium of the rod, the torques about the point of suspension must balance:

$T_X x = T_Y (1 - x)$

The strain in a wire is given by $\epsilon = \dfrac{T}{AY}$.

Since the strains in both wires are equal:

$\dfrac{T_X}{A_X Y_X} = \dfrac{T_Y}{A_Y Y_Y}$

$\dfrac{T_X}{T_Y} = \dfrac{A_X Y_X}{A_Y Y_Y}$

Given $A_X = 0.1\ \text{cm}^2$, $A_Y = 0.3\ \text{cm}^2$, and $\dfrac{Y_X}{Y_Y} = \dfrac{3}{1}$.

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{T_X}{T_Y} = \left(\dfrac{0.1}{0.3}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{3}{1}\right) = 1$

This gives $T_X = T_Y$.

Substituting this into the torque equation:

$x = 1 - x$

$2x = 1 \Rightarrow x = 0.5\ \text{m}$

Answer: $0.5\ \text{m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The stress verses strain graph of four metals A,B,C and D are as shown. Which of the graph represent the metal having greatest Young's modulus?
questions.solution:
The Young's modulus $Y$ of a material is defined as the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit, which corresponds to the slope of the stress-strain graph.

$Y = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}} = \tan(\theta)$

where $\theta$ is the angle that the stress-strain line makes with the strain axis.

Comparing the slopes of the given lines OA, OB, OC, and OD, the line OA makes the largest angle with the strain axis. Therefore, the slope of line OA is the greatest.

Since the slope represents the Young's modulus, the metal represented by graph OA has the greatest Young's modulus.

Answer: Graph OA

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One end of a nylon rope of length 1 and diameter 10 mm is fixed to free limb. A monkey weighing 100 N jumps to catch the free end and stays there. The change in diameter of the rope is (Young's modulus of the wire is Y and Poisson Ratio is $\sigma$ )
questions.solution:
The Young modulus $Y$ is defined as the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain. The longitudinal stress is $\sigma_{stress} = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{F}{\pi r^2} = \dfrac{F}{\pi (d/2)^2} = \dfrac{4F}{\pi d^2}$, where $F = 100$ N and $d = 10$ mm = $0.01$ m.

The longitudinal strain is $\epsilon_L = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \dfrac{\sigma_{stress}}{Y} = \dfrac{4F}{\pi d^2 Y}$.

The Poisson ratio $\sigma$ is defined as the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain: $\sigma = - \dfrac{\epsilon_D}{\epsilon_L}$, where $\epsilon_D = \dfrac{\Delta d}{d}$ is the lateral strain.

Therefore, the change in diameter $\Delta d$ is given by $\Delta d = - \sigma \epsilon_L d = - \sigma \left( \dfrac{4F}{\pi d^2 Y} \right) d = - \dfrac{4F \sigma}{\pi d Y}$.

Substituting the given values $F = 100$ N and $d = 0.01$ m:

$\Delta d = - \dfrac{4 \times 100 \times \sigma}{\pi \times 0.01 \times Y} = - \dfrac{400 \sigma}{0.01 \pi Y} = - \dfrac{40000 \sigma}{\pi Y}$.

The magnitude of the change in diameter is $\dfrac{40000 \sigma}{\pi Y}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{40000 \sigma}{\pi Y}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Select the correct statement from the following:
options: The bulk modulus of an ideal liquid is zero
Rubber is more elastic than steel
Shear modulus of an ideal liquid is infinite
The bulk modulus of a perfect rigid body is infinite
questions.solution:
The bulk modulus $B$ is defined as $B = -V \dfrac{dP}{dV}$. For a perfectly rigid body, the change in volume $dV$ is zero for any applied pressure $dP$. Thus, $B = -V \dfrac{dP}{0} = \infty$.

Regarding other options: The bulk modulus of an ideal liquid is finite and positive, not zero. Steel is more elastic than rubber because the Young's modulus of steel is much higher than that of rubber, meaning it requires more stress to produce the same strain. The shear modulus of an ideal liquid is zero because it cannot sustain any shear stress.

Answer: The bulk modulus of a perfect rigid body is infinite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Young's modulus of the material of wires X and Y are in the ratio $4: 1$ and the areas of cross sections of the wires X and Y are in the ratio 2:1. If the same amount of load is applied to both the wires, the ratio of elongation produced in the wires X and Y will be: (Assume length of the wires X and Y initially are the same)
questions.solution:
The Young's modulus $Y$ is defined as $Y = \dfrac{FL}{A \Delta L}$, where $F$ is the applied force, $L$ is the initial length, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, and $\Delta L$ is the elongation.

Rearranging for elongation, we get $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$.

Given that the force $F$ and initial length $L$ are the same for both wires X and Y, the elongation $\Delta L$ is inversely proportional to the product of area $A$ and Young's modulus $Y$, i.e., $\Delta L \propto \dfrac{1}{AY}$.

The ratio of elongations is $\dfrac{\Delta L_X}{\Delta L_Y} = \dfrac{A_Y Y_Y}{A_X Y_X}$.

Given $\dfrac{Y_X}{Y_Y} = \dfrac{4}{1}$ and $\dfrac{A_X}{A_Y} = \dfrac{2}{1}$, we substitute these values:

$\dfrac{\Delta L_X}{\Delta L_Y} = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

Therefore, the ratio of elongation produced in wires X and Y is $1:8$.

Answer: $1: 8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An elevator cable is to have a maximum stress of $7 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$ to allow for appropriate safety factors. Its maximum upward acceleration is $1.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. If the cable has to support the total weight of 2000 kg of a loaded elevator, the area of cross-section of the cable should be
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} \\ & T_{\max }=m(g+a)=(2000)(9.8+1.5)=22600 \mathrm{~N} \\ \\ & \text { Maximum stress }=\frac{T_{\max }}{\text { Area }} \\ \end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} \\ \therefore \text { Area } & =\frac{T_{\max }}{\text { Maximum stress }}=\frac{22600}{7 \times 10^7} \\ \\ & =3.22 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2=3.22 \mathrm{~cm}^2 \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature of a wire is doubled. The Young's modulus of elasticity
questions.solution:
Young's modulus of elasticity $Y$ is a material property that depends primarily on the nature of the material and the temperature. When the temperature of a solid increases, the interatomic distances increase due to thermal expansion, which weakens the interatomic forces.

As the temperature increases, the atomic vibrations increase, leading to a decrease in the stiffness of the material. Consequently, the Young's modulus of elasticity decreases with an increase in temperature.

Therefore, when the temperature of a wire is doubled, its Young's modulus of elasticity will decrease.

Answer: Will decrease

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the ratio of lengths, radii and Young's Moduli of steel and brass wires in the figure are $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}$ and $\mathrm{c}$ respectively, then the corresponding ratio of increase in their lengths would be
questions.solution:
Let $L_s, r_s, Y_s$ be the length, radius, and Young's modulus of the steel wire, and $L_b, r_b, Y_b$ be those of the brass wire. Given ratios are $\dfrac{L_s}{L_b} = a$, $\dfrac{r_s}{r_b} = b$, and $\dfrac{Y_s}{Y_b} = c$.

The tension in the steel wire is $T_s = 2Mg$ (supporting the $2M$ mass). The tension in the brass wire is $T_b = (M + 2M)g = 3Mg$ (supporting both masses).

The elongation $\Delta L$ is given by $\Delta L = \dfrac{TL}{AY} = \dfrac{TL}{\pi r^2 Y}$.

The ratio of increase in lengths is $\dfrac{\Delta L_s}{\Delta L_b} = \dfrac{T_s L_s}{\pi r_s^2 Y_s} \times \dfrac{\pi r_b^2 Y_b}{T_b L_b} = \left( \dfrac{T_s}{T_b} \right) \left( \dfrac{L_s}{L_b} \right) \left( \dfrac{r_b}{r_s} \right)^2 \left( \dfrac{Y_b}{Y_s} \right)$.

Substituting the given values: $\dfrac{T_s}{T_b} = \dfrac{2Mg}{3Mg} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, $\dfrac{L_s}{L_b} = a$, $\dfrac{r_b}{r_s} = \dfrac{1}{b}$, and $\dfrac{Y_b}{Y_s} = \dfrac{1}{c}$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{\Delta L_s}{\Delta L_b} = \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right) (a) \left( \dfrac{1}{b^2} \right) \left( \dfrac{1}{c} \right) = \dfrac{2a}{3b^2c}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2 a}{3 b^2 c}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wire of same material having radius in ratio $2: 1$ and lengths in ratio $1: 2$. If same force is applied on them, then ratio of their change in length will be
questions.solution:
Given, ratio of radius of two wires,
$\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{2}{1}$
and ratio in their lengths,
$\frac{l_1}{l_2}=\frac{1}{2}$
When same force is applied on them, then ratio change in their lengths,
$\frac{\Delta l_1}{\Delta l_2}=\text { ? }$
We known that, Young's modulus,
$\begin{gathered}
Y=\frac{F l}{A \Delta l} \Rightarrow \Delta l=\frac{F l}{A Y} \\
\Delta l \propto \frac{l}{A} \\
\therefore \quad \frac{\Delta l_1}{\Delta l_2}=\frac{l_1 / A_1}{l_2 / A_2}=\frac{l_1 A_2}{l_2 A_2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\Delta l_1}{\Delta l_2}=\frac{l_1 / A_1}{r_2^2 / r_1^2}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{8}
\end{gathered}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wires are made of the same material and have the same volume. The first wire has cross-sectional area $A$ and the second wire has cross-sectional area $3 A$. If the length of the first wire is increased by $\Delta l$ on applying a force $F$, how much force is needed to stretch the second wire by the same amount?
questions.solution:
According to the question, For wire 1 : Area of cross-section $=A_1$, Force applied $=F_1$ and increase in length $=\Delta l$. From the relation of Young's modulus of elasticity, $Y=\frac{F l}{A \Delta l}$ Substituting the values for wire 1 in the above relation, we get
For wire $2:$ Area of cross-section $=A_2$ Force applied $=F_2$ increase in length $=\Delta l$
$\because$ Volume, $V=A l$ or $l=\frac{V}{A}$ Substituting the value of $l$ in Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $Y_1=\frac{F_1 V}{A_1^2 \Delta l} \text { and } Y_2=\frac{F_2 V}{A_2^2 \Delta l}$ As it is given that the wires are made up of same material, i.e. $\quad Y_1=Y_2\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{F_1 V}{A_1^2 \Delta l}=\frac{F_2 V}{A_2^2 \Delta l} \Rightarrow \frac{F_1}{F_2}= & \frac{A_1^2}{A_2^2}=\frac{A^2}{9 A^2}=\frac{1}{9} \\ & \left(\because A_1=A \text { and } A_2=3 A\right)\end{aligned}$ or $\quad F_2=9 F_1=9 F \quad$ (given, $\left.F_1=F\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A man grows into a giant such that his height increases to 8 times his original height. Assuming that his density remains same, the stress in the leg will change by a factor of
questions.solution:
Let the original height of the man be $h$ and the original cross-sectional area of his legs be $A$. The mass of the man is $m = \rho V$, where $\rho$ is the density and $V$ is the volume. Since the man grows geometrically similar, the volume $V$ is proportional to $h^3$. Thus, $m \propto h^3$.

The stress $\sigma$ in the legs is defined as the force per unit area, $\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{mg}{A}$.

Since the man grows geometrically similar, the cross-sectional area $A$ of the legs scales as $h^2$.

Substituting the scaling relations $m \propto h^3$ and $A \propto h^2$ into the stress formula, we get $\sigma \propto \dfrac{h^3}{h^2} = h$.

Given that the height increases by a factor of 8, the stress in the legs will also increase by a factor of 8.

Answer: 8

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wire of same material having radius in ratio 2 : 1 and lengths in ratio 1: 2. If same force is applied on them, then ratio of their change in length will be
questions.solution:
The change in length $\Delta L$ of a wire is given by the formula $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$, where $F$ is the applied force, $L$ is the original length, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, and $Y$ is Young's modulus of the material.

Since both wires are made of the same material, $Y$ is the same for both. The force $F$ applied is also the same. Thus, $\Delta L \propto \dfrac{L}{A}$.

The area $A$ is given by $\pi r^2$, so $\Delta L \propto \dfrac{L}{r^2}$.

Given the ratio of radii $r_1 : r_2 = 2 : 1$ and the ratio of lengths $L_1 : L_2 = 1 : 2$, we have:

$\dfrac{\Delta L_1}{\Delta L_2} = \left( \dfrac{L_1}{L_2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} \right)^2$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{\Delta L_1}{\Delta L_2} = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

Answer: $1: 8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two wires are made of the same material and have the same volume. The first wire has cross-sectional area $A$ and the second wire has cross-sectional area $3 A$. If the length of the first wire is increased by $\Delta l$ on applying a force $F$, how much force is needed to stretch the second wire by the same amount?
questions.solution:
Let the length and area of the first wire be $L_1$ and $A_1 = A$. Let the length and area of the second wire be $L_2$ and $A_2 = 3A$.

Since the volumes are equal, $V_1 = V_2$, we have $A_1 L_1 = A_2 L_2$. Substituting the given values, $A L_1 = 3A L_2$, which implies $L_1 = 3 L_2$.

The Young modulus $Y$ is the same for both wires. The force $F$ required to produce an extension $\Delta l$ is given by $F = \dfrac{Y A \Delta l}{L}$.

For the first wire, $F = \dfrac{Y A \Delta l}{L_1}$.

For the second wire, let the force be $F'$. Then $F' = \dfrac{Y A_2 \Delta l}{L_2} = \dfrac{Y (3A) \Delta l}{L_2}$.

Substituting $L_2 = \dfrac{L_1}{3}$ into the expression for $F'$, we get $F' = \dfrac{Y (3A) \Delta l}{L_1 / 3} = 9 \times \dfrac{Y A \Delta l}{L_1}$.

Since $F = \dfrac{Y A \Delta l}{L_1}$, it follows that $F' = 9F$.

Answer: 9F

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A copper and a steel wire of same diameter are connected end to end. A deforming force $F_1$ is applied to the wire which causes an elongation of $1 \mathrm{~cm}$. The two wires will have
questions.solution:
Let the copper wire have Young's modulus $Y_C$ and the steel wire have Young's modulus $Y_S$. Both wires have the same diameter, so they have the same cross-sectional area $A$.

When connected end to end and subjected to a deforming force $F_1$, the tension in both wires is the same, equal to $F_1$.

The stress in each wire is given by $\sigma = \dfrac{F_1}{A}$. Since $F_1$ and $A$ are the same for both wires, the stress is the same in both wires.

The strain in each wire is given by $\epsilon = \dfrac{\sigma}{Y}$. Since the Young's moduli $Y_C$ and $Y_S$ are different for copper and steel, the strains $\epsilon_C = \dfrac{F_1}{A Y_C}$ and $\epsilon_S = \dfrac{F_1}{A Y_S}$ will be different.

Therefore, the two wires will have different strains.

Answer: different strain

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force $F$ applied on the wire of radius $r$ and length $L$ and change in the length of the wire is l. If the same force $F$ is applied on the wire of the same material and radius $4 r$ and length $4 l$, then change in length of the other wire is,
questions.solution:
Young's modulus $Y$ is defined as $Y = \dfrac{F L}{A l}$, where $A = \pi r^2$ is the cross-sectional area of the wire.

For the first wire, $Y = \dfrac{F L}{(\pi r^2) l}$.

For the second wire, let the change in length be $l'$. The material is the same, so $Y$ remains constant. The force is $F$, the radius is $4r$, and the length is $4L$.

$Y = \dfrac{F (4L)}{\pi (4r)^2 l'} = \dfrac{4 F L}{16 \pi r^2 l'} = \dfrac{F L}{4 \pi r^2 l'}$.

Equating the expressions for $Y$:

$\dfrac{F L}{\pi r^2 l} = \dfrac{F L}{4 \pi r^2 l'}$

$\dfrac{1}{l} = \dfrac{1}{4 l'}$

$l' = \dfrac{l}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{l}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Within the elastic limit, the corresponding stress is known as
questions.solution:
In the stress-strain curve of a material, the elastic limit is the maximum stress that a material can withstand without undergoing permanent deformation. The stress corresponding to the elastic limit is defined as the yield strength of the material. Beyond this point, the material begins to deform plastically.

Answer: yield strength

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire is stretched to double of its length. The strain is
questions.solution:
Strain is defined as the ratio of the change in length to the original length of the wire.

Let the original length of the wire be $L$.

The wire is stretched to double its length, so the new length $L' = 2L$.

The change in length $\Delta L = L' - L = 2L - L = L$.

Strain = $\dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{L}{L} = 1$.

Answer: 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The Poisson's ratio of a material is $0.1$. If the longitudinal strain of a rod of this material is $10^{-3}$, then the percentage change in the volume of the rod will be
questions.solution:
If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the longitudinal strain and lateral strain respectively, then
$\alpha=\frac{l_{2}-l_{1}}{l_{1}}=10^{-3}=0.001\Rightarrow \quad \frac{l_{2}}{l_{1}}=1.001$
Poisson's ratio, $\sigma=\frac{\text { Lateral strain }}{\text { Longitudinal strain }}=\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \beta=\sigma \alpha=0 \\ \text { But, } & \beta=\frac{r_{1}-r_{2}}{r_{1}}\end{array}
$\therefore \quad \frac{r_{1}-r_{2}}{n_{1}}=10^{-4}=0.0001\Rightarrow \quad \frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}=0.9999$
Hence, percentage increase in vol
$=\frac{V_{2}-V_{1}}{V_{1}} \times 100=\frac{\pi r_{2}^{2} l_{2}-\pi r_{1}^{2} l_{1}}{\pi r_{1}^{2} l_{1}} \times 100=\left[\left(\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{l_{2}}{l_{1}}\right)^{2}-1\right] \times 100=\left[(0.9999)^{2} \times(1.0001)^{2}-1\right] \times 100=0.0008 \times 100=0.08 \%

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object is dropped from a certain point A at a height 'h' from the ground. During it's journey straight downwards, the object passes points B and C such that the ratio of time taken $t_1$ to cover AB and $t_2$ to cover BC is 1: $(\sqrt{2} - 1)$. What is the ratio of distances AB:BC ?
questions.solution:
Let the time taken to travel from A to B be $t_1 = t$.

The time taken to travel from B to C is $t_2 = (\sqrt{2} - 1)t$.

The total time taken to travel from A to C is $t_{AC} = t_1 + t_2 = t + (\sqrt{2} - 1)t = \sqrt{2}t$.

Since the object is dropped from rest at A, the initial velocity is zero.

The distance AB is given by $AB = \dfrac{1}{2}gt_1^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$.

The distance AC is given by $AC = \dfrac{1}{2}gt_{AC}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}g(\sqrt{2}t)^2 = gt^2$.

The distance BC is $BC = AC - AB = gt^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$.

The ratio of distances AB and BC is $AB : BC = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 : \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 1 : 1$.

Answer: $1:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle moves along a parabolic path $y = 9x^2$ in such a way that the x component of velocity remains constant. If, the acceleration of the particle is $2j\ ms^{-2}$, find the x component of velocity.
questions.solution:
The equation of the path is given by $y = 9x^2$.

Differentiating with respect to time $t$, we get the y-component of velocity:

$v_y = \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 18x \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 18x v_x$

Differentiating again with respect to time $t$, we get the y-component of acceleration:

$a_y = \dfrac{dv_y}{dt} = 18 \left( \dfrac{dx}{dt} v_x + x \dfrac{dv_x}{dt} \right)$

Since the x-component of velocity $v_x$ is constant, its derivative $\dfrac{dv_x}{dt} = 0$.

Substituting $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v_x$ and $\dfrac{dv_x}{dt} = 0$, we get:

$a_y = 18 v_x^2$

It is given that the acceleration of the particle is $2\hat{j}\ ms^{-2}$, which means $a_y = 2\ ms^{-2}$.

$18 v_x^2 = 2$

$v_x^2 = \dfrac{2}{18} = \dfrac{1}{9}$

$v_x = \dfrac{1}{3}\ ms^{-1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}\ ms^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car, starting from rest, accelerates at a rate of $\beta$ through a distance S, then continues at constant speed for time t and then decelerates at a rate of $\dfrac{\beta}{2}$ to come to rest. If the total distance travelled is $10\ S$, then ratio $\dfrac{S}{t^2}$ is
questions.solution:
Let the maximum speed reached by the car be $v$.

For the first part of the motion, the car accelerates from rest at $\beta$ over a distance $S$. Using the equation of kinematics:

$v^2 = 0 + 2\beta S \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2\beta S}$

For the second part of the motion, the car travels at a constant speed $v$ for time $t$. The distance covered is:

$S_2 = vt$

For the third part of the motion, the car decelerates at $\dfrac{\beta}{2}$ to come to rest. The distance covered $S_3$ is given by:

$0 = v^2 - 2\left(\dfrac{\beta}{2}\right)S_3 \Rightarrow S_3 = \dfrac{v^2}{\beta}$

Substituting $v^2 = 2\beta S$ gives:

$S_3 = \dfrac{2\beta S}{\beta} = 2S$

The total distance travelled is given as $10S$. Therefore:

$S + S_2 + S_3 = 10S$

$S + vt + 2S = 10S$

$vt = 7S$

Substituting $v = \sqrt{2\beta S}$:

$\sqrt{2\beta S} \cdot t = 7S$

Squaring both sides:

$2\beta S \cdot t^2 = 49S^2$

$\dfrac{S}{t^2} = \dfrac{2\beta}{49}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2\beta}{49}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bus covers the first half of the total distance 6 km at a speed ' $u$ ' and the second half at speed of $30 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. If the average speed is $15 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ the value of ' $u$ ' is:
questions.solution:
Let the total distance be $D = 6$ km. The bus covers the first half distance $d = 3$ km at speed $u$ and the second half distance $d = 3$ km at speed $v = 30$ km h$^{-1}$.

The time taken for the first half is $t_1 = \dfrac{d}{u} = \dfrac{3}{u}$.

The time taken for the second half is $t_2 = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{3}{30} = \dfrac{1}{10}$ h.

The average speed $v_{avg}$ is defined as the total distance divided by the total time:

$v_{avg} = \dfrac{D}{t_1 + t_2} = \dfrac{6}{\dfrac{3}{u} + \dfrac{1}{10}}$

Given $v_{avg} = 15$ km h$^{-1}$, we have:

$15 = \dfrac{6}{\dfrac{3}{u} + \dfrac{1}{10}}$

Dividing both sides by 3:

$5 = \dfrac{2}{\dfrac{3}{u} + \dfrac{1}{10}}$

Rearranging the terms:

$\dfrac{3}{u} + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

$\dfrac{3}{u} = \dfrac{2}{5} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{4 - 1}{10} = \dfrac{3}{10}$

Therefore, $u = 10$ km h$^{-1}$.

Answer: $10 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car, starting from rest, accelerates at the rate (f) through a distance (S), then continues at constant speed for some time $(\mathrm{t})$ and then decelerates at the rate $\dfrac{f}{2}$ to come to rest. If the total distance is 5 S , then
questions.solution:
Let the car accelerate from rest at rate $f$ for distance $S$. The final velocity $v$ reached is given by $v^2 = 0^2 + 2fS$, so $v = \sqrt{2fS}$. The time taken for this phase is $t_1 = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2fS}}{f} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2S}{f}}$.

The car then travels at constant speed $v$ for time $t$. The distance covered in this phase is $S_2 = vt = t\sqrt{2fS}$.

Finally, the car decelerates at rate $\dfrac{f}{2}$ to come to rest. Let the distance covered be $S_3$. Using $v^2 = 2aS_3$, we have $v^2 = 2(\dfrac{f}{2})S_3$, which gives $S_3 = \dfrac{v^2}{f} = \dfrac{2fS}{f} = 2S$.

The total distance is given as $5S$. Thus, $S + S_2 + S_3 = 5S$. Substituting the values, $S + t\sqrt{2fS} + 2S = 5S$.

Simplifying, $t\sqrt{2fS} = 2S$. Squaring both sides, $t^2(2fS) = 4S^2$.

Dividing by $2S$ (assuming $S \neq 0$), we get $t^2 f = 2S$, which implies $S = \dfrac{1}{2} f t^2$.

Answer: $S=\dfrac{1}{2} f t^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Select the graph which represents the motion of a particle along a straight line with uniform acceleration.
questions.solution:
For a particle moving in a straight line with uniform acceleration $a$, the velocity $v$ at time $t$ is given by the equation $v = u + at$, where $u$ is the initial velocity.

If the particle starts from rest ($u = 0$), the equation becomes $v = at$. This represents a linear relationship between velocity and time, which is a straight line passing through the origin with a slope equal to the acceleration $a$.

Among the given options, the third graph shows a velocity-time graph that is a straight line passing through the origin, which corresponds to motion with uniform acceleration starting from rest.

Answer:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle moves towards west with a velocity of $10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. After 10s its direction changes towards south and it moves with the same velocity. The average acceleration of the particle is:
questions.solution:
The initial velocity vector is $\vec{v}_i = -10 \hat{i} \text{ m/s}$ (towards west).

The final velocity vector is $\vec{v}_f = -10 \hat{j} \text{ m/s}$ (towards south).

The change in velocity is $\Delta \vec{v} = \vec{v}_f - \vec{v}_i = -10 \hat{j} - (-10 \hat{i}) = 10 \hat{i} - 10 \hat{j} \text{ m/s}$.

The time interval is $\Delta t = 10 \text{ s}$.

The average acceleration is $\vec{a}_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{10 \hat{i} - 10 \hat{j}}{10} = 1 \hat{i} - 1 \hat{j} \text{ m/s}^2$.

The magnitude of the average acceleration is $|\vec{a}_{avg}| = \sqrt{1^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{2} \text{ m/s}^2$.

The direction is given by the vector $\hat{i} - \hat{j}$, which points towards the South-East (SE) direction.

Answer: $\sqrt{2} m s^{-2} S E$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stone is dropped from a height $h$. It hits the ground with a certain momentum ' $p$ '. If the same stone is dropped from a different height h' such that percentage change in momentum is $41.4 \%$, then the height from which the stone is dropped is $\mathrm{h}^\prime=x \mathrm{~h}$, where $x$ is:
questions.solution:
The momentum $p$ of a stone dropped from height $h$ is given by $p = mv$, where $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. Thus, $p = m\sqrt{2gh}$, which implies $p \propto \sqrt{h}$.

Let $p$ be the initial momentum and $p'$ be the final momentum. The percentage change in momentum is given as $41.4\%$.

$\dfrac{p' - p}{p} = 0.414$

$\dfrac{p'}{p} = 1 + 0.414 = 1.414$

Since $p \propto \sqrt{h}$, we have $\dfrac{p'}{p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{h'}{h}}$.

Substituting the values, $\sqrt{\dfrac{h'}{h}} = 1.414$.

Squaring both sides, $\dfrac{h'}{h} = (1.414)^2$.

Since $1.414 \approx \sqrt{2}$, we have $\dfrac{h'}{h} = (\sqrt{2})^2 = 2$.

Therefore, $h' = 2h$, which gives $x = 2$.

Answer: $2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle starts from rest and moves along the x -axis with a velocity that varies as $\mathrm{v}=\sqrt{100+4 x} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. The acceleration of the particle is:
questions.solution:
Given the velocity $v = \sqrt{100 + 4x}$.

The acceleration $a$ of a particle moving in one dimension is given by $a = v \dfrac{dv}{dx}$.

Differentiating $v = (100 + 4x)^{1/2}$ with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2} (100 + 4x)^{-1/2} \times 4 = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{100 + 4x}}$.

Substituting $v$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ into the expression for acceleration:

$a = \sqrt{100 + 4x} \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{100 + 4x}}$.

$a = 2 \text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Answer: $2 m s^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A man standing in a truck moving with constant velocity throws a ball vertically into air, ball falls
options: Exactly in the hand of the boy
In the truck behind the boy
In the truck ahead of the boy
questions.solution:
The truck is moving with a constant velocity $v$ in the horizontal direction. When the man throws the ball vertically upward, the ball possesses the same initial horizontal velocity $v$ as the truck and the man.

Since there is no horizontal acceleration acting on the ball (ignoring air resistance), its horizontal velocity remains constant at $v$ throughout the flight.

The truck also continues to move with the same constant horizontal velocity $v$.

Because both the ball and the truck cover the same horizontal distance in the same time interval, the ball remains directly above the point from which it was thrown relative to the truck.

Therefore, the ball falls exactly back into the hand of the man.

Answer: Exactly in the hand of the boy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The graph of an object moving with speed v for a time t is shown below. The graph that shows the distance s travelled by the same object for a time t is
questions.solution:
Since $v = \dfrac{ds}{dt}$, the slope of the $s$-$t$ graph equals speed at every instant.

At $t = 0$: $v = 0 \Rightarrows$-$t$ graph starts with zero slope (horizontal tangent).

First half (increasing $v$): slope of $s$-$t$ increases \Rightarrow curve bends upward (concave up).

At peak $v$: steepest slope on $s$-$t$ graph (inflection point).

Second half (decreasing $v$): slope decreases \Rightarrow curve bends downward (concave down).

At end: $v = 0$ again \Rightarrow slope returns to zero (curve flattens).

Since speed is always $\geq 0$, distance never decreases. The $s$-$t$ graph starts flat, steepens, then flattens again — an S-shaped curve, which matches option (4).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When two objects are moving along a straight line in the same direction, the distance between them increases by $6 \mathrm{~m}$ in one second. If the objects move with their constant speed towards each other the distance decreases by $8 \mathrm{~m}$ in one second, then the speed of the objects are :
questions.solution:
Let the speeds of the two objects be $v_1$ and $v_2$ in $\text{ms}^{-1}$, where $v_1 \gt v_2$.

When moving in the same direction, the relative speed is $v_1 - v_2$. The distance between them increases by $6 \text{ m}$ in $1 \text{ s}$, so $v_1 - v_2 = \dfrac{6 \text{ m}}{1 \text{ s}} = 6 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

When moving towards each other, the relative speed is $v_1 + v_2$. The distance between them decreases by $8 \text{ m}$ in $1 \text{ s}$, so $v_1 + v_2 = \dfrac{8 \text{ m}}{1 \text{ s}} = 8 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Adding the two equations: $(v_1 - v_2) + (v_1 + v_2) = 6 + 8 \Rightarrow 2v_1 = 14 \Rightarrow v_1 = 7 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Subtracting the first equation from the second: $(v_1 + v_2) - (v_1 - v_2) = 8 - 6 \Rightarrow 2v_2 = 2 \Rightarrow v_2 = 1 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

The speeds of the objects are $7 \text{ ms}^{-1}$ and $1 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $7 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ and $1 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is projected vertically upwards. The times corresponding to height $h$ while ascending and while descending are $t_1$ and $t_2$, respectively. Then, the velocity of projection will be (take, $g$ as acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Let $v$ be initial velocity of vertical projection and $t$ be the time taken by the body to reach a height $h$ from ground.
Here, $\quad u=u, a=-g, s=h, t=t$
Using,
$s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2$, we have
$\begin{aligned}
& h=u t+\frac{1}{2}(-g) t^2 \\
& g t^2-2 u t+2 h=0 \\
& t=\frac{2 u \pm \sqrt{4 u^2-4 g \times 2 h}}{2 g}=\frac{u \pm \sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g}
\end{aligned}$
It means $t$ has two values, i.e.
$\begin{aligned}
t_1 & =\frac{u+\sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g} \Rightarrow t_2=\frac{u-\sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g} \\
t_1+t_2 & =\frac{2 u}{g} \text { or } u=\frac{g\left(t_1+t_2\right)}{2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A drone is flying due west, a little above the train, with a speed of $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. A 270 meter long train is moving due east at a speed of $20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The time taken by the drone to cross the train is
questions.solution:
Let the velocity of the drone be $\vec{v}_{d} = -10 \hat{i} \text{ m/s}$ (due west).

Let the velocity of the train be $\vec{v}_{t} = 20 \hat{i} \text{ m/s}$ (due east).

The relative velocity of the drone with respect to the train is $\vec{v}_{dt} = \vec{v}_{d} - \vec{v}_{t} = -10 \hat{i} - 20 \hat{i} = -30 \hat{i} \text{ m/s}$.

The magnitude of the relative velocity is $|\vec{v}_{dt}| = 30 \text{ m/s}$.

The length of the train is $L = 270 \text{ m}$.

The time taken by the drone to cross the train is $t = \dfrac{L}{|\vec{v}_{dt}|} = \dfrac{270}{30} = 9 \text{ s}$.

Answer: 9 s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The nucleus of a helium atom travels along the inside of a straight hollow tube $4 \mathrm{~m}$ long which forms part of a particle accelerator. If one assumes uniform acceleration, how long is the particle in the tube if it enters at a speed of $2000 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and leaves at $8000 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
questions.solution:
Given the length of the tube $s = 4 \text{ m}$, the initial velocity $u = 2000 \text{ m/s}$, and the final velocity $v = 8000 \text{ m/s}$.

Assuming uniform acceleration, the average velocity $v_{avg}$ is given by the formula $v_{avg} = \dfrac{u + v}{2}$.

Substituting the given values, $v_{avg} = \dfrac{2000 + 8000}{2} = \dfrac{10000}{2} = 5000 \text{ m/s}$.

The time $t$ taken to travel the distance $s$ is given by $t = \dfrac{s}{v_{avg}}$.

Substituting the values, $t = \dfrac{4}{5000} = \dfrac{4}{5 \times 10^3} = 0.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$.

Converting this to scientific notation, $t = 8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}$.

Answer: $8 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is projected vertically upwards. The times corresponding to height $h$ while ascending and while descending are $t_1$ and $t_2$, respectively. Then, the velocity of projection will be (take, $g$ as acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Let $u$ be the velocity of projection. The equation of motion for a body at height $h$ is given by $h = ut - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$.

Rearranging the terms, we get a quadratic equation in $t$: $\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 - ut + h = 0$.

The roots of this equation are $t_1$ and $t_2$, which correspond to the times at which the body is at height $h$ during ascent and descent, respectively.

From the properties of quadratic equations, the sum of the roots is $t_1 + t_2 = \dfrac{u}{g/2} = \dfrac{2u}{g}$.

The product of the roots is $t_1 t_2 = \dfrac{h}{g/2} = \dfrac{2h}{g}$.

The total time of flight $T$ is the time taken to reach the maximum height and return to the ground, which is $T = t_1 + t_2 = \dfrac{2u}{g}$.

Therefore, the velocity of projection $u$ is given by $u = \dfrac{g(t_1 + t_2)}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{g\left(t_1+t_2\right)}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to a speed of $180 \mathrm{~kmh}^{-1}$ in $10 \mathrm{~s}$. The distance covered by the car in this time interval is
questions.solution:
The initial velocity $u = 0$ m/s. The final velocity $v = 180 \text{ kmh}^{-1}$.

Converting $v$ to m/s: $v = 180 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 50 \text{ m/s}$.

The time interval $t = 10 \text{ s}$.

Since the acceleration is uniform, the average velocity is $\dfrac{u + v}{2} = \dfrac{0 + 50}{2} = 25 \text{ m/s}$.

The distance covered $s = \text{average velocity} \times t = 25 \text{ m/s} \times 10 \text{ s} = 250 \text{ m}$.

Answer: 250 m

questions.q: The displacement $x$ of a particle in a straight line motion is given by $x = 1 - t^2$. The correct representation of the motion is
questions.solution:
Given $x = 1 - t^2$

At $t = 0$: $x = 1$, so the graph must start at a positive value on the $x$-axis. This eliminates graph (1) which starts at the origin.

Velocity: $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -2t$. At $t = 0$, $v = 0$, so the slope of the $x$-$t$ graph must be zero (horizontal) at the start. This eliminates graph (4) which has a positive initial slope.

Acceleration: $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -2$, a negative constant, so the $x$-$t$ graph must be a downward-opening parabola. This eliminates graph (3) which opens upward.

Graph (2) starts at a positive $x$-value, has zero initial slope, and forms a downward-opening parabola — consistent with $x = 1 - t^2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which graph shows the correct $v-x$ graph of a freely falling body?
questions.solution:
For a body falling freely under gravity from rest, the initial velocity $u = 0$ and acceleration $a = g$.

The equation of motion is $v^2 - u^2 = 2as$.

Substituting $u = 0$, $a = g$, and displacement $s = x$, we get $v^2 = 2gx$.

This implies $v = \sqrt{2gx}$, which can be written as $v = \sqrt{2g} \cdot \sqrt{x}$.

This equation represents a parabolic relationship between $v$ and $x$, specifically of the form $v^2 \propto x$.

The graph of $v$ versus $x$ is a parabola opening along the positive $x$-axis, starting from the origin $(0,0)$.

Comparing this with the given options, the first graph shows this parabolic behavior starting from the origin.

Answer:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The displacement $x$ of a particle varies with time $t, x=a e^{-p t}+b e^{q t}$, where $a, b, p$ and $q$ are positive constant. The velocity of the particle will
questions.solution:
The displacement of the particle is given by $x = a e^{-pt} + b e^{qt}$, where $a, b, p, q \gt 0$.

The velocity $v$ is the time derivative of displacement $x$:

$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(a e^{-pt} + b e^{qt})$

$v = -ap e^{-pt} + bq e^{qt}$

To determine the behavior of velocity with time, we find the acceleration $a_{acc}$ by differentiating $v$ with respect to $t$:

$a_{acc} = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(-ap e^{-pt} + bq e^{qt})$

$a_{acc} = ap^2 e^{-pt} + bq^2 e^{qt}$

Since $a, b, p, q \gt 0$, the terms $ap^2 e^{-pt}$ and $bq^2 e^{qt}$ are always positive for all $t \ge 0$. Therefore, $a_{acc} \gt 0$ for all $t$.

Since the acceleration is positive, the velocity $v$ must be an increasing function of time. As $t$ increases, $e^{qt}$ grows exponentially, causing $v$ to increase without bound.

Answer: go on increasing forever

questions.q:
A bullet moving with a speed of $100 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ can just penetrate two planks of equal thickness.
Then, the number of such planks penetrated by the same bullet when the speed is doubled will be
questions.solution:
Given, velocity of the bullet $v=100 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$
Let, thickness of one plank, $t=s$
According to third equation of motion, we get
$v^{2}-u^{2}=2 a s(0)-(100)^{2}=2 \times a \times(2 s)$
( $\because$ two planks are penetrated)
$\Rightarrow \quad-1000=4 a s \quad \ldots$. (i)
When velocity of bullet is doubled, $v=200 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$
Applying third equation of motion again, we get
$\Rightarrow \quad 0-(200)^{2}=2 \times a \times(n s)$
(where, $n$ is number of planks)
$-40000=2 a n s$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\frac{-40000}{-10000}=\frac{2 a n s}{4 a s}\Rightarrow \quad n=8$
Hence, 8 planks can be penetrated by the same bullet if speed is doubled.

questions.q:
A simple pendulum is suspended from the
ceiling of a lift. When the lift is at rest its time
period is T. With what acceleration should the
lift be accelerated upwards in order to reduce
its period to T / 2 ?
(g is acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Time-period of simple pendulum is given as

T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}

If $a$ be the acceleration of the lift, so that time-period of simple pendulum is reduced to $T / 2$.
$\begin{aligned} \text { i.e. } & T^{\prime}=T / 2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g+a}} &=\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} \end{aligned}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{l}{g+a}=\frac{1}{4}, \frac{l}{g}\Rightarrow \quad g+a=4 g\Rightarrow \quad a=3 g$

questions.solution:

When a lift containing a simple pendulum is accelerated upwards with acceleration $a$, then its time period becomes
$T^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{l}{(g+a)}}$
Clearly, $\quad T^{\prime} \angle T$
Hence, its time period decreases.

questions.q: A boy, standing at a certain height, kicks a football horizontally with a velocity of $19.6\ ms^{-1}$. What will be the ratio of horizontal and vertical components of velocities after 2s?
questions.solution:
Initial horizontal velocity, $u_x = 19.6\ ms^{-1}$

Initial vertical velocity, $u_y = 0\ ms^{-1}$

Acceleration in horizontal direction, $a_x = 0$

Acceleration in vertical direction, $a_y = g = 9.8\ ms^{-2}$

Time, $t = 2\ s$

Horizontal velocity after $2\ s$, $v_x = u_x + a_x t = 19.6\ ms^{-1}$

Vertical velocity after $2\ s$, $v_y = u_y + a_y t = 0 + 9.8 \times 2 = 19.6\ ms^{-1}$
