If the rate of flow of heat through the rods is equal, the ratio of area of cross section of $A$ to that of $B$ is
questions.solution:
The rate of heat flow $H$ through a rod is given by the formula $H = \dfrac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}$, where $K$ is the thermal conductivity, $A$ is the area of cross-section, $L$ is the length, and $(T_1 - T_2)$ is the temperature difference across the ends.

Given that the rate of heat flow is equal for both rods, we have $H_A = H_B$.

Let $L_A = L$ and $L_B = 2L$ based on the ratio $1:2$. Let $A_A$ and $A_B$ be the areas of cross-section of rods $A$ and $B$ respectively.

Equating the heat flow rates:
$\dfrac{K_1 A_A (T_1 - T_2)}{L_A} = \dfrac{K_2 A_B (T_1 - T_2)}{L_B}$

Since the temperature difference $(T_1 - T_2)$ is the same for both rods, it cancels out:
$\dfrac{K_1 A_A}{L} = \dfrac{K_2 A_B}{2L}$

Simplifying the equation by cancelling $L$ from both sides:
$K_1 A_A = \dfrac{K_2 A_B}{2}$

Rearranging to find the ratio $\dfrac{A_A}{A_B}$:
$\dfrac{A_A}{A_B} = \dfrac{K_2}{2 K_1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{K_2}{2 K_1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The rate of heat conduction in the given two metal rods having the same length is found to be the same when the temperature difference between the ends is kept $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ If the area of cross section of the first rod is $8 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$ then what will be area of cross section of the second rod? [ Given that the ratio of the thermal conductivity of the first rod to that of the second rod is $1: 4$ ]
questions.solution:
The rate of heat conduction $H$ through a rod is given by the formula $H = \dfrac{KA \Delta T}{L}$, where $K$ is the thermal conductivity, $A$ is the area of cross-section, $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference, and $L$ is the length of the rod.

Given that the rate of heat conduction is the same for both rods, we have $H_1 = H_2$. Substituting the formula for both rods:

$\dfrac{K_1 A_1 \Delta T_1}{L_1} = \dfrac{K_2 A_2 \Delta T_2}{L_2}$

Since the lengths $L_1 = L_2$ and the temperature differences $\Delta T_1 = \Delta T_2 = 30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ are the same, the equation simplifies to:

$K_1 A_1 = K_2 A_2$

Rearranging to solve for $A_2$:

$A_2 = A_1 \times \left( \dfrac{K_1}{K_2} \right)$

Given $A_1 = 8 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$ and the ratio $\dfrac{K_1}{K_2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$, we substitute these values:

$A_2 = (8 \times 10^{-2}) \times \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = 2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$

Answer: $2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of metal A is connected in series with another block of metal B such that the two metal blocks have the same area of cross sections. The thermal conductivity of metal A is K and the free end of metal A is at $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The temperature of the interface is $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the free end of metal B is at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Assuming the two metals have the same thickness, the conductivity of metal B is:
questions.solution:
In a steady state, the rate of heat flow through two blocks connected in series is the same. Let $A$ be the cross-sectional area and $L$ be the thickness of each block. The rate of heat flow $H$ is given by $H = \dfrac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}$.

For metal A, the temperature difference is $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C} - 60^{\circ} \mathrm{C} = 20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Thus, $H_A = \dfrac{KA(80 - 60)}{L} = \dfrac{20KA}{L}$.

For metal B, let $K_B$ be its thermal conductivity. The temperature difference is $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C} - 20^{\circ} \mathrm{C} = 40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Thus, $H_B = \dfrac{K_B A(60 - 20)}{L} = \dfrac{40K_B A}{L}$.

Since the blocks are in series, $H_A = H_B$. Therefore, $\dfrac{20KA}{L} = \dfrac{40K_B A}{L}$.

Simplifying the equation, $20K = 40K_B$, which gives $K_B = \dfrac{20K}{40} = \dfrac{K}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{K}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin copper wire of length $L$ increases in length by $1 \%$, when heated from temperature $T_1$ to $T_2$. What is the percentage change in area when a thin copper plate having dimensions $(10 L \times 2 L)$ is heated from $T_1$ to $T_2$ ?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} &  A=10 L \times 2 L=20 L^2 \\ & \frac{\Delta A}{A} \times 100=2 \frac{\Delta L}{L} \times 100=2 \times 1=2 \%\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 100 g of ice at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is mixed with 100 g of water at $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The final temperature of the mixture is (Given, latent heat of fusion of ice, $L_f=80 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}$ and specific heat capacity of water, $S_{\text {water }}=1 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )
questions.solution:
Let the final temperature of mixture be $T^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
From principle of calorimetry,
Heat given by 100 g of water $=$ Heat taken by 100 g of ice
$m_1 S_{\text {water }}\left(\Delta T_1\right)=m_2 L_f+m_2 S_{\text {water }} \Delta T_2$
Substituting the given values, we get
$\begin{aligned} \\ & 100 \times 1 \times(80-T)=100 \times 80+100 \times 1 \times(T-0) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 80-T=80+T \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 2 T=0 \Rightarrow T=0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the given substances $A, B$ and $C$ have more specific heat?
questions.solution:
Substnnces having more specific heat take longer time to get heated to a higher temperature and longer time to get cooled.

If we draw a line parallel to the time axis, then it cuts the given graphs at three different points.
Corresponding points on the time axes shows that,
$\begin{array}{ll}
& t_C \gt t_B \gt t_A \\
\Rightarrow \quad & c_C \gt c_B \gt c_A
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the coefficient of volume expansion of brass is $6 \times 10^{-5}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$, then fractional change in its density for a $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ rise in temperature will be
questions.solution:
Density at temperature $T$ is given by
$\begin{aligned} \\ \rho & =\rho_0(1-\alpha \Delta T) \\ \\ \rho & =\rho_0-\rho_0 \alpha \Delta T \\ \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\rho-\rho_0}{\rho_0} & =-\alpha \Delta T \\ \end{aligned}$
$\therefore$ Fractional change in density,
$\begin{aligned} \\ & \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho_0}=-\alpha \Delta T=-6 \times 10^{-5} \times 60 \\ \\ & \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho_0}=-3.6 \times 10^{-3} \\ \end{aligned}$
Note: Negative sign indicates that density decreases with rise in temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The thickness of a metallic plate is 0.4 cm . The temperature between its two surfaces is $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The quantity of heat flowing per second is 50 cal from $5 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ area. In CGS system, the coefficient of thermal conductivity will be
questions.solution: $\begin{array}{ll} & \frac{Q}{t}=\frac{K A(\Delta \theta)}{l} \\ \Rightarrow & 50=\frac{5 \times 20 K}{0.4} \\ \Rightarrow & K=\frac{1}{5}=0.2\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An iron piece of mass $200 \mathrm{~g}$ is kept inside a furnace for some time and then put in a calorimeter of water equivalent $20 \mathrm{~g}$ containing $230 \mathrm{~g}$ of water at $20 \mathrm{C}$. The steady state temperature attained by the mixture is $60^{\circ}$. The temperature of the furnace is (Specific heat capacity of iron is $470 \mathrm{~J~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
Let $T$ be the temperature of the furnace. The heat lost by the iron piece is equal to the heat gained by the calorimeter and the water.

Mass of iron $m_{Fe} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$.
Specific heat of iron $c_{Fe} = 470 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \text{ C}^{-1}$.
Water equivalent of calorimeter $w = 0.02 \text{ kg}$.
Mass of water $m_w = 0.23 \text{ kg}$.
Specific heat of water $c_w = 4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \text{ C}^{-1}$.
Initial temperature of water and calorimeter $T_i = 20^{\circ} \text{C}$.
Final steady state temperature $T_f = 60^{\circ} \text{C}$.

Heat lost by iron = $m_{Fe} c_{Fe} (T - T_f) = 0.2 \times 470 \times (T - 60) = 94(T - 60)$.

Heat gained by calorimeter and water = $(w + m_w) c_w (T_f - T_i) = (0.02 + 0.23) \times 4200 \times (60 - 20) = 0.25 \times 4200 \times 40 = 42000 \text{ J}$.

Equating heat lost and heat gained:
$94(T - 60) = 42000$
$T - 60 = \dfrac{42000}{94} \approx 446.81$
$T = 446.81 + 60 = 506.81^{\circ} \text{C}$.

Answer: 506.8$^\circ$C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The coefficient of volume expansion of glycerine is $49 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$. The percentage change in its density for a $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ rise in temperature is
questions.solution:
The density $\rho$ of a liquid at temperature $T$ is related to its density $\rho_0$ at initial temperature $T_0$ by the relation $\rho = \dfrac{\rho_0}{1 + \gamma \Delta T}$, where $\gamma$ is the coefficient of volume expansion and $\Delta T$ is the change in temperature.

The change in density $\Delta \rho = \rho - \rho_0 = \rho_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{1 + \gamma \Delta T} - 1 \right) = \rho_0 \left( \dfrac{1 - 1 - \gamma \Delta T}{1 + \gamma \Delta T} \right) = - \dfrac{\rho_0 \gamma \Delta T}{1 + \gamma \Delta T}$.

For small values of $\gamma \Delta T$, the expression simplifies to $\Delta \rho \approx -\rho_0 \gamma \Delta T$.

The percentage change in density is given by $\left| \dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho_0} \right| \times 100 = \gamma \Delta T \times 100$.

Given $\gamma = 49 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$ and $\Delta T = 50^{\circ} \text{C} = 50 \text{ K}$.

Percentage change $= 49 \times 10^{-5} \times 50 \times 100 = 49 \times 50 \times 10^{-3} = 2450 \times 10^{-3} = 2.45$.

Answer: 2.45

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A one $\mathrm{kg}$ block of ice at $-1.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ falls from a height of $1.5 \mathrm{~km}$ and is found melting. The amount of ice melted due to fall, if $60 \%$ energy is converted into heat is (Specific heat capacity of ice is $0.5 \mathrm{~cal} \mathrm{~g}^{-1} \mathrm{~C}^{-1}$, Latent heat of fusion of ice $=80 \mathrm{~cal~g}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
PE lost $= mgh = 1 \times 9.8 \times 1500 = 14700$ J

Heat generated $= 0.6 \times 14700 = 8820$ J $= \dfrac{8820}{4.2} = 2100$ cal

Heat to warm ice from $-1.5°C$ to $0°C$:
$Q_1 = 1000 \times 0.5 \times 1.5 = 750$ cal

Heat available for melting:
$Q_{melt} = 2100 - 750 = 1350$ cal

Mass melted $= \dfrac{Q_{melt}}{L} = \dfrac{1350}{80} \approx 16.9$ g

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A glass of hot water cools from $90^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $70^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in 3 minutes when the temperature of surroundings is $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. What is the time taken by the glass of hot water to cool from $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ if the surrounding temperature remains the same at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?
questions.solution:
According to Newton's law of cooling, the rate of cooling is given by $\dfrac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_s)$, where $T$ is the temperature of the body, $T_s$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k$ is a constant.

For the first interval, $T_1 = 90^{\circ} \text{C}$, $T_2 = 70^{\circ} \text{C}$, $T_s = 20^{\circ} \text{C}$, and $t = 3 \text{ minutes}$. Using the average temperature approximation $\dfrac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k \left( \dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_s \right)$, we get $\dfrac{90 - 70}{3} = k \left( \dfrac{90 + 70}{2} - 20 \right)$.

$\dfrac{20}{3} = k(80 - 20) = 60k$, which implies $k = \dfrac{20}{3 \times 60} = \dfrac{1}{9}$.

For the second interval, $T_1 = 60^{\circ} \text{C}$, $T_2 = 40^{\circ} \text{C}$, $T_s = 20^{\circ} \text{C}$, and we need to find $t'$. Using the same formula, $\dfrac{60 - 40}{t'} = k \left( \dfrac{60 + 40}{2} - 20 \right)$.

$\dfrac{20}{t'} = \dfrac{1}{9} (50 - 20) = \dfrac{30}{9} = \dfrac{10}{3}$.

Solving for $t'$, $t' = \dfrac{20 \times 3}{10} = 6 \text{ minutes}$.

Answer: 6 minutes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two slabs are of the thicknesses $d_1$ and $d_2$. Their thermal conductivities are $K_1$ and $K_2$, respectively. They are in series. The free ends of the combination of these two slabs are kept at temperatures $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$. Assume $\theta_1 \gt \theta_2$. The temperature $\theta$ of their common junction is
questions.solution:
For first slab,
Heat current, $H_1=\frac{K_1\left(\theta_1-\theta\right) A}{d_1}$ For second slab, Heat current, $H_2=\frac{K_2\left(\theta-\theta_2\right) A}{d_2}$ As slabs are in series, $H_1=H_2\begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \frac{K_1\left(\theta_1-\theta\right) A}{d_1}=\frac{K_2\left(\theta-\theta_2\right) A}{d_2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \theta & \quad \theta=\frac{K_1 \theta_1 d_2+K_2 \theta_2 d_1}{K_2 d_1+K_1 d_2} \end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylinder of radius $r$ and of thermal conductivity $K_1$ is surrounded by a cylindrical shell of inner radius $r$ and outer radius $2 r$ made of a material of thermal conductivity $K_2$. The effective thermal conductivity of the system is
questions.solution:
Both the cylinders are in parallel, for the heat flow from one end as shown
So, $K_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{K_1 A_1+K_2 A_2}{A_1+A_2}$ where, $A_1=$ area of cross-section of inner cylinder $=\pi R^2$ and $\quad A_2=$ area of cross-section of cylindrical shell $\begin{aligned} & =\pi\left\{(2 R)^2-(R)^2\right\}=3 \pi R^2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad K_{\mathrm{eq}} & =\frac{K_1\left(\pi R^2\right)+K_2\left(3 \pi R^2\right)}{\pi R^2+3 \pi R^2}=\frac{1}{4}\left(K_1+3 K_2\right) \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two black bodies $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{Q}$ have equal surface areas and are kept at temperatures $127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ respectively. The ratio of thermal power radiated by A to that by B is
questions.solution:
The thermal power radiated by a black body is given by the Stefan-Boltzmann law: $P = \sigma A T^{4}$, where $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $A$ is the surface area, and $T$ is the absolute temperature in Kelvin.

Given the temperatures in Celsius:
$T_{P} = 127^{\circ} \text{C} = 127 + 273 = 400 \text{ K}$
$T_{Q} = 27^{\circ} \text{C} = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$

The ratio of thermal power radiated by P to that by Q is:
$\dfrac{P_{P}}{P_{Q}} = \dfrac{\sigma A T_{P}^{4}}{\sigma A T_{Q}^{4}} = \left( \dfrac{T_{P}}{T_{Q}} \right)^{4}$

Substituting the values:
$\dfrac{P_{P}}{P_{Q}} = \left( \dfrac{400}{300} \right)^{4} = \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)^{4}$

Calculating the power:
$\dfrac{P_{P}}{P_{Q}} = \dfrac{4^{4}}{3^{4}} = \dfrac{256}{81}$

Answer: $256: 81$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylinder of radius $r$ and of thermal conductivity $K_1$ is surrounded by a cylindrical shell of inner radius $r$ and outer radius $2 r$ made of a material of thermal conductivity $K_2$. The effective thermal conductivity of the system is
questions.solution:
Consider a length $L$ of the composite cylinder. The system consists of two cylindrical layers in parallel for radial heat flow. The thermal resistance $R$ of a cylindrical shell of inner radius $r_1$, outer radius $r_2$, length $L$, and thermal conductivity $K$ is given by $R = \dfrac{\ln(r_2/r_1)}{2 \pi K L}$.

For the inner cylinder of radius $r$, we consider it as a solid cylinder. However, in the context of effective thermal conductivity for radial heat flow, we treat the cross-sectional area. The total cross-sectional area $A$ of the composite cylinder is $\pi (2r)^2 = 4 \pi r^2$.

The thermal resistance of the inner cylinder of radius $r$ is $R_1 = \dfrac{\ln(r/0)}{2 \pi K_1 L}$, which is not well-defined for a solid cylinder. Instead, we use the area-weighted average conductivity for parallel heat flow across the cross-section. The effective thermal conductivity $K_{eff}$ is given by $K_{eff} = \dfrac{\sum K_i A_i}{\sum A_i}$.

The area of the inner cylinder is $A_1 = \pi r^2$. The area of the outer shell is $A_2 = \pi (2r)^2 - \pi r^2 = 3 \pi r^2$.

The total area is $A = A_1 + A_2 = 4 \pi r^2$.

Therefore, $K_{eff} = \dfrac{K_1 A_1 + K_2 A_2}{A_1 + A_2} = \dfrac{K_1 (\pi r^2) + K_2 (3 \pi r^2)}{4 \pi r^2} = \dfrac{K_1 + 3 K_2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}(K_1 + 3 K_2)$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4}\left(K_1+3 K_2\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two slabs are of the thicknesses $d_1$ and $d_2$. Their thermal conductivities are $K_1$ and $K_2$, respectively. They are in series. The free ends of the combination of these two slabs are kept at temperatures $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$. Assume $\theta_1 \gt  \theta_2$. The temperature $\theta$ of their common junction is
questions.solution:
In a series combination of two slabs, the rate of heat flow $H$ through each slab must be the same in the steady state.

The rate of heat flow through the first slab is $H = \dfrac{K_1 A (\theta_1 - \theta)}{d_1}$, where $A$ is the cross-sectional area.

The rate of heat flow through the second slab is $H = \dfrac{K_2 A (\theta - \theta_2)}{d_2}$.

Equating the two expressions for $H$:

$\dfrac{K_1 A (\theta_1 - \theta)}{d_1} = \dfrac{K_2 A (\theta - \theta_2)}{d_2}$

Canceling $A$ and rearranging the terms:

$\dfrac{K_1}{d_1} (\theta_1 - \theta) = \dfrac{K_2}{d_2} (\theta - \theta_2)$

$\dfrac{K_1 \theta_1}{d_1} - \dfrac{K_1 \theta}{d_1} = \dfrac{K_2 \theta}{d_2} - \dfrac{K_2 \theta_2}{d_2}$

$\theta \left( \dfrac{K_1}{d_1} + \dfrac{K_2}{d_2} \right) = \dfrac{K_1 \theta_1}{d_1} + \dfrac{K_2 \theta_2}{d_2}$

$\theta \left( \dfrac{K_1 d_2 + K_2 d_1}{d_1 d_2} \right) = \dfrac{K_1 \theta_1 d_2 + K_2 \theta_2 d_1}{d_1 d_2}$

$\theta = \dfrac{K_1 \theta_1 d_2 + K_2 \theta_2 d_1}{K_1 d_2 + K_2 d_1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{K_1 \theta_1 d_2+K_2 \theta_2 d_1}{K_1 d_2+K_2 d_1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In which mode of transmission, the heat waves travel along straight line with the speed of light?
questions.solution:
Thermal radiation is the process by which heat is transferred in the form of electromagnetic waves. These waves travel through a vacuum or a medium at the speed of light, $c \approx 3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s, and propagate in straight lines.

Answer: Thermal radiation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a compound slab consisting of two different materials having equal lengths, thickness and thermal conductivities $K$ and $2 K$ respectively. The equivalent thermal conductivity of the slab is
questions.solution:
Let the length of each slab be $L$ and the cross-sectional area be $A$. The thermal conductivities are $K_1 = K$ and $K_2 = 2K$.

When the slabs are connected in series, the total thermal resistance $R_{eq}$ is the sum of individual resistances $R_1$ and $R_2$.

$R_1 = \dfrac{L}{K_1 A} = \dfrac{L}{KA}$

$R_2 = \dfrac{L}{K_2 A} = \dfrac{L}{2KA}$

$R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 = \dfrac{L}{KA} + \dfrac{L}{2KA} = \dfrac{2L + L}{2KA} = \dfrac{3L}{2KA}$

The equivalent thermal conductivity $K_{eq}$ for a slab of total length $2L$ and area $A$ is given by $R_{eq} = \dfrac{2L}{K_{eq} A}$.

Equating the expressions for $R_{eq}$:

$\dfrac{2L}{K_{eq} A} = \dfrac{3L}{2KA}$

$\dfrac{2}{K_{eq}} = \dfrac{3}{2K}$

$K_{eq} = \dfrac{4K}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{3} K$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two conductors of the same material have their diameters in the ratio $1: 2$ and their lengths in the ratio $2: 1$. If the temperature difference between their ends is the same, then the ratio of amounts of heat conducted per second through them will be
questions.solution:
Ratio of diameters, $\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$
Ratio of lengths, $\frac{l_{1}}{l_{2}}=\frac{2}{1}$
The rate of heat conduction is given by the formula,

H=\frac{d Q}{d t}=k \frac{A}{l} \Delta T

where, $d Q$ is the amount of heat transferred in $d t$ time, $k$ is coefficient of heat conduction for a particular material. Since, $\Delta T$ is same in both cases, the ratio is

\begin{aligned}
\frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}} &=\frac{A_{1} l_{2}}{A_{2} l_{1}} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}} &=\frac{d_{1}^{2} l_{2}}{d_{2}^{2} l_{1}}=\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow R=1: 8
\end{aligned}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $\gamma$ is the ratio of specific heats and $R$ is the universal gas constant, then the molar specific heat at constant volume $C_{V}$ is given by
questions.solution:
According to Mayer's formula,
$C_{p}-C_{V}=R$
where, $C_{p}=$ specific heat at constant pressure,
$C_{V}=$ specific heat at constant volume
$R=$ gas constant .
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}}-1=\frac{R}{C_{V}}\Rightarrow \quad \gamma-1=\frac{R}{C_{V}}\Rightarrow \quad C_{V}=\frac{R}{\gamma-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The coefficient of thermal conductivity of copper is 9 times that of steel. In the composite cylindrical bar shown in the figure, what will be the temperature at the junction of copper and steel?
questions.solution:
The given situation is shown below

Thermal conductivity of copper $=9 \times$ thermal conductivity of steel K_{c}=9 K_{s} Since, both bar are connected in series, hence heat current along the bar will be same. i. e $\quad \frac{d Q}{d t}=\frac{K_{e} \mathrm{~A}\left(T_{1}-T\right)}{l_{1}}=\frac{K_{s} A\left(T-T_{2}\right)}{l_{2}}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{9 K_{\mathrm{S}} A(100-T)}{18}=\frac{K_{s} A(T-0)}{6}\Rightarrow \quad 3(100-T)=T300-3 T=T\Rightarrow \quad 4 T=300\Rightarrow \quad T=75^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A piece of blue glass heated to a high temperature and a piece of red glass at room temperature are taken inside a dimly lit room. Then
options: the blue piece will look blue and red will look as usual
red will look brighter red and blue will look ordinary blue
blue will shines like brighter red compared to the red piece
Both the pieces will look equally red
questions.solution: When blue glass is heated to a high temperature, it absorbs all radiations of higher wavelength except red. So, when it is taken inside a dimly lit room, it emits all radiations and hence looks brighter red compared to the red piece. This happens according to Kirchhoff's law of radiation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wavelength of the radiation emitted by a body depends upon
questions.solution:
According to Wien's law, the wavelength of radiation emitted by a body is
$\lambda \propto \frac{1}{T}$
i.e., it depends on the temperature of the surface.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two rods of same area of cross-section and lengths and conductivities $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ are connected in series. Then in steady state, conductivity of the combination is
questions.solution:
The thermal resistance of a rod is given by
$R=\frac{l}{K A}$
As, length and area of two rods are same, then in series combination,
$\begin{aligned} R &=R_{1}+R_{2} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2 l}{K_{s} A} &=\frac{l}{K_{1} A}+\frac{l}{K_{2} A} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2}{K_{s}} &=\frac{1}{K_{1}}+\frac{1}{K_{2}}=\frac{K_{1}+K_{2}}{K_{1} K_{2}} \\ \Rightarrow & K_{s} &=\frac{2 K_{1} K_{2}}{K_{1}+K_{2}} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: Two conductors of the same material have their diameters in the ratio $1: 2$ and their lengths in the ratio $2: 1$. If the temperature difference between their ends is the same, then the ratio of amounts of heat conducted per second through them will be
questions.solution:
The rate of heat conduction is given by

H=\frac{d \theta}{d t}=\frac{k A}{l} \Delta T

Here, $\Delta T$ is same for both conductors, so ratio of heat conduction,
$\begin{aligned} \frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}} &=\frac{A_{1}}{l_{1}} \times \frac{l_{2}}{A_{2}} \\ &=\frac{d_{1}^{2}}{l_{1}} \times \frac{l_{2}}{d_{2}^{2}} \quad\left(\because A=\frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}\right) \\ &=\left(\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}\right)^{2} \cdot \frac{l_{2}}{l_{1}} \\ &=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Following graph shows four different processes, adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric for an ideal gas, from the same initial state. Study the graph carefully and state which of the following statements is correct?
questions.solution:
From the given $P-V$ graph, we can analyze the four processes starting from the same initial state:

1. Process 1 is a vertical line parallel to the $P$-axis. This indicates that the volume $V$ remains constant while the pressure changes. Therefore, Process 1 is an isochoric process.

2. Process 4 is a horizontal line parallel to the $V$-axis. This indicates that the pressure $P$ remains constant while the volume changes. Therefore, Process 4 is an isobaric process.

3. Processes 2 and 3 are curves representing expansion (volume increases and pressure decreases). We know that the magnitude of the slope of an adiabatic curve on a $P-V$ diagram is $\gamma$ times the magnitude of the slope of an isothermal curve $\left( \left| \dfrac{dP}{dV} \right|_{\text{adiabatic}} = \gamma \dfrac{P}{V} \text{ and } \left| \dfrac{dP}{dV} \right|_{\text{isothermal}} = \dfrac{P}{V} \right)$. Since $\gamma \gt 1$, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve. Thus, the steeper curve 2 is the adiabatic process, and curve 3 is the isothermal process.

Evaluating the given options:
(A) Process 4 is adiabatic - Incorrect (it is isobaric).
(B) Process 1 is isochoric - Correct.
(C) Process 2 is isobaric - Incorrect (it is adiabatic).
(D) Process 3 is isochoric - Incorrect (it is isothermal).

Answer: Process 1 is isochoric

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two vessels A and B contain same mass of Oxygen and Hydrogen respectively at the same temperature. The volume of B is twice that of A. The ratio of gas pressure in A to that in B is
questions.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT = \dfrac{m}{M}RT$, where $m$ is the given mass and $M$ is the molar mass.

For vessel A containing Oxygen ($O_2$, $M_A = 32$):
$P_A = \dfrac{mRT}{32 V_A}$

For vessel B containing Hydrogen ($H_2$, $M_B = 2$):
$P_B = \dfrac{mRT}{2 V_B}$

Given that the volume of B is twice that of A ($V_B = 2V_A$), we get:
$P_B = \dfrac{mRT}{2(2V_A)} = \dfrac{mRT}{4V_A}$

Taking the ratio of the pressures:
$\dfrac{P_A}{P_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{mRT}{32 V_A}}{\dfrac{mRT}{4 V_A}} = \dfrac{4}{32} = \dfrac{1}{8}$

The ratio of gas pressure in A to that in B is $1:8$.

Answer: $1:8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 1 kg of water at $100^\circ$C is converted to steam at the same temperature. Volume of 1 cc of water changes to $1671 \times 10^3$ cc on boiling. The change in internal energy of the system is (Latent Heat of vaporisation of water is $22.68 \times 10^5\ J\ kg^{-1}$; 1 atm $= 1.0 \times 10^5$ Pa)
questions.solution:
Given the final volume of 1 kg of steam is $1671 \times 10^3$ cc $= 1.671$ m$^3$.

Initial volume of 1 kg of water is $1000$ cc $= 10^{-3}$ m$^3$.

Change in volume, $\Delta V = 1.671 - 0.001 = 1.670$ m$^3$.

Work done, $W = P\Delta V = 1.0 \times 10^5 \times 1.670 = 1.67 \times 10^5$ J.

Heat supplied, $Q = mL = 1 \times 22.68 \times 10^5 = 22.68 \times 10^5$ J.

Using the first law of thermodynamics, $Q = \Delta U + W$.

$\Delta U = Q - W = 22.68 \times 10^5 - 1.67 \times 10^5 = 21.01 \times 10^5$ J.

Answer: $21.01 \times 10^5\ J$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thermal source supplies heat at a rate of $300 \mathrm{Js}^{-1}$. By using that heat a system performs work at a rate of $125 \mathrm{Js}^{-1}$. What is the rate at which the internal energy of the system increases?
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the rate of heat supplied to the system is equal to the sum of the rate of work done by the system and the rate of change of internal energy of the system.

Let $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}$ be the rate of heat supply, $\dfrac{dW}{dt}$ be the rate of work done, and $\dfrac{dU}{dt}$ be the rate of change of internal energy.

The equation is given by $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{dW}{dt} + \dfrac{dU}{dt}$.

Given values are $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 300 \text{ Js}^{-1}$ and $\dfrac{dW}{dt} = 125 \text{ Js}^{-1}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$300 = 125 + \dfrac{dU}{dt}$

$\dfrac{dU}{dt} = 300 - 125 = 175 \text{ Js}^{-1}$.

Answer: $175 \mathrm{Js}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monoatomic ideal gas, initially at temperature $T_1$, is enclosed in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston. The gas is allowed to expand adiabatically to a temperature $T_2$ by releasing the piston suddenly. If $L$ and $2 L$ are the lengths of the gas column before and after expansion respectively, then $\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}$ is
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process of an ideal gas, the relationship between temperature and volume is given by $T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$.

For a monoatomic gas, the adiabatic index $\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}$. Thus, $\gamma - 1 = \dfrac{5}{3} - 1 = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

The volume of the gas is proportional to the length of the gas column, $V \propto L$. Therefore, $T_1 L_1^{2/3} = T_2 L_2^{2/3}$.

Given $L_1 = L$ and $L_2 = 2L$, we have $T_1 L^{2/3} = T_2 (2L)^{2/3}$.

Rearranging to find the ratio $\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}$:

$\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \dfrac{(2L)^{2/3}}{L^{2/3}} = \left(\dfrac{2L}{L}\right)^{2/3} = 2^{2/3}$.

Answer: $2^{2 / 3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is expanding such that $P T^2=$ constant. The coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is
questions.solution:
The equation of state for an ideal gas is $PV = nRT$.

Given $PT^{2} = C$, where $C$ is a constant, we can write $P = C T^{-2}$.

Substituting this into the ideal gas equation, we get $(C T^{-2}) V = nRT$.

Rearranging for $V$, we have $V = \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{3}$.

The coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma$ is defined as $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \left( \dfrac{dV}{dT} \right)_{P}$.

Differentiating $V$ with respect to $T$ from the relation $V = \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{3}$, we get $\dfrac{dV}{dT} = 3 \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{2}$.

Substituting $V$ and $\dfrac{dV}{dT}$ into the expression for $\gamma$:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\left( \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{3} \right)} \left( 3 \dfrac{nR}{C} T^{2} \right) = \dfrac{3}{T}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The heat required to increase the temperature of 4 moles of a mono-atomic ideal gas from $273^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $473^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ at constant volume is
questions.solution:
The heat required at constant volume is given by the formula $Q = n C_{v} \Delta T$.

For a mono-atomic ideal gas, the molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_{v} = \dfrac{3}{2} R$.

Given values are $n = 4$ moles, $T_{1} = 273^{\circ} \text{C}$, and $T_{2} = 473^{\circ} \text{C}$.

The change in temperature is $\Delta T = T_{2} - T_{1} = 473 - 273 = 200 \text{ K}$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$Q = 4 \times \left( \dfrac{3}{2} R \right) \times 200$

$Q = 4 \times 1.5 R \times 200$

$Q = 6 R \times 200 = 1200 R$.

Answer: 1200 R

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A given volume of gas at NTP is allowed to expand 6 times of its original volume, first under isothermal condition and then under adiabatic condition. Which of the given statement is correct?
[Given $\dfrac{C_p}{C_v}=\gamma=1.4$ ]
options: The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.
Pressure remains same in both adiabatic and isothermal expansion
The final temperature after the adiabatic expansion is 1.4 times less than the final temperature after the isothermal expansion.
The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is 1.4 times greater than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.
questions.solution:
Let the initial pressure be $P_0$, initial volume be $V_0$, and initial temperature be $T_0$. The gas expands to a final volume $V_f = 6V_0$.

For isothermal expansion, the final pressure $P_{iso}$ is given by $P_0 V_0 = P_{iso} (6V_0)$, which gives $P_{iso} = \dfrac{P_0}{6}$.

For adiabatic expansion, the final pressure $P_{adia}$ is given by $P_0 V_0^{\gamma} = P_{adia} (6V_0)^{\gamma}$, which gives $P_{adia} = P_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^{\gamma}$.

Given $\gamma = 1.4$, we have $P_{adia} = P_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^{1.4}$.

Comparing $P_{iso} = P_0 (6)^{-1}$ and $P_{adia} = P_0 (6)^{-1.4}$, since $6^{1.4} \gt 6^1$, it follows that $\dfrac{1}{6^{1.4}} \lt \dfrac{1}{6^1}$.

Therefore, $P_{adia} \lt P_{iso}$. The final pressure after adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after isothermal expansion.

Answer: The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sample of an ideal gas is taken through the cyclic process ABCA as shown in figure below. It absorbs 60J of heat during the part AB and rejects 80 J of heat during CA . There is no heat exchanged during the process BC . A work of 40 J is done on the gas during the part BC . If the internal energy of the gas at A is 1450 J , then the work done by the gas during the part CA is:
questions.solution:
The process is a cycle ABCA. We are given the heat exchange $Q$ and work done $W$ for each part of the cycle.

For process AB: $Q_{AB} = 60$ J. Since $W_{AB} = 0$ (as it is a vertical line on the P-V diagram, volume is constant), the change in internal energy is $\Delta U_{AB} = Q_{AB} - W_{AB} = 60 - 0 = 60$ J. Thus, $U_B - U_A = 60$ J.

For process BC: $Q_{BC} = 0$ J. Work is done on the gas, so $W_{BC} = -40$ J. The change in internal energy is $\Delta U_{BC} = Q_{BC} - W_{BC} = 0 - (-40) = 40$ J. Thus, $U_C - U_B = 40$ J.

For process CA: $Q_{CA} = -80$ J (heat is rejected). Let $W_{CA}$ be the work done by the gas during CA. The change in internal energy is $\Delta U_{CA} = Q_{CA} - W_{CA} = -80 - W_{CA}$.

Since the process is cyclic, the total change in internal energy over the cycle is zero: $\Delta U_{AB} + \Delta U_{BC} + \Delta U_{CA} = 0$.

Substituting the values: $60 + 40 + (-80 - W_{CA}) = 0$.

$100 - 80 - W_{CA} = 0$.

$20 - W_{CA} = 0 \Rightarrow W_{CA} = 20$ J.

Answer: 20 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of specific heat capacities at constant pressure to that at constant volume for a given mass of a gas is $\dfrac{5}{2}$. If the percentage increase in volume of the gas while undergoing an adiabatic change is $\dfrac{3}{2}$, then the percentage decrease in pressure will be:
questions.solution:
The ratio of specific heat capacities is given as $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v} = \dfrac{5}{2}$.

For an adiabatic process, the relation between pressure and volume is $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

Taking the logarithmic derivative, we get $\dfrac{dP}{P} + \gamma \dfrac{dV}{V} = 0$, which implies $\dfrac{dP}{P} = -\gamma \dfrac{dV}{V}$.

The percentage increase in volume is $\dfrac{dV}{V} \times 100 = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5$.

Substituting the values, the percentage change in pressure is $\dfrac{dP}{P} \times 100 = -\gamma \times \left( \dfrac{dV}{V} \times 100 \right) = -\dfrac{5}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{2} = -\dfrac{15}{4}$.

The negative sign indicates a decrease in pressure. Thus, the percentage decrease in pressure is $\dfrac{15}{4}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{15}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The molar heat capacity in a process of a diatomic gas if it does a work of $\frac{Q}{4}$, when a heat of $Q$ is supplied to it is
questions.solution:
$d U=C_V d T=\left(\frac{5}{2} R\right) d T$ or $d T=\frac{2(d U)}{5 R}$
From first law of thermodynamics,
$d U=d Q-d W=Q-\frac{Q}{4}=\frac{3 Q}{4}$
Now, molar heat capacity,
$C=\frac{d Q}{d T}=\frac{Q}{\frac{2(d U)}{5 R}}=\frac{5 R Q}{2\left(\frac{3 Q}{4}\right)}=\frac{10}{3} R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thermally insulated rigid container contains an ideal gas heated by a filament of resistance $100 \Omega$ through a current of 1 A for 5 min , then change in internal energy is
questions.solution:
Volume of the ideal gas is constant, so $W=0$.
Using first law of thermodynamics,
$\begin{aligned} \\ \Delta Q & =\Delta U \Rightarrow \Delta U=i^2 R t \\ \\ & =1^2 \times 100 \times 5 \times 60 \\ \\ & =30 \times 10^3=30 \mathrm{~kJ} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thermodynamic system changes its state from A to C in two different paths ABC and AC. The internal energy of the system at state C is $20\text{ J}$ and at state A is $10\text{ J}$. Heat supplied to the system to go from A to C along path AC is
questions.solution:
$\Delta U = U_C - U_A = 20 - 10 = 10$ J (state function, path independent)

Work done along path AC (area of trapezium under P-V curve):

$W_{AC} = \dfrac{1}{2}(P_A + P_C)(V_C - V_A) = \dfrac{1}{2}(5+15)(9-3) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 6 = 60$ J

By first law: $Q_{AC} = \Delta U + W_{AC} = 10 + 60 = 70$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylinder of fixed capacity 44.81 contains hydrogen gas at STP. What is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of the gas in the cylinder by $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ? ($R=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
At STP, the volume of 1 mole of an ideal gas is $22.4 \text{ L}$.

Given the volume of the cylinder is $44.8 \text{ L}$, the number of moles $n$ of hydrogen gas is $n = \dfrac{44.8}{22.4} = 2 \text{ moles}$.

Hydrogen is a diatomic gas, so its molar heat capacity at constant volume $C_V$ is given by $C_V = \dfrac{f}{2}R$, where $f = 5$ is the degrees of freedom for a diatomic molecule.

$C_V = \dfrac{5}{2} \times 8.31 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1} = 20.775 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$.

The heat required $Q$ to raise the temperature by $\Delta T = 20^{\circ} \text{C}$ (which is equivalent to $20 \text{ K}$) at constant volume is $Q = n C_V \Delta T$.

$Q = 2 \times 20.775 \times 20 = 40 \times 20.775 = 831 \text{ J}$.

Answer: 831 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The latent heat of vaporisation of water is $2240 \mathrm{~J}$. If the work done in the process of vaporisation of $1 \mathrm{~g}$ is $168 \mathrm{~J}$, the increase in internal energy is
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the heat supplied $Q$ is equal to the sum of the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ and the work done $W$ by the system during the process of vaporisation.

$Q = \Delta U + W$

Given that the latent heat of vaporisation $L = 2240 \text{ J}$ for $1 \text{ g}$ of water, the heat supplied $Q$ is $2240 \text{ J}$.

The work done $W$ during the process is given as $168 \text{ J}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$2240 \text{ J} = \Delta U + 168 \text{ J}$

Solving for the change in internal energy $\Delta U$:

$\Delta U = 2240 \text{ J} - 168 \text{ J}$

$\Delta U = 2072 \text{ J}$

Answer: 2072 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas is taken through the cycle $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$, as shown in figure. What is the net work done by the gas?
questions.solution:
Net work done by the gas $=$ Area enclosed in $p-V$ curve, i.e. area of $\triangle A B C$.
$W_{\text {net }}=\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~J}=10^3 \mathrm{~J}=1000 \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas goes from state $A$ to state $B$ via three different processes as indicated in the $p-V$ diagram. If $Q_1, Q_2$ and $Q_3$ indicate the heat absorbed by the three processes and $\Delta U_1, \Delta U_2$ and $\Delta U_3$ indicate the change in internal energy along the three processes respectively, then
options: $Q_1 \gt Q_2 \gt Q_3$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$
$Q_3 \gt Q_2 \gt Q_1$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$
$Q_3 \gt Q_2 \gt Q_1$ and $\Delta U_1 \gt \Delta U_2 \gt \Delta U_3$
questions.solution:
For all processes 1,2 and 3
Change in internal energy, i.e.
$\begin{gathered}
\Delta U=U_B-U_A \\
\therefore \Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3 \Rightarrow Q=\Delta U+\Delta W
\end{gathered}$
Now, $\Delta W=$ work done by the gas, i.e. area under $p-V$ curve.
As, area $(1) \gt $ area $(2) \gt $ area $(3)\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \Delta W_1 \gt \Delta W_2 \gt \Delta W_3 \\
\therefore & Q_1 \gt Q_2 \gt Q_3
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $150 \mathrm{~J}$ of heat is added to a system and the work done by the system is $110 \mathrm{~J}$, then change in internal energy will be

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an adiabatic expansion of air, the volume is increased by $6.2 \%$. The percentage change in pressure is $(\gamma=1.4)$
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process, the relation between pressure $P$ and volume $V$ is given by $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

Taking the logarithmic differentiation of the equation $PV^{\gamma} = C$, we get $\ln P + \gamma \ln V = \ln C$.

Differentiating both sides, we obtain $\dfrac{dP}{P} + \gamma \dfrac{dV}{V} = 0$, which implies $\dfrac{dP}{P} = -\gamma \dfrac{dV}{V}$.

Given that the volume increases by $6.2 \%$, we have $\dfrac{dV}{V} = 0.062$.

Substituting the values $\gamma = 1.4$ and $\dfrac{dV}{V} = 0.062$ into the expression for the fractional change in pressure:

$\dfrac{dP}{P} = -1.4 \times 0.062 = -0.0868$.

The percentage change in pressure is $\dfrac{dP}{P} \times 100 = -0.0868 \times 100 = -8.68 \%$.

The magnitude of the percentage change in pressure is $8.68 \%$.

Answer: 8.68

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the ratio of specific heat of a gas at constant pressure to that at constant volume is $\gamma$, the change in internal energy of a mass of a gas when the volume changes from $\mathrm{V}$ to $3 \mathrm{~V}$ at constant pressure is
questions.solution:
The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ for an ideal gas is given by the formula $\Delta U = n C_{v} \Delta T$.

For an ideal gas, $C_{v} = \dfrac{R}{\gamma - 1}$. Thus, $\Delta U = n \left( \dfrac{R}{\gamma - 1} \right) \Delta T$.

Using the ideal gas law $PV = nRT$, at constant pressure $P$, we have $P \Delta V = nR \Delta T$.

Substituting $nR \Delta T = P \Delta V$ into the expression for internal energy, we get $\Delta U = \dfrac{P \Delta V}{\gamma - 1}$.

Given the volume changes from $V$ to $3V$, the change in volume is $\Delta V = 3V - V = 2V$.

Therefore, $\Delta U = \dfrac{P(2V)}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{2PV}{\gamma - 1}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2 P V}{(\gamma-1)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas is taken through the cycle $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$, as shown in figure. What is the net work done by the gas?
questions.solution:
Net work done = area enclosed in P-V diagram. Cycle $A \to B \to C \to A$ is clockwise \to work done is positive.

The enclosed area is a right-angled triangle.

Base $= V_C - V_A = (7 - 3) \times 10^{-3} = 4 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^3$

Height $= P_B - P_C = (6 - 2) \times 10^5 = 4 \times 10^5$ Pa

$W_{net} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 10^{-3} \times 4 \times 10^5 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 10^2 = 800$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $150 \mathrm{~J}$ of heat is added to a system and the work done by the system is $110 \mathrm{~J}$, then change in internal energy will be
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ is given by the equation:

$\Delta U = Q - W$

where $Q$ is the heat added to the system and $W$ is the work done by the system.

Given values are $Q = 150 \text{ J}$ and $W = 110 \text{ J}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$\Delta U = 150 \text{ J} - 110 \text{ J} = 40 \text{ J}$

Answer: 40 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas goes from state $A$ to state $B$ via three different processes as indicated in the $p$-$V$ diagram. If $Q_1, Q_2$ and $Q_3$ indicate the heat absorbed by the three processes and $\Delta U_1, \Delta U_2$ and $\Delta U_3$ indicate the change in internal energy along the three processes respectively, then
options: $Q_1 \gt  Q_2 \gt  Q_3$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$
$Q_3 \gt  Q_2 \gt  Q_1$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$
$Q_3 \gt  Q_2 \gt  Q_1$ and $\Delta U_1 \gt  \Delta U_2 \gt  \Delta U_3$
questions.solution:
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, which is a state function. Since all three processes start at state A and end at state B, the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ is the same for all three paths. Therefore, $\Delta U_1 = \Delta U_2 = \Delta U_3$.

According to the first law of thermodynamics, $Q = \Delta U + W$, where $W$ is the work done by the gas. The work done $W$ is equal to the area under the $p-V$ curve. From the given diagram, the area under path 1 is the largest, followed by path 2, and then path 3. Thus, $W_1 \gt W_2 \gt W_3$.

Since $\Delta U$ is constant for all paths, the heat absorbed $Q$ follows the same order as the work done $W$. Therefore, $Q_1 \gt Q_2 \gt Q_3$.

Answer: $Q_1 \gt Q_2 \gt Q_3$ and $\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2=\Delta U_3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a Carnot heat engine has a sink at a temperature of $27^\circ\text{C}$ and takes $100\text{ kcal}$ of heat from a source at a temperature of $627^\circ\text{C}$, the work done (in J) is:
questions.solution:
$T_2 = 27 + 273 = 300\,\text{K}$, $T_1 = 627 + 273 = 900\,\text{K}$

$\eta = 1 - \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 1 - \dfrac{300}{900} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

$Q_1 = 100\,\text{kcal} = 10^5 \times 4.2\,\text{J} = 4.2 \times 10^5\,\text{J}$

$W = \eta \times Q_1 = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 4.2 \times 10^5 = 2.8 \times 10^5 = 0.28 \times 10^6\,\text{J}$

Correct option: (1)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: From the following $p$-V diagram, an ideal gas undergoing a change of state from $A$ to $B$. Four different processes I, II, III and IV as shown in the figure may lead to same change of state.
options: Work done is minimum in case II
Change in internal energy is same in all the four cases
Change in internal energy is same in IV and III cases, but not in I and II
questions.solution:
The internal energy $U$ of an ideal gas is a state function, which depends only on the temperature $T$ of the gas. For an ideal gas, the internal energy is given by $U = \dfrac{f}{2} nRT$, where $f$ is the degrees of freedom.

Since the change of state is from $A$ to $B$ in all four processes, the initial state $(P_A, V_A, T_A)$ and the final state $(P_B, V_B, T_B)$ are the same for all paths.

The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ is given by $\Delta U = U_B - U_A = \dfrac{f}{2} nR(T_B - T_A)$.

Because $T_A$ and $T_B$ are fixed for all four processes, the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ must be the same for all four processes I, II, III, and IV.

Answer: Change in internal energy is same in all the four cases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is taken through the cycle $A \to B \to C \to A$, as shown in the figure (assume Volume $V$ is in $m^3$). If the net heat supplied to the gas in the cycle is 5 J, the work done by the gas in the process $C \to A$ is,
questions.solution:
For a complete cycle, $\Delta U_{net} = 0$, so by the first law: $W_{net} = Q_{net} = 5$ J

$W_{net} = W_{A \to B} + W_{B \to C} + W_{C \to A}$

Process $A \to B$: Constant pressure $p = 10$ N/m$^2$, volume increases from $V_A = 1$ m$^3$ to $V_B = 2$ m$^3$
$W_{A \to B} = p\Delta V = 10 \times (2-1) = 10$ J

Process $B \to C$: Constant volume ($\Delta V = 0$)
$W_{B \to C} = 0$ J

Substituting:
$5 = 10 + 0 + W_{C \to A}$
$W_{C \to A} = -5$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: There are two identical containers $C_1$ and $C_2$ containing to identical gases. Gas in $C_1$ is reduced to half of its original volume adiabatically, while the gas in container $C_2$ is also reduced to half of its initial volume isothermally. Find the ratio of final pressure in these containers. ( $\gamma$ be the adiabatic constant).
questions.solution:
Let the initial pressure and volume of the gas in both containers be $P_0$ and $V_0$ respectively.

For container $C_1$, the process is adiabatic. The relation between pressure and volume is $P V^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

Given the final volume $V_1 = \dfrac{V_0}{2}$, the final pressure $P_1$ is given by $P_0 V_0^{\gamma} = P_1 \left( \dfrac{V_0}{2} \right)^{\gamma}$.

$P_1 = P_0 \left( \dfrac{V_0}{V_0/2} \right)^{\gamma} = P_0 (2)^{\gamma}$.

For container $C_2$, the process is isothermal. The relation between pressure and volume is $P V = \text{constant}$.

Given the final volume $V_2 = \dfrac{V_0}{2}$, the final pressure $P_2$ is given by $P_0 V_0 = P_2 \left( \dfrac{V_0}{2} \right)$.

$P_2 = P_0 \left( \dfrac{V_0}{V_0/2} \right) = 2 P_0$.

The ratio of final pressures is $\dfrac{P_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{P_0 2^{\gamma}}{2 P_0} = \dfrac{2^{\gamma}}{2} = 2^{\gamma-1}$.

Thus, the ratio is $2^{\gamma-1} : 1$.

Answer: $2^{\gamma-1}: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an adiabatic process with the ratio of two specific heat, $\gamma=\dfrac{3}{2}$, pressure is increased by $\dfrac{2}{3} \%$, then decrease in the volume will be
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process, the relation between pressure $P$ and volume $V$ is given by $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$.

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides, we get $\ln P + \gamma \ln V = \text{constant}$.

Differentiating both sides, we obtain $\dfrac{dP}{P} + \gamma \dfrac{dV}{V} = 0$, which implies $\dfrac{dV}{V} = -\dfrac{1}{\gamma} \dfrac{dP}{P}$.

Given $\gamma = \dfrac{3}{2}$ and the percentage increase in pressure $\dfrac{dP}{P} = \dfrac{2}{3} \%$.

Substituting these values, the percentage change in volume is $\dfrac{dV}{V} = -\dfrac{1}{3/2} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \% = -\dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \% = -\dfrac{4}{9} \%$.

The negative sign indicates a decrease in volume. Therefore, the decrease in volume is $\dfrac{4}{9} \%$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{9} \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For an ideal gas, coefficient of volume expansion is given by
questions.solution:
The equation of state for an ideal gas is $PV = nRT$.

The coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma$ is defined as $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_{P}$.

From the ideal gas equation, $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P}$.

Differentiating $V$ with respect to $T$ at constant pressure $P$, we get $\left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_{P} = \dfrac{nR}{P}$.

Substituting this into the expression for $\gamma$, we have $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \left( \dfrac{nR}{P} \right)$.

Since $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P}$, we can write $\dfrac{nR}{P} = \dfrac{V}{T}$.

Therefore, $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{V} \left( \dfrac{V}{T} \right) = \dfrac{1}{T}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Carnot cycle of an engine is given below

Total work done by the gas in one cycle is
questions.solution:
The Carnot cycle has two isothermal and two adiabatic processes.

$P \to Q$: Isothermal expansion at $T_1$ ($T_1 = T_2$): $W_{PQ} = \mu RT_1 \ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$

$Q \to R$: Adiabatic expansion: $W_{QR} = \dfrac{\mu R(T_2 - T_3)}{\gamma - 1}$

$R \to S$: Isothermal compression at $T_3$ ($T_3 = T_4$): $W_{RS} = -\mu RT_3 \ln\dfrac{V_3}{V_4}$

$S \to P$: Adiabatic compression: $W_{SP} = \dfrac{\mu R(T_4 - T_1)}{\gamma - 1}$

Since $T_1 = T_2$ and $T_3 = T_4$, the adiabatic work terms cancel: $W_{QR} + W_{SP} = 0$

Total work: $W = \mu RT_1 \ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} - \mu RT_3 \ln\dfrac{V_3}{V_4}$

$= \mu RT_1 \log\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} - \mu RT_2 \log\dfrac{V_3}{V_4}$

Correct option: (2)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The dimensional formula for specific resistance is:
questions.solution:
Specific resistance $\rho$ is given by $\rho = \dfrac{R A}{L}$.

Resistance $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{W}{q I} = \dfrac{W}{I^2 t}$.

Dimensional formula of work $W = [M L^2 T^{-2}]$.

Dimensional formula of current $I = [A]$ and time $t = [T]$.

Dimensional formula of resistance $R = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[A^2 T]} = [M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-2}]$.

Dimensional formula of area $A = [L^2]$ and length $L = [L]$.

Dimensional formula of specific resistance $\rho = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-2}] [L^2]}{[L]} = [M L^3 T^{-3} A^{-2}]$.

Answer: $[M\,L^3\,T^{-3}\,A^{-2}]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the equation $X = G^{-1/2}\,h^{1/2}\,c^{5/2}$, where G- universal gravitation constant, h- Planck's constant and c- velocity of light, the dimensions of X are that of
questions.solution:
The dimensional formulas for the given physical quantities are:

$[G] = [M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}]$

$[h] = [M L^2 T^{-1}]$

$[c] = [L T^{-1}]$

Given the expression $X = G^{-1/2} h^{1/2} c^{5/2}$, substituting the dimensions:

$[X] = [M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}]^{-1/2} [M L^2 T^{-1}]^{1/2} [L T^{-1}]^{5/2}$

$[X] = [M^{1/2} L^{-3/2} T^1] [M^{1/2} L^1 T^{-1/2}] [L^{5/2} T^{-5/2}]$

Combining the powers of $M$, $L$, and $T$:

$[X] = [M^{\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}} L^{-\dfrac{3}{2} + 1 + \dfrac{5}{2}} T^{1 - \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{5}{2}}]$

$[X] = [M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]$

The dimensions $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$ correspond to Energy.

Answer: Energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The velocity of a body moving in a viscous medium is given by $v = \dfrac{A}{B+C}\left[1 - e^{\frac{-t}{B}}\right]$ where t is time; dimensions of A and C are
questions.solution:
The exponent of an exponential function must be dimensionless. Therefore, the dimension of $\dfrac{t}{B}$ is $[M^0L^0T^0]$.

$[B] = [t] = [M^0L^0T^1]$

By the principle of homogeneity, quantities added or subtracted must have the same dimensions. Since $B$ and $C$ are added in the denominator, $[C] = [B] = [M^0L^0T^1]$.

The term $\left[1 - e^{\dfrac{-t}{B}}\right]$ is dimensionless. Thus, the dimensions of velocity $v$ must equal the dimensions of $\dfrac{A}{B+C}$.

$[v] = \dfrac{[A]}{[B+C]}$

$[M^0L^1T^{-1}] = \dfrac{[A]}{[M^0L^0T^1]}$

$[A] = [M^0L^1T^{-1}] \times [M^0L^0T^1] = [M^0L^1T^0]$

The dimensions of $A$ and $C$ are $[M^0L^1T^0]$ and $[M^0L^0T^1]$ respectively.

Answer: $[M^0L^1T^0],\ [M^0L^0T^1]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the dimensional formula for electric flux?
questions.solution:
Electric flux $\phi_E$ is defined as the product of electric field $E$ and area $A$, given by $\phi_E = E \cdot A$.

The electric field $E$ is defined as force per unit charge, $E = \dfrac{F}{q}$. The dimensional formula for force $F$ is $[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]$ and for charge $q$ is $[A^1 T^1]$.

Thus, the dimensional formula for electric field $E$ is $\dfrac{[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]}{[A^1 T^1]} = [M^1 L^1 T^{-3} A^{-1}]$.

The dimensional formula for area $A$ is $[L^2]$.

Therefore, the dimensional formula for electric flux $\phi_E$ is $[M^1 L^1 T^{-3} A^{-1}] \times [L^2] = [M^1 L^3 T^{-3} A^{-1}]$.

Answer: $\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the expression $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{El}^2 \mathrm{~m}^{-5} \mathrm{G}^{-2}$ where $\mathrm{E}, 1, \mathrm{~m}$ and G represent Energy, Angular Momentum, Mass and Gravitational Constant, the dimensions of P are
questions.solution:
The dimensions of the given physical quantities are as follows:

Energy (E) = $[M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]$

Angular Momentum (l) = $[M^1 L^2 T^{-1}]$

Mass (m) = $[M^1]$

Gravitational Constant (G): From $F = G \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, we have $G = \dfrac{F r^2}{m^2} = \dfrac{[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}] [L^2]}{[M^2]} = [M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}]$

Now, substitute these dimensions into the expression $P = E l^2 m^{-5} G^{-2}$:

$P = [M^1 L^2 T^{-2}] \times ([M^1 L^2 T^{-1}])^2 \times ([M^1])^{-5} \times ([M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}])^{-2}$

$P = [M^1 L^2 T^{-2}] \times [M^2 L^4 T^{-2}] \times [M^{-5}] \times [M^2 L^{-6} T^4]$

Combine the powers of M, L, and T:

M: $1 + 2 - 5 + 2 = 0$

L: $2 + 4 + 0 - 6 = 0$

T: $-2 - 2 + 0 + 4 = 0$

Therefore, $P = [M^0 L^0 T^0]$.

Answer: $\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}^0\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two physical quantities having the same dimensional formula $\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$ are
questions.solution:
The dimensional formula for Stress is $\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}} = \dfrac{[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]}{[L^2]} = [M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

The dimensional formula for Pressure is $\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}} = \dfrac{[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]}{[L^2]} = [M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Since both Stress and Pressure have the same dimensional formula $[M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$, they are the correct pair.

Answer: Stress and Pressure

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $R$ and $L$ denote resistance and inductance of a material, then the dimension of $L R$ will be:
questions.solution:
The dimension of resistance $R$ is given by $V = IR$, so $[R] = [V][I]^{-1}$. Since $V = W/q$, $[V] = [M L^2 T^{-2}][A T]^{-1} = [M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-1}]$. Thus, $[R] = [M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-2}]$.

The dimension of inductance $L$ is given by $V = L(dI/dt)$, so $[L] = [V][T][I]^{-1} = [M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-1}][T][A]^{-1} = [M L^2 T^{-2} A^{-2}]$.

The dimension of the product $LR$ is $[L][R] = [M L^2 T^{-2} A^{-2}] \times [M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-2}] = [M^2 L^4 T^{-5} A^{-4}]$.

Answer: $M^2 L^4 T^{-5} A^{-4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If units of mass, length and gravitational constant are chosen to fundamental units, the dimensions of time would be
questions.solution:
The dimension of the gravitational constant $G$ is given by the formula $F = G \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, which implies $[G] = \dfrac{[F][r^2]}{[m^2]} = \dfrac{MLT^{-2} L^2}{M^2} = M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}$.

We express time $T$ in terms of mass $M$, length $L$, and gravitational constant $G$ as $T = M^a L^b G^c$.

Substituting the dimensions, we get $[T] = M^a L^b (M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2})^c = M^{a-c} L^{b+3c} T^{-2c}$.

Comparing the powers of $T$ on both sides: $-2c = 1 \Rightarrow c = -1/2$.

Comparing the powers of $M$ on both sides: $a - c = 0 \Rightarrow a = c = -1/2$.

Comparing the powers of $L$ on both sides: $b + 3c = 0 \Rightarrow b = -3c = -3(-1/2) = 3/2$.

Thus, the dimensions of time are $M^{-1/2} L^{3/2} G^{-1/2}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{M}^{-1 / 2} \mathrm{~L}^{3 / 2} \mathrm{G}^{-1 / 2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The dimension $[\mathrm{ML}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}]$ is the physical quantity of
questions.solution:
The given dimension is $[M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Pressure is defined as $\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}} = \dfrac{[M L T^{-2}]}{[L^2]} = [M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Energy density is defined as $\dfrac{\text{Energy}}{\text{Volume}} = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[L^3]} = [M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Since both Pressure and Energy density have the dimension $[M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$, we evaluate the options provided.

Option (1) Energy density has the dimension $[M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Option (2) Pressure \times Area is Force, which has dimension $[M L T^{-2}]$.

Option (3) Power \times Time is Energy, which has dimension $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$.

Option (4) $\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Pressure}}$ is Area, which has dimension $[L^2]$.

Therefore, Energy density is the correct physical quantity.

Answer: Energy density

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Joule second is the unit of
questions.solution:
The unit of energy is Joule (J) and the unit of time is second (s).

The unit Joule second (J s) corresponds to the product of energy and time.

From the relation $E = h \nu$, where $E$ is energy and $\nu$ is frequency, the unit of Planck constant $h$ is $\dfrac{J}{s^{-1}} = J s$.

Angular momentum $L$ is defined as $L = mvr$. The dimensional formula for angular momentum is $[M L^2 T^{-1}]$.

The dimensional formula for energy is $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$. Multiplying by time $T$, we get $[M L^2 T^{-2}] \times [T] = [M L^2 T^{-1}]$.

Since the dimensions of energy multiplied by time are equivalent to the dimensions of angular momentum, the unit Joule second represents angular momentum.

Answer: Angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Find the value of '$n$' in the given equation $P=\rho^n v^2$ where '$P$' is the pressure, '$\rho$' density and '$v$' velocity.
questions.solution:
The dimensional formula for pressure $P$ is $[M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

The dimensional formula for density $\rho$ is $[M L^{-3}]$.

The dimensional formula for velocity $v$ is $[L T^{-1}]$.

Substituting these into the equation $P = \rho^n v^2$, we get:

$[M L^{-1} T^{-2}] = [M L^{-3}]^n [L T^{-1}]^2$

$[M L^{-1} T^{-2}] = [M^n L^{-3n}] [L^2 T^{-2}]$

$[M L^{-1} T^{-2}] = [M^n L^{-3n+2} T^{-2}]$

Comparing the powers of $M$ on both sides, we get $n = 1$.

Checking the powers of $L$: $-1 = -3n + 2 \Rightarrow 3n = 3 \Rightarrow n = 1$.

Checking the powers of $T$: $-2 = -2$, which is consistent.

Answer: $\mathrm{n}=1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the given dimensional formula represents heat capacity
questions.solution:
Heat capacity $C$ is defined as the amount of heat energy $Q$ required to raise the temperature of a substance by an amount $\Delta T$.

The formula is $C = \dfrac{Q}{\Delta T}$.

The dimensional formula for heat energy $Q$ is the same as work or energy, which is $[ML^2T^{-2}]$.

The dimensional formula for temperature change $\Delta T$ is $[K]$.

Substituting these into the formula, we get $C = \dfrac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[K]} = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$.

Answer: $\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $C$ be the capacitance and $V$ be the electric potential, then the dimensional formula of $\mathrm{CV}^2$ is
questions.solution:
We know that energy, $E=\frac{1}{2} C V^2$
Dimensions of $C V^2=$ Dimensions of energy, $E=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2} \mathrm{~A}^0\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The time dependence of a physical quantity P is give by $\mathrm{P=P}_0 \exp \left(-\alpha t^2\right)$ where $\alpha$ is a constant and $t$ is time. The constant $\alpha$ will
options: Have dimensions equal to that of $\mathrm{Pt}^2$
questions.solution:
The given equation is $P = P_0 \exp(-\alpha t^2)$.

In any exponential function of the form $e^x$, the exponent $x$ must be dimensionless. Therefore, the term $\alpha t^2$ must be dimensionless.

$[\alpha t^2] = [M^0 L^0 T^0] = 1$.

Since $t$ represents time, its dimension is $[T]$. Thus, $[\alpha] [T^2] = 1$.

$[\alpha] = [T^{-2}]$.

This implies that the constant $\alpha$ has dimensions of $t^{-2}$.

Answer: Have dimensions of $t^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $R$ and $C$ denote resistance and capacitance of a material, then the dimension of $C R$ will be :
questions.solution:
The dimension of resistance $R$ is given by $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$. Since $V = \dfrac{W}{q}$, we have $R = \dfrac{W}{Iq} = \dfrac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[A][AT]} = [ML^2T^{-3}A^{-2}]$.

The dimension of capacitance $C$ is given by $C = \dfrac{q}{V}$. Since $V = \dfrac{W}{q}$, we have $C = \dfrac{q^2}{W} = \dfrac{[AT]^2}{[ML^2T^{-2}]} = [M^{-1}L^{-2}T^4A^2]$.

The product $CR$ has dimensions $[M^{-1}L^{-2}T^4A^2] \times [ML^2T^{-3}A^{-2}] = [M^{1-1}L^{2-2}T^{4-3}A^{2-2}] = [M^0L^0T^1]$.

Thus, the dimension of $CR$ is $[T]$, which corresponds to $[M^0L^0T]$.

Answer: $\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following quantity represents the dimensions of momentum?
questions.solution:
The dimension of momentum $p$ is given by $p = mv$, where $m$ is mass ($M$) and $v$ is velocity ($LT^{-1}$). Thus, the dimensions of momentum are $[MLT^{-1}]$.

Impulse $J$ is defined as the change in momentum, $J = \Delta p = F \Delta t$. The dimensions of force $F$ are $[MLT^{-2}]$ and time $\Delta t$ is $[T]$. Therefore, the dimensions of impulse are $[MLT^{-2}] \times [T] = [MLT^{-1}]$.

Pressure is force per unit area, $[MLT^{-2}] / [L^2] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$.

Viscosity (coefficient of viscosity) has dimensions $[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]$.

Power is work per unit time, $[ML^2T^{-2}] / [T] = [ML^2T^{-3}]$.

Comparing these, impulse has the same dimensions as momentum.

Answer: Impulse

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The physical quantity having the same dimensions as Planck's constant $h$ is
questions.solution:
Dimensional formula of Planck's constant $=\left[\mathrm{M}^{1} \mathrm{~L}^{2} \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]$
Similarly,
Boltzmann constant is given

K=\frac{\text { Energy }}{\text { Temperature }}

$\therefore$ The dimension of $K$ is

=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{[K]}=\left[M^{1} L^{2} T^{-2} K^{-1}\right]

Dimensional formula of force is $\left[\mathrm{M}^{\mathrm{l}} \mathrm{L}^{1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$.
Dimensional formula of linear momentum is $\left[M^{1} L^{1} T^{-1}\right]$.
Dimensional formula of angular momentum is $\left[\mathrm{M}^{1} \mathrm{~L}^{2} \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]$.
Hence, angular momentum and Planck's constant have same dimensional formula.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The dimensional formula for inductance is
questions.solution:
EMF induced in circular coil of self-inductance $L$ is given by $\varepsilon=-L \frac{d I}{d t}\mathrm{EMF}$ is equal to the potential difference dimensionally.
Hence,

\varepsilon=V

We know,

V=\frac{W}{q}

Thus, dimensional formula of potential difference is given as

\begin{aligned}
V &=\frac{\left[M^{1} L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{[A T]} \\
&=\left[M^{1} L^{2} T^{-3} A^{-1}\right]
\end{aligned}

The self-inductance is given by, $L=V \times \frac{d t}{d I}$
Dimensional formula of self-inductance is given by,

L=\left[\mathrm{M}^{1} \mathrm{~L}^{-2} \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}\right] \times \frac{[\mathrm{T}]}{[\mathrm{A}]}

Dimensional formula of self-inductance,

L=\left[\mathrm{M}^{1} \mathrm{~L}^{2} \mathrm{~T}^{-2} \mathrm{~A}^{-2}\right]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Dimensional formula for the universal gravitational constant $G$ is
questions.solution:
According to Newton's law of gravitation,

F=\frac{G m_{1} m_{2}}{r^{2}}

where, $F$ = gravitational force between two bodies of masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$,
$r=$ distance between the two masses
and $G=$ universal gravitational constant.
$\therefore \quad G=\frac{F r^{2}}{m_{1} m_{2}} .\therefore \quad[G]=\frac{[F]\left[r^{2}\right]}{\left[m_{1}\right]\left[m_{2}\right]}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right]\left[\mathrm{L}^{2}\right]}{[\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{M}]}=\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^{3} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Out of the following four dimensional quantities. which one qualifies to be called a dimensional constant?
options: Weight of a standard kilogram mass
questions.solution: The velocity of light in vacuum is $3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, which is a dimensional constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which one of the following is not a tunit of Young's modulus?
questions.solution:
Young's modulus, $Y=\frac{\text { Stress }}{\text { Strain }}$
Here, strain is a dimensionless quantity and stress is measured in SI unit of $\mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$, dyne $\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ or pascal.
So, the Young's modulus has the same unit as stress.
$\therefore \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ is not a unit of Young's modulus.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The square root of the product of inductance and capacitance has the dimension of
questions.solution:
We know that, in $L-C-R$ series resonant circuit, resonance frequency,
$\begin{aligned} f &=\frac{1}{2 \pi \sqrt{L C}} \\ \Rightarrow \sqrt{L C} &=\frac{1}{2 \pi f} \end{aligned}\Rightarrow \sqrt{L C}=\frac{1}{\omega} \quad[\omega=$ angular frequency $]\begin{aligned}
&\therefore \text { Dimension of } \sqrt{L C}=\frac{1}{\text { Dimension of } \omega} \\
&\Rightarrow \quad[\sqrt{L C}]=\frac{1}{[\omega]}=\frac{1}{\left[\mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]}=[\mathrm{T}]
\end{aligned}$
Hence, square root of the product of inductance $[L]$ and capacitance $[\mathrm{C}]$ has the dimension of time.

questions.q: Which two of the following quantities are dimensionally equivalent?
questions.solution:
We know that,
Force $=$ Mass \times  Acceleration
$\Rightarrow \quad F=m \times a\Rightarrow \quad[F]=[\mathrm{m}][\mathrm{a}]=[\mathrm{M}]\left[\mathrm{LT}^{-2}\right]=\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right]$
Pressure $(p)=\frac{\text { Force }(F)}{\operatorname{Area}(A)}\Rightarrow \quad[p]=\frac{[\mathrm{F}]}{[\mathrm{A}]}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{L}^{2}\right]}=\left[\mathrm{ML}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$
Young's modulus, $Y=\frac{\text { Stress }}{\text { Strain }}\Rightarrow \quad[Y]=\frac{[\text { Stress }]}{[\text { Strain }]}=\frac{[F / A]}{[\text { Strain }]}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{ML}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{M}^{0} \mathrm{~L}^{0} \mathrm{~T}^{0}\right]}=\left[\mathrm{ML}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$
Energy $=$ Work done $=$ Force \times  Displacement
$\Rightarrow[$ Energy $]=[$ Force $] \times[$ Displacement $]=\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right][\mathrm{L}]=\left[\mathrm{ML}^{2} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$
Hence, we see that dimensions of pressure and Young's modulus is same.

Impulse $=$ Force \times  Time  =\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right][\mathrm{T}]=\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-1}\right]  Surface tension $=\frac{\text { Force }}{\text { Length }}$ =\frac{\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right]}{[\mathrm{L}]}=\left[\mathrm{ML}^{0} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]

&=\frac{\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right] \times[\mathrm{L}]}{\left[\mathrm{L}^{2}\right] \times[\mathrm{L}]}=\left[\mathrm{ML}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]
